subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
unit_title: Health Care and Development of Nursing Services in India
question: Explain the planning and development of nursing services and nursing education at the global and national levels.
tags: Global Strategic Directions for Nursing and Midwifery 2021-2025
International Year of the Nurse and Midwife 2020
National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act 2023
answer_html:
Introduction Nurses and midwives form the largest group of health workers and deliver most of the care in hospitals and communities. Planning the number, education, deployment and leadership of nurses is therefore central to achieving universal health coverage (UHC) and the health-related Sustainable Development Goals.

A. Global level

  1. World Health Organization (WHO)
    • The Global Strategic Directions for Nursing and Midwifery (SDNM) 2021–2025, adopted by the World Health Assembly, set out four directions – education, jobs, leadership and service delivery – with policy priorities that countries adapt to their needs.
    • The State of the World's Nursing 2025 report (WHO, ICN and partners) showed that the global nursing workforce grew from 27.9 million (2018) to 29.8 million (2023); the shortage fell from 6.2 million to 5.8 million and is projected to fall to about 4.1 million by 2030, but 78% of nurses work in countries with only 49% of the world's population, and 85% of nurses are women.
  2. International Council of Nurses (ICN) – sets the Code of Ethics for Nurses, advocates for nurses' pay, safety and leadership, and leads International Nurses Day (12 May).
  3. Global campaigns – the Nursing Now campaign (2018–2020) and the International Year of the Nurse and the Midwife (2020), marking Florence Nightingale's bicentenary, raised the profile of nursing.
  4. Migration – international recruitment of nurses is guided by the WHO Global Code of Practice, which discourages active recruitment from countries with critical shortages.

B. National level (India)

  1. Regulation
    • The Indian Nursing Council Act, 1947 set up the INC to maintain uniform standards of nursing education; State Nursing Councils register nurses and midwives.
    • The National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act, 2023 provides for a Commission to replace the INC; until it is constituted, the INC continues to function.
    • The Nurses Registration and Tracking System (NRTS) gives every nurse a unique identity and links renewal of registration with continuing nursing education.
  2. Workforce – India had 46.02 lakh registered nursing personnel on 31 December 2025 (about 34.9 lakh RN & RM and 10.6 lakh ANMs, the rest LHVs), a nurse–population ratio of about 2.6 per 1,000 – still below the WHO benchmark of 3 per 1,000 – with wide differences between States.
  3. Education
    • More than 5,200 nursing institutions produce nearly 3.9 lakh nursing personnel every year.
    • The revised competency-based B.Sc. Nursing curriculum (2021) with a semester system; post-graduate, M.Phil. and Ph.D. programmes; nurse practitioner programmes in critical care and midwifery.
    • New nursing colleges co-located with medical colleges (157 approved in 2023), increase in permissible seats and raising of the retirement age of nursing faculty to address faculty shortage.
  4. Services
    • Nurses are designated Nursing Officers in Central Government hospitals; posts of Nursing Superintendent and Chief Nursing Officer lead the nursing departments.
    • Community health officers (mostly nurses with a bridge course) run Ayushman Arogya Mandirs; Nurse Practitioners in Midwifery strengthen midwifery-led care in labour rooms.
    • Nurses implement every national health programme – immunisation, maternal and child health, NCDs, TB, mental health.

Conclusion Globally, WHO's SDNM 2021–2025 and the State of the World's Nursing reports guide investment in nursing education, jobs, leadership and services, while in India regulation by the INC (and in future the NNMC), rapid expansion of education, new advanced roles and community health officers are shaping nursing services, although shortages and maldistribution remain.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
unit_title: Health Care and Development of Nursing Services in India
question: Explain the recent trends and issues in nursing service and management in India.
answer_html:
A. Recent trends

  1. Advanced and expanded roles – nurse practitioners in critical care and midwifery, community health officers at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, nurse educators and nurse counsellors, nurse-led clinics (diabetes, wound care, lactation, stoma).
  2. Specialisation – oncology, critical care, emergency, cardiothoracic, neonatal, psychiatric, infection control and dialysis nursing.
  3. Evidence-based practice and standardised protocols, care bundles and clinical pathways.
  4. Digital health – electronic health records, the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, telenursing and Tele-MANAS, use of mobile applications and decision-support tools.
  5. Quality and accreditation – NABH accreditation and its nursing excellence certification, National Quality Assurance Standards, Kayakalp and LaQshya in public hospitals; patient safety culture and incident reporting.
  6. Participative management – shared governance, nursing councils within hospitals, quality circles and magnet-style recognition of nursing.
  7. Shift of care to the community and home – home-based care, palliative care, geriatric care and day-care services.
  8. Changing workforce – more male nurses, more graduate and post-graduate nurses, and greater international mobility.

B. Issues

  1. Shortage and maldistribution – the nurse–population ratio is below the WHO benchmark, with concentration in southern States and in cities, and shortages in rural and tribal areas.
  2. Migration of experienced nurses to other countries, causing loss of skilled staff.
  3. Heavy workload and inadequate staffing – poor nurse–patient ratios, many non-nursing duties, long or double shifts.
  4. Low salaries and job insecurity – especially in small private hospitals and on contract posts; an expert committee set up on the Supreme Court's direction in 2016 recommended minimum salaries linked to hospital size.
  5. Workplace violence and safety – assault by patients' relatives, unsafe night duties, needle-stick injuries and exposure to infections.
  6. Stress and burnout, leading to absenteeism and turnover.
  7. Limited autonomy and recognition – little say in policy-making; few nurses in top health leadership posts.
  8. Quality of education – rapid growth of private institutions, shortage of qualified faculty and inadequate clinical facilities in some colleges.
  9. Regulatory transition – delay in constituting the National Nursing and Midwifery Commission.

Role of nurse managers – advocate for safe staffing and fair pay, ensure safety at work, support professional development and research, encourage participation in decision-making and prepare nurses for leadership.

Conclusion Nursing in India is moving towards advanced practice, specialisation, evidence-based and digital care, quality accreditation and community-based services, but it still faces shortage, migration, heavy workload, poor pay in some sectors, workplace violence and limited autonomy, which nurse leaders must address.

question: What are the Global Strategic Directions for Nursing and Midwifery 2021–2025?
answer_html:
• The Global Strategic Directions for Nursing and Midwifery (SDNM) 2021–2025 were adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2021 to help countries ensure that nurses and midwives contribute fully to universal health coverage and other health goals.
  • They set four strategic directions, each with policy priorities:
    1. Education – educating enough nurses and midwives with competencies to meet population health needs.
    2. Jobs – creating jobs, managing migration, and recruiting and retaining nurses where they are most needed.
    3. Leadership – increasing the number of nurses and midwives in health leadership and policy positions.
    4. Service delivery – ensuring that nurses and midwives work to their full scope in safe, supportive environments.

question: (a) Define management and explain its features and importance. (4 marks) (b) Explain the principles of management given by Henri Fayol, with their application in nursing. (6 marks) (c) Explain the role of the nurse as a manager. (5 marks)

answer_html:
(a) Definition, features and importance of management (4 marks)

Definitions

  • Management is "the process of designing and maintaining an environment in which individuals, working together in groups, efficiently accomplish selected aims" (Koontz and Weihrich).
  • Henri Fayol: "To manage is to forecast and plan, to organise, to command, to coordinate and to control."
  • In nursing, nursing management is the process of planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling the work of nursing personnel and the use of resources so that safe, high-quality and cost-effective nursing care is provided to patients and communities.

Features of management

  1. Goal-oriented – it exists to achieve the objectives of the organisation, such as quality patient care.
  2. Universal – needed in every organisation – a hospital, a ward, a nursing college or a PHC – and at every level.
  3. A continuous process of planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling.
  4. Getting things done through others – the manager works through people.
  5. Integrates resources – the "6 Ms": men (people), money, materials, machines, methods and minutes (time).
  6. Group activity that requires coordination of individual efforts.
  7. Both an art and a science – it has principles that can be learned, and it needs skill, judgement and creativity in application.
  8. Dynamic – it adapts to changes in technology, policies and patient needs.
  9. A distinct profession with its own body of knowledge and ethics.
  10. Intangible – it is seen in its results, such as satisfied patients and an efficient ward.

Importance

  • Achievement of the goals of the organisation – safe, effective and patient-centred care.
  • Optimum use of resources – staff, money, equipment, supplies and time; reduction of wastage.
  • Coordination between nursing, medical and support departments.
  • Quality and safety of care through standards and monitoring.
  • Staff development and satisfaction – fair assignment, motivation, growth.
  • Adaptation to change – new technology, policies and accreditation requirements.
  • Accountability to patients, the institution and society.

(b) Fayol's principles of management and their application in nursing (6 marks) Henri Fayol (1916), the "father of modern management", described 14 principles:

  1. Division of work – work is divided according to skill so that people specialise. Nursing: staff are assigned to ICU, OT, wards and OPD according to their training; in team nursing, tasks are divided according to competence.
  2. Authority and responsibility – authority (the right to give orders) must match responsibility. Nursing: a ward in-charge responsible for the ward must have authority to assign duties and requisition supplies.
  3. Discipline – obedience to rules and agreements, maintained by good supervision, clear rules and fair penalties. Nursing: punctuality, uniform, following procedures and policies.
  4. Unity of command – each employee should receive orders from one superior only, to avoid confusion. Nursing: a staff nurse takes instructions about nursing work from her ward in-charge.
  5. Unity of direction – one plan and one head for a group of activities with the same objective. Nursing: all infection-control activities follow one plan under the infection control committee and nurse.
  6. Subordination of individual interest to the general interest – the interests of the organisation and patients come before personal interests. Nursing: duty rosters ensure patient care is covered before personal requests.
  7. Remuneration – fair pay and benefits that satisfy both staff and the organisation. Nursing: fair salary, night-duty and risk allowances, recognition.
  8. Centralisation – the degree to which decision-making is concentrated at the top must suit the situation. Nursing: policies are decided centrally by the nursing department, while day-to-day patient assignment is decentralised to wards.
  9. Scalar chain – a clear line of authority from top to bottom (the chain of command); communication normally follows it, but "Fayol's gang plank" allows direct communication between equals in emergencies. Nursing: Chief Nursing Officer → Nursing Superintendent → Deputy and Assistant Nursing Superintendents → Ward in-charge → Nursing officers.
  10. Order – "a place for everything and everything in its place", and the right person in the right job. Nursing: an organised ward store, crash cart and records; correct placement of staff.
  11. Equity – kindness and justice towards all employees. Nursing: fair distribution of night duties and holidays, no favouritism.
  12. Stability of tenure of personnel – frequent transfers and high turnover reduce efficiency. Nursing: nurses in specialised units (ICU, NICU, dialysis) are not rotated too often.
  13. Initiative – staff should be allowed to suggest and carry out plans. Nursing: encouraging nurses to propose improvements in procedures or patient education.
  14. Esprit de corps – "union is strength"; harmony and team spirit. Nursing: team meetings, recognition, celebrating achievements such as Nurses' Day.

(c) Role of the nurse as a manager (5 marks) Every nurse is a manager – of her patients' care, of her time and of the people and resources she works with. The ward in-charge (nursing officer in-charge) is the first-line manager.

Managerial functions in the ward

  1. Planning – plan patient care, ward activities, staff requirements, supplies, in-service education and improvement projects; set objectives for the ward.
  2. Organising – organise the ward physically and functionally; assign patients and duties (team or primary nursing); delegate tasks; coordinate with other departments.
  3. Staffing – prepare duty rosters, ensure skill mix in each shift, orient new staff and students, request additional staff when needed.
  4. Directing – give clear instructions, supervise and guide staff, motivate, resolve conflicts, communicate through handover, rounds and meetings.
  5. Controlling – maintain standards of care, check records, conduct audits, monitor infection control and patient safety, evaluate staff performance and patient satisfaction.

Mintzberg's managerial roles applied to the nurse manager

  • Interpersonal roles – figurehead (representing the ward on official occasions), leader (guiding and motivating staff), liaison (linking with doctors, pharmacy, laboratory, maintenance and families).
  • Informational roles – monitor (collecting information on patients, staff and supplies), disseminator (sharing policies and changes with staff), spokesperson (reporting to higher authorities and communicating with families).
  • Decisional roles – entrepreneur (introducing improvements), disturbance handler (managing emergencies, complaints and conflicts), resource allocator (assigning staff, beds, equipment and supplies), negotiator (with other departments and staff).

Other responsibilities

  • Patient advocate – protecting patients' rights, dignity and safety.
  • Material manager – indenting, stock keeping and care of equipment.
  • Teacher – clinical teaching of students and in-service education of staff.
  • Quality and safety officer – incident reporting, audits, infection control and accreditation requirements.
  • Record keeper – ward census, registers and reports.
  • Change agent and researcher – introducing evidence-based practices.

Nursing importance Good management in the ward means enough skilled staff on every shift, equipment that works, supplies that do not run out, clear communication and safe, timely care. Nurses who understand management principles can turn limited resources into high-quality care and can grow into senior leadership roles.

Conclusion Management is the goal-oriented process of planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling resources through people. Fayol's fourteen principles – such as division of work, unity of command, scalar chain, equity and esprit de corps – apply directly to the organisation of nursing services. As a manager, the nurse plans, organises, staffs, directs and controls ward activities and fulfils interpersonal, informational and decisional roles to ensure safe, efficient and patient-centred care.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain the theories (schools) of management and their relevance to nursing.
answer_html:
1. Classical theories

  • Scientific management – Frederick W. Taylor (1911)
    • Work should be studied scientifically (time and motion studies) to find the "one best way" of doing a task; workers should be selected and trained scientifically; incentive pay for higher output; division of planning (managers) and doing (workers).
    • Nursing: standardised procedures, work-study to reduce walking time and wastage, task lists, equipment trays arranged for efficiency.
    • Limitation: treats workers like machines and ignores human needs.
  • Administrative (management process) theory – Henri Fayol (1916)
    • Focuses on the whole organisation; describes the functions of management and the 14 principles (unity of command, scalar chain and others).
    • Nursing: the organisational structure of the nursing department and the management process used by nurse managers.
  • Bureaucratic theory – Max Weber
    • An ideal organisation has a clear hierarchy of authority, written rules and procedures, division of labour, impersonal relationships, selection and promotion on merit, and careful records.
    • Nursing: government hospitals with fixed hierarchy, service rules and written policies.
    • Limitation: rigidity, "red tape" and slow decisions.

2. Neo-classical (human relations and behavioural) theories

  • Human relations theory – Elton Mayo (Hawthorne studies, 1924–1932)
    • Productivity is influenced more by social and psychological factors – attention, recognition, group norms and morale – than by physical conditions alone (the Hawthorne effect).
    • Nursing: recognising staff, good interpersonal relationships, participation and team spirit improve performance.
  • Behavioural science theories – Maslow's hierarchy of needs, McGregor's Theory X and Y, Herzberg's two-factor theory – emphasise motivation, leadership and job satisfaction.

3. Modern theories

  • Systems theory (Ludwig von Bertalanffy)
    • An organisation is an open system with inputs (staff, patients, money, supplies, information), throughput (processes of care and management), outputs (recovered patients, satisfied clients, trained students) and feedback, interacting with its environment; a change in one part affects the others.
    • Nursing: the ward is a sub-system of the hospital; a shortage in pharmacy affects nursing care.
  • Contingency (situational) theory – there is no single best way to manage; the right approach depends on the situation – the size of the organisation, technology, environment and people.
    • Nursing: an emergency demands firm, directive management, while a stable, experienced team benefits from participative management.
  • Other modern approaches – management by objectives (Peter Drucker), total quality management (Deming) and evidence-based management.

Conclusion Classical theories gave nursing management its structure, rules and efficiency; human relations theories emphasised people, morale and participation; and systems and contingency theories show that nursing services are interdependent parts of a larger system that must be managed according to the situation. A modern nurse manager combines all these insights.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Differentiate between management and administration, and explain the levels of management in the nursing service.
answer_html:
A. Management and administration

  • Administration is the policy-making, goal-setting function concerned with determining objectives, major policies and allocation of resources – the "thinking" function at the top.
  • Management is the executive function of putting those policies into action through planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling – the "doing" function.
  • In practice the terms overlap, and in hospitals both are performed at different levels.
Basis Administration Management
Nature Policy-making, determinative Policy-executing, executive
Level Top level Middle and lower levels
Main functions Planning goals, policies, budget Organising, directing, controlling
Concern What to do How to do
Example in nursing Chief Nursing Officer framing nursing policies Ward in-charge implementing them

B. Levels of management in the nursing service

  1. Top-level management
    • Chief Nursing Officer / Nursing Superintendent (in large hospitals, a Director of Nursing).
    • Functions – formulate the philosophy, objectives and policies of the nursing department; long-term (strategic) planning; preparation of the nursing budget; staffing policies and recruitment; representing nursing in hospital committees and at higher levels; overall control of quality.
  2. Middle-level management
    • Deputy Nursing Superintendents and Assistant Nursing Superintendents (supervisors) in charge of groups of wards or departments.
    • Functions – interpret and implement policies; coordinate units; supervise ward in-charges; prepare departmental rosters and plans; in-service education; handle problems and report to top management.
  3. First-line (lower-level) management
    • Ward in-charge / senior nursing officer (ward sister) and team leaders.
    • Functions – day-to-day management of the ward – patient assignment, duty roster, supervision of nursing officers and students, care of equipment and supplies, ward records, maintaining standards and communicating with patients and families.

Managerial skills needed at each level (Katz)

  • Technical skills (clinical and procedural knowledge) – most needed at the first-line level.
  • Human skills (communication, motivation, teamwork) – needed equally at all levels.
  • Conceptual skills (seeing the organisation as a whole, planning and policy-making) – most needed at the top level.

Conclusion Administration decides policies and goals, while management carries them out. In the nursing service, top-level managers set policies and plans, middle-level managers coordinate and supervise groups of units, and first-line managers run the wards day to day, each requiring a different balance of technical, human and conceptual skills.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain the functions of management (the management process), with examples from the nursing service.
answer_html:
Introduction The functions of management form a continuous, interrelated cycle. Luther Gulick (1937) summarised them as POSDCORB – Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Coordinating, Reporting and Budgeting. They are commonly grouped into five main functions:

1. Planning – deciding in advance what to do, how, when and by whom; setting objectives, policies, procedures and programmes.

  • Example: the nursing department plans to reduce hospital-acquired pressure injuries by half in one year, with a schedule of training, risk assessment and equipment purchase.

2. Organising – arranging people, tasks and resources into a structure with defined roles, authority and relationships; delegation and coordination.

  • Example: dividing a 40-bed ward into two teams, each with a team leader, and assigning nurses to patients.

3. Staffing – recruiting, selecting, placing, training and retaining the right number and type of personnel.

  • Example: calculating staff needs for a new dialysis unit, recruiting trained nurses and arranging their orientation.

4. Directing – guiding, supervising, motivating and communicating with staff so that plans are carried out; includes leadership.

  • Example: the ward in-charge conducts handover, supervises procedures, gives feedback and recognises good work.

5. Controlling – setting standards, measuring performance, comparing it with standards and taking corrective action.

  • Example: monthly audit of medication administration records, analysis of errors and retraining of staff.

Other functions

  • Coordinating – linking the work of different units and professionals (nursing, medical, pharmacy, laboratory, dietary, housekeeping) so that they work in harmony.
  • Reporting – keeping superiors and staff informed through records, reports, meetings and inspections.
  • Budgeting – fiscal planning, accounting and control of expenditure, such as preparing the annual budget for nursing equipment.

Interrelationship – the functions are not separate steps; controlling provides feedback for new planning, and directing and coordinating go on throughout.

Importance of the management process for nurse managers

  • It gives a systematic framework for running a ward or department instead of managing from crisis to crisis.
  • It ensures that objectives, people and resources are linked – plans are converted into duties, staff are prepared for them, work is guided and results are checked.
  • It promotes accountability, because standards are set in advance and performance is measured against them.
  • It helps in continuous improvement, as the findings of controlling feed back into the next cycle of planning.
  • The same process is used by managers at all levels; only the scope differs – the Chief Nursing Officer plans for the whole hospital, the ward in-charge plans for one ward and one shift.

Conclusion The management process – planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling, supported by coordinating, reporting and budgeting – is used by nurse managers at every level to turn objectives into safe, efficient and high-quality patient care.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is POSDCORB?
answer_html:
POSDCORB is an acronym given by Luther Gulick (1937), with Lyndall Urwick, for the seven functions of management (administration):

  • P – Planning; O – Organising; S – Staffing; D – Directing; CO – Coordinating; R – Reporting; B – Budgeting.

  • It describes the work of the chief executive of any organisation and is widely used to explain the duties of nursing administrators, from the Chief Nursing Officer to the ward in-charge.

  • In nursing, for example, the Nursing Superintendent plans services, organises the department, staffs the wards, directs supervisors, coordinates with other departments, reports to the Medical Superintendent and budgets for nursing needs.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is the Hawthorne effect?
answer_html:
• The Hawthorne effect is the improvement in people's performance or behaviour because they know they are being observed or are receiving special attention, rather than because of the change being tested.
  • It was identified in the Hawthorne studies (1924–1932) at the Western Electric Company, USA, by Elton Mayo and colleagues, where workers' productivity rose whether lighting was increased or decreased.
  • Significance – it showed the importance of human and social factors (attention, recognition, group morale) in work, and it is a source of bias in research and audits, where staff may perform better only while being watched.

question: (a) Define planning and state its characteristics and importance. (4 marks) (b) Explain the principles and types of planning. (5 marks) (c) Describe the steps of planning, with an example from the nursing service. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Steps of planning
labels: awareness of the problem or opportunity (situation analysis

SWOT) → setting SMART objectives → developing planning premises → identifying alternatives → evaluating alternatives → selecting the best course → formulating supporting plans → budgeting → implementing → evaluating and revising (feedback loop)

answer_html:
(a) Definition, characteristics and importance of planning (4 marks)

Definitions

  • "Planning is deciding in advance what to do, how to do it, when to do it and who is to do it. Planning bridges the gap from where we are to where we want to go." – Koontz and O'Donnell
  • In nursing, planning is the process of setting objectives for the nursing service and deciding the policies, programmes, resources and schedules needed to provide safe and effective care.

Characteristics

  1. Primary function of management – it comes first; organising, staffing, directing and controlling follow from it.
  2. Goal-oriented – every plan aims at specific objectives.
  3. Future-oriented – it involves forecasting patient load, staff needs and changes in technology.
  4. Pervasive – done at all levels, from the Chief Nursing Officer (long-term plans) to the ward in-charge (daily and shift plans).
  5. Continuous and dynamic – plans are revised as conditions change.
  6. An intellectual process – it requires thinking, judgement and creativity.
  7. Involves choice – selecting the best among alternative courses of action.
  8. Flexible – allows adjustment to unexpected events.
  9. Basis of control – plans provide the standards against which performance is measured ("planning and controlling are inseparable").

Importance

  • Gives direction and unity of purpose to all nursing staff.
  • Reduces uncertainty and risk by anticipating problems such as staff shortage or epidemics.
  • Ensures economical use of resources – staff, money, equipment, time.
  • Facilitates coordination between units and departments.
  • Provides standards for control and evaluation.
  • Encourages innovation and improvement of care.
  • Prepares the organisation for emergencies and disasters.
  • Improves decision-making and motivates staff by involving them in setting goals.

(b) Principles and types of planning (5 marks)

Principles of planning

  1. Principle of contribution to objectives – every plan must help achieve the objectives of the organisation.
  2. Principle of primacy – planning precedes all other managerial functions.
  3. Principle of pervasiveness – every manager plans, within his or her own area.
  4. Principle of efficiency – a plan should achieve objectives at the lowest cost in money, effort and time.
  5. Principle of planning premises – plans must be based on clear, agreed assumptions about the future (patient census, budget, staff availability).
  6. Principle of flexibility – plans should allow for change without high cost.
  7. Principle of commitment – plans should cover a period long enough to fulfil the commitments they involve (for example, training staff for a new unit).
  8. Principle of the limiting factor – identify and plan around the factor that most restricts achievement (such as shortage of trained ICU nurses).
  9. Principle of navigational change – plans are reviewed periodically and redirected, like a ship's course.
  10. Principle of participation – those who will carry out the plan should take part in making it, which improves acceptance.
  11. Principle of timing – plans must be made and implemented at the right time.

Types of planning

  1. According to time
    • Long-term plans (three to five years or more) – for example, starting a cardiac centre or upgrading the school of nursing to a college.
    • Medium-term plans (one to three years).
    • Short-term plans (up to one year) – annual budget, monthly in-service education programme, weekly duty roster.
  2. According to the level of management
    • Strategic planning – by top management; long-term, concerned with the vision, mission and major goals of the organisation.
    • Tactical planning – by middle management; converts strategic plans into specific programmes for departments.
    • Operational planning – by first-line managers; day-to-day plans such as patient assignment, shift plans and indents.
  3. According to use
    • Standing plans – used repeatedly: objectives, policies, procedures, methods and rules (such as a visitors' policy or the procedure for blood transfusion).
    • Single-use plans – made for a particular purpose and discarded when it is achieved: programmes, projects, budgets and schedules (such as a plan for a vaccination campaign or a ward renovation).
  4. Functional planning – plans for a particular function: nursing service, finance, human resources, materials.
  5. Contingency planning – alternative plans for emergencies such as fire, disasters, epidemics or power failure.
  6. Formal and informal planning – written, systematic plans versus unwritten plans of small units.

(c) Steps of planning, with an example (6 marks)

Example used – the ward in-charge of a 30-bed medical ward finds that the catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) rate has risen over the last three months and plans to reduce it.

  1. Being aware of the problem or opportunity (situation analysis)
    • Collect data – CAUTI rate per 1,000 catheter-days, number of catheterised patients, duration of catheterisation, practices of staff.
    • Analyse strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (SWOT) – for example, motivated staff (strength), lack of a catheter removal protocol (weakness), support from the infection control committee (opportunity), heavy workload (threat).
  2. Establishing objectives
    • Objectives must be SMART – Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound: "To reduce the CAUTI rate in the medical ward by 50% within six months."
  3. Developing planning premises – assumptions on which the plan rests: hospital administration will support the plan, closed drainage systems will be supplied, staff numbers will remain stable.
  4. Identifying alternative courses of action
    • Alternative 1 – only buy better catheters and bags.
    • Alternative 2 – staff education alone.
    • Alternative 3 – a CAUTI prevention bundle: indications checklist, aseptic insertion, closed drainage, daily review of need and a nurse-driven protocol for early removal, with education and audit.
  5. Evaluating the alternatives – compare cost, feasibility, acceptability to staff, time required and expected effectiveness; evidence shows that bundles combined with education and audit are most effective.
  6. Selecting the best course of action – alternative 3 is chosen.
  7. Formulating derivative (supporting) plans
    • Training schedule for all nurses and doctors of the ward.
    • Checklists for insertion and daily maintenance; a removal protocol approved by the medical team.
    • Indent for closed drainage systems, catheter fixation devices and hand-rub.
    • Assignment of a "CAUTI champion" nurse on each shift.
  8. Budgeting (numbering the plan) – estimate the cost of training material, supplies and staff time and obtain approval.
  9. Implementing the plan – communicate the plan to all staff, start training, put checklists into use, display progress charts.
  10. Evaluating and revising (follow-up)
    • Monitor the CAUTI rate and catheter-days every month, audit compliance with the bundle and give feedback to staff.
    • If the target is not met, identify causes and revise the plan; if it is met, standardise the practice and extend it to other wards.

Barriers to effective planning – lack of reliable data, resistance to change, inadequate resources, unrealistic objectives, lack of participation and poor follow-up; these are overcome through participation, realistic goals and regular review.

Nursing importance Planning turns good intentions into organised action. A nurse manager who plans systematically can anticipate needs, use scarce staff and supplies wisely, prevent crises and show measurable improvement in patient outcomes.

Conclusion Planning is the primary, goal-oriented and continuous function of deciding in advance what is to be done. Guided by principles such as contribution to objectives, planning premises, flexibility and the limiting factor, nurse managers prepare strategic, tactical and operational plans and standing and single-use plans. The planning process – situation analysis, SMART objectives, premises, alternatives, selection, supporting plans, budgeting, implementation and evaluation – can be applied to any problem in the nursing service.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain the vision, mission, philosophy and objectives of the nursing service department, with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction Every nursing service department needs clear statements of where it wants to go (vision), why it exists (mission), what it believes (philosophy) and what it will achieve (objectives). These statements guide policies, plans, staff behaviour and evaluation.

1. Vision

  • A brief, inspiring statement of the desired future of the nursing service – what it aspires to become.
  • Example: "To be recognised as a centre of excellence in compassionate, safe and evidence-based nursing care."

2. Mission

  • A statement of the purpose of the nursing service – what it does, for whom and how – consistent with the mission of the hospital.
  • Example: "The nursing department provides holistic, patient-centred care to all patients regardless of their background, through competent and caring nurses, continuous learning and teamwork with other health professionals."

3. Philosophy

  • A written statement of the beliefs and values of the nursing staff about people, health, nursing, the environment, education and staff, which guides their practice.
  • Example statements – "We believe that:
    • every patient is a unique individual with physical, psychological, social and spiritual needs and has the right to dignity, privacy and participation in decisions about care;
    • nursing is a profession based on scientific knowledge, skill and ethical principles;
    • safe, quality care requires adequate, competent and motivated staff;
    • continuing education and research are essential for professional growth;
    • patients, families and the community are partners in care."

4. Objectives

  • Specific statements of the results to be achieved, derived from the mission and philosophy; they should be SMART and are reviewed every year.
  • Examples:
    • To maintain a nurse–patient ratio as per approved norms in every unit.
    • To reduce patient falls by 30% in one year.
    • To provide at least 30 hours of in-service education to every nurse each year.
    • To achieve a patient satisfaction score of at least 90% with nursing care.

Developing and using the statements

  • Prepared by a committee of nurses from all levels, in line with the hospital's vision and mission, and approved by the nursing administration.
  • Displayed and communicated – in wards, orientation programmes and the nursing manual – so that every nurse knows them.
  • Reviewed periodically (every two to three years for philosophy and mission; every year for objectives).
  • Uses – guide policy-making, planning, staff selection and orientation, performance appraisal and evaluation of services, and give staff a shared identity.

Conclusion The vision describes the future the nursing service aims for, the mission its purpose, the philosophy its beliefs and values, and the objectives the measurable results it will achieve. Developed participatively and reviewed regularly, they give direction and meaning to everyday nursing practice.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain nursing service policies and procedures, and the preparation and uses of a nursing procedure manual.
answer_html:
1. Policies

  • Definition – a policy is a standing plan that serves as a general guide to thinking and decision-making, stating the organisation's position on a matter and leaving some freedom in its application.
  • Examples in nursing – visitors' policy, policy on verbal orders, medication administration policy, restraint policy, policy on patient identification, policy on night-duty allocation, leave policy, policy on students' clinical posting.
  • Types – originated (by top management), appealed (made in response to problems or requests from staff), implied (understood from practice) and externally imposed (by laws and regulators, such as biomedical waste rules or MHCA requirements).
  • Characteristics of good policies – consistent with the objectives and the law, clear and written, stable yet flexible, known to all, fair, and reviewed periodically.

2. Procedures

  • Definition – a procedure is a detailed chronological sequence of steps for carrying out a particular activity; it tells how a policy is to be implemented.
  • Examples – procedure for blood transfusion, admission of a patient, insertion of a urinary catheter, care of the dead body.
  • Policy versus procedure – a policy is broad and allows judgement ("all blood products shall be checked by two nurses"), whereas a procedure is specific and gives step-by-step instructions for the check. Rules are precise statements of what must or must not be done, with no discretion ("No smoking in the hospital").

3. Nursing procedure manual

  • Definition – a written collection of approved nursing procedures (and related policies) of an institution, used as an official reference for nursing practice.
  • Contents of each procedure – title and code; purpose and scope; definitions; responsible personnel; equipment; steps with scientific rationale; precautions and special considerations; aftercare; documentation; references; date of issue, date of review and approving authority.
  • Steps of preparation
    1. Form a procedure committee of experienced nurses from different units, with the nursing educator.
    2. List the procedures performed in the hospital and decide priorities.
    3. Review current evidence, standards (INC, NABH, national guidelines) and existing practice.
    4. Draft each procedure in a standard format; obtain comments from staff and other departments (infection control, pharmacy).
    5. Pilot the procedure in selected wards and revise it.
    6. Approve through the nursing administration and hospital authorities.
    7. Distribute copies (print and digital) to all units; train staff.
    8. Review and update every two to three years, or earlier when evidence or equipment changes.
  • Uses – standardises care and reduces variation; guides new staff and students during orientation; serves as a basis for supervision, audits and performance appraisal; provides a legal reference of the accepted standard of practice; and is required for accreditation.

Conclusion Policies are broad guides to decision-making, procedures are step-by-step methods of carrying them out, and the nursing procedure manual brings the approved procedures together. Prepared by a committee on the basis of evidence and reviewed regularly, it standardises care, guides staff and supports quality, safety and legal protection.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Describe the planning of a patient care unit (ward).
answer_html:
Introduction A patient care unit (ward) is the area of a hospital where a group of patients receives nursing care under a ward in-charge. Its planning determines how safely, efficiently and comfortably care can be given, so nurses must be part of the planning committee with the administrator, architect, engineers, doctors and infection control team.

Principles

  • Plan according to the type of patients (medical, surgical, paediatric, maternity, critical care), expected workload and future expansion.
  • Follow national standards (such as the Indian Public Health Standards and accreditation norms) for space, services and safety.
  • Ensure patient safety, privacy, infection control, efficiency of work and comfort.

Physical planning

  1. Size and layout – a ward of about 20–30 beds is convenient for one nursing team; layouts include the open (Nightingale) ward, the racetrack ward with central services, and wards with single and two-bed rooms for privacy and isolation.
  2. Nurses' station – centrally placed with a clear view of all patients, close to the treatment room and emergency equipment.
  3. Patient area – adequate space around each bed for care and equipment, bedside locker, curtains or screens for privacy, an oxygen outlet, suction point and call bell at each bed, good natural light and ventilation, and hand-hygiene facilities (wash basins and alcohol hand-rub at the point of care).
  4. Supporting rooms
    • Treatment and procedure room; clean utility room (preparation of medicines and sterile supplies); dirty utility/sluice room (bedpans, soiled linen); store for equipment and linen; pantry.
    • Isolation room(s) with attached toilet.
    • Toilets and bathrooms for patients, separate for men and women, with grab bars and accessible design.
    • Doctors' duty room, staff changing and rest room, counselling or interview room, day room for ambulatory patients, space for biomedical waste segregation.
  5. Safety and services – fire extinguishers and exit routes, emergency lighting and power back-up, ramps and wide doors for trolleys and wheelchairs, non-slip floors, and a nurse call system.

Functional planning

  • Equipment and supplies – list of beds, monitors, crash cart, infusion pumps, linen and consumables, with a system for indent and maintenance.
  • Staffing – number and categories of staff according to norms and patient classification.
  • Policies and procedures – admission, visiting hours, infection control, handover and emergency procedures.
  • Communication and records – telephones, computers for electronic records, notice boards.

Role of the nurse manager

  • Give nursing input on layout, workflow and space.
  • Prepare the list of equipment and staff requirements and the policies of the unit.
  • Commission the unit – check installations, arrange supplies, orient staff and test emergency systems before admitting patients.

Conclusion Planning a patient care unit involves both physical planning – size, layout, nurses' station, patient area, supporting rooms and safety services – and functional planning of equipment, staff, policies and communication. Active participation of nurses ensures a ward that is safe, efficient and comfortable for patients and staff.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain the planning for emergencies and disasters in the hospital and the role of the nurse manager.
answer_html:
Introduction A hospital must be ready to continue functioning during internal emergencies (fire, power or oxygen failure, flooding, violence) and to receive large numbers of casualties during external disasters (accidents, floods, earthquakes, epidemics). This requires a written hospital emergency and disaster management plan, in which the nursing department plays a major part.

Components of the hospital disaster plan

  1. Hazard vulnerability analysis – identifying likely hazards for the hospital and area (floods, fire, road and rail accidents, industrial accidents, epidemics) and their probable impact.
  2. Command structure – Hospital Incident Command System – an incident commander (usually the Medical Superintendent) and sections for operations, planning, logistics and finance, with clear roles; the Chief Nursing Officer heads nursing operations.
  3. Activation and alerts – criteria for declaring a disaster and code alerts (for example, Code Red for fire and Code Blue for cardiac arrest); a staff recall (call-in) system.
  4. Surge capacity – plans to free and add beds (early discharge, postponing elective surgery, opening extra areas), extra staff, equipment and supplies.
  5. Triage and treatment areas – a designated triage area at the entrance with colour-coded triage, and areas for red, yellow, green and black categories.
  6. Communication plan – internal and external communication, coordination with district authorities, ambulance services and other hospitals; a public information desk.
  7. Logistics – stockpile of emergency drugs, IV fluids, dressings, oxygen, linen and personal protective equipment; arrangements for water, food, power and transport.
  8. Evacuation plan – routes, assembly points and methods of moving non-ambulatory patients.
  9. Training and mock drills – regular drills (fire, mass casualty), evaluation and revision of the plan.

Role of the nurse manager

  • Before – prepare the nursing component of the plan; keep updated call-in lists; assign roles (triage nurses, area in-charges); maintain emergency stock and check it regularly; train staff in triage, first aid, fire safety and evacuation; conduct and evaluate drills.
  • During – report to the incident commander; deploy nursing staff according to need; open additional beds; ensure supplies; supervise triage and care; maintain records of casualties; set up a family information centre; protect patients already in the hospital.
  • After – return to routine services, replenish stock, ensure documentation, debrief staff, look after their welfare (rest, psychological support) and revise the plan using lessons learned.

Conclusion Hospital emergency and disaster planning includes hazard analysis, an incident command structure, alerts, surge capacity, triage, communication, logistics, evacuation and drills. The nurse manager prepares the nursing plan, trains and deploys staff, ensures supplies and supports staff, so that the hospital can respond quickly and safely.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain cost–benefit analysis and cost-effectiveness analysis in nursing services.
answer_html:
Introduction Resources in health care are limited, so nurse managers must show that new programmes, equipment or staff are worth their cost. Economic evaluation compares the costs and consequences of alternative choices.

1. Cost–benefit analysis (CBA)

  • Definition – a method that compares the total costs of a programme with its total benefits, both expressed in money.
  • Results – net benefit (benefits minus costs) and benefit–cost ratio (benefits ÷ costs); a programme is worthwhile when the net benefit is positive or the ratio is greater than one.
  • Costs – direct (staff time, equipment, supplies, training), indirect (time off work) and intangible (pain, anxiety) costs.
  • Illustrative example – a CAUTI prevention bundle costs ₹2,00,000 a year (training, closed drainage systems, audits). It prevents 10 infections, each of which would have cost about ₹40,000 in extra stay and antibiotics, so the benefits are ₹4,00,000; the net benefit is ₹2,00,000 and the benefit–cost ratio is 2:1.

2. Cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA)

  • Definition – compares alternatives that have the same kind of outcome, expressed in natural units (infections prevented, falls prevented, lives saved, days of stay reduced), and calculates the cost per unit of outcome.
  • Example – in the above case, the cost per CAUTI prevented is ₹2,00,000 ÷ 10 = ₹20,000; this can be compared with another option, such as only staff education, to see which achieves the outcome at lower cost.
  • It is useful when benefits are hard to express in money, such as patient comfort or lives saved.

3. Related methods

  • Cost-utility analysis – outcome expressed as quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) or disability-adjusted life years.
  • Cost-minimisation analysis – when outcomes are equal, the cheaper option is chosen (for example, two dressing materials with equal healing rates).

Steps – define the problem and alternatives; identify and measure costs; identify and measure outcomes or benefits; calculate ratios; perform sensitivity analysis (test how results change if assumptions change); interpret and decide.

Uses in nursing services – justifying new posts (a lactation nurse, an infection control nurse), equipment (pressure-relieving mattresses, infusion pumps), programmes (fall prevention, discharge education) and choice of supplies; preparing budget proposals; and showing the economic value of nursing.

Limitations – difficulty in valuing intangible benefits, need for reliable data, assumptions that may not hold and ethical concerns if cost alone decides care.

Conclusion Cost–benefit analysis measures costs and benefits in money, while cost-effectiveness analysis measures cost per unit of health outcome. Both help nurse managers choose the best use of limited resources and present convincing proposals to administrators.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is a Gantt chart?
answer_html:
• A Gantt chart, developed by Henry L. Gantt (1910s), is a bar chart that shows the activities of a project against a time scale – each activity is a horizontal bar whose length shows its start, duration and finish.
  • Uses in nursing – planning a CNE programme, an accreditation preparation schedule, a ward renovation, an in-service education calendar or a research project; it helps monitor progress against the plan.
  • A milestone chart is a Gantt chart that marks important completion points (milestones).
  • Limitation – it does not clearly show the interdependence of activities, for which PERT and CPM are used.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is SWOT analysis?
answer_html:
• SWOT analysis is a planning tool for situation analysis that examines an organisation's internal Strengths and Weaknesses and its external Opportunities and Threats.
  • Example (nursing department) – Strengths: experienced, motivated nurses; Weaknesses: shortage of ICU-trained staff, outdated procedure manual; Opportunities: new government schemes, accreditation, tie-up with a nursing college; Threats: migration of nurses, rising patient load, competition from other hospitals.
  • It helps managers build on strengths, correct weaknesses, use opportunities and prepare for threats when setting objectives and strategies.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Differentiate between strategic planning and operational planning.
answer_html:
Strategic planning Operational planning
Done by top management (Chief Nursing Officer, hospital administration) Done by first-line managers (ward in-charges)
Long-term – three to five years or more Short-term – daily, weekly, monthly, up to one year
Broad – vision, mission, major goals and strategies Specific – activities, schedules, assignments
Deals with uncertainty in the environment Deals with routine, known conditions
Example: plan to start a cardiac care centre Example: duty roster and patient assignment for the week
  • Relationship – operational plans are the means of carrying out strategic plans; for example, the strategic goal of starting a cardiac centre is achieved through operational plans for recruiting and training nurses, procuring equipment and scheduling staff.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: (a) Define organising and explain the principles of organisation. (5 marks) (b) Explain the types of organisational structure, with organisational charts. (5 marks) (c) Describe the organisation of the nursing service department in a hospital. (5 marks)

diagram.caption: Organisational chart of the nursing service department of a teaching hospital
labels: Medical Superintendent / Director – Chief Nursing Officer / Nursing Superintendent – Deputy Nursing Superintendents (administration
quality) – Assistant Nursing Superintendents (groups of wards
night duty) – Senior Nursing Officers (ward in-charges) – Nursing Officers – nursing students
multipurpose workers and ward attendants; staff positions: infection control nurse

answer_html:
(a) Definition and principles of organisation (5 marks)

Definition

  • Organising is "the establishment of an intentional structure of roles through determination of the activities required to achieve goals, grouping of these activities, assignment of these groups to managers, delegation of authority to carry them out, and provision for coordination horizontally and vertically" (Koontz and Weihrich).
  • Simply, it is the process of arranging people, tasks, authority and resources so that the plans of the nursing service can be carried out effectively.

Process of organising

  1. Identify and classify the activities needed (patient care, education, supplies, records).
  2. Group activities into units or departments (wards, OT, ICU, OPD) – departmentation.
  3. Assign each group to a person or team (ward in-charge, team leader).
  4. Delegate authority to perform the duties.
  5. Establish relationships of authority, responsibility and communication, and provide for coordination.

Principles of organisation

  1. Principle of objectives – the organisation and every unit in it must contribute to its objectives.
  2. Specialisation (division of work) – work is divided so that each person does a limited range of tasks in which he or she is skilled.
  3. Unity of command – each person reports to one superior.
  4. Span of control (span of management) – the number of subordinates a manager can supervise effectively is limited; it is narrower for complex, varied work and wider for routine work.
  5. Scalar principle (chain of command) – a clear, unbroken line of authority from the top to the bottom.
  6. Delegation – authority must be delegated to those at the point where decisions are needed.
  7. Parity of authority and responsibility – authority delegated should be equal to the responsibility assigned.
  8. Absoluteness of accountability – a superior cannot escape accountability for the work delegated.
  9. Unity of direction – one plan and one head for each group of activities having the same objective.
  10. Coordination – activities of all units must be harmonised.
  11. Balance – between centralisation and decentralisation, and between line and staff.
  12. Flexibility – the structure should adapt to changing needs, such as an epidemic.
  13. Continuity – the structure should continue despite changes of personnel.
  14. Exception principle – routine decisions are taken at lower levels; only exceptional matters are referred upward.
  15. Efficiency – objectives should be achieved with the minimum of cost and effort.

(b) Types of organisational structure (5 marks)

1. Line (military or scalar) organisation

  • Authority flows directly from top to bottom in a straight line; each person has one superior.
  • Merits – simple, clear authority and responsibility, quick decisions, discipline.
  • Demerits – overload of top managers, lack of specialists, rigidity.
  • Nursing example – Nursing Superintendent → Assistant Nursing Superintendent → ward in-charge → nursing officers.

2. Line and staff organisation

  • Line managers have authority over operations, while staff specialists advise and support them without direct command authority.
  • Nursing example – the infection control nurse, nurse educator and quality coordinator advise ward in-charges, who remain in the line of command.
  • Merits – specialist expertise with unity of command. Demerits – possible conflict between line and staff.

3. Functional organisation (F. W. Taylor)

  • Work is grouped by function, and each functional specialist has authority over that function in all units.
  • Example – a dietician has authority over the diets in all wards.
  • Merits – specialisation and expertise. Demerits – violates unity of command; workers may receive orders from several bosses.

4. Matrix organisation

  • A two-way structure in which staff report both to a functional head and to a project or programme head.
  • Example – a nurse in the oncology programme reports to the nursing department and to the oncology programme coordinator.
  • Merits – flexibility and teamwork for complex projects. Demerits – dual authority, confusion and conflict.

5. Committee organisation – groups of people (committees) take decisions or advise on specific matters, such as the infection control committee or the nursing procedure committee.

6. Tall and flat structures – tall structures have many levels and narrow spans of control (more control, slower communication); flat structures have few levels and wide spans (faster communication, more autonomy).

Formal and informal organisation – the formal organisation is the official structure shown in the chart; the informal organisation is the network of personal relationships and groups ("grapevine") that also influences work.

Organisational chart

  • A diagram showing the structure of an organisation – its positions, levels, lines of authority and communication.
  • Types – vertical (top to bottom), horizontal (left to right) and circular (top position at the centre).
  • Uses – shows who reports to whom, the span of control and gaps or overlaps; helps orientation of new staff and planning of changes.
  • Limitations – shows only formal relationships, may become outdated and does not show the degree of authority.

(c) Organisation of the nursing service department (5 marks)

Position in the hospital – the nursing department is the largest department of the hospital; its head, the Chief Nursing Officer or Nursing Superintendent, reports to the Medical Superintendent or Hospital Director and is a member of the hospital's management committees.

Hierarchy (typical teaching hospital)

  1. Chief Nursing Officer / Nursing Superintendent – head of the department; responsible for policies, planning, staffing, budget, quality and liaison with hospital administration.
  2. Deputy Nursing Superintendents – assist the head, often in charge of administration, nursing education or quality.
  3. Assistant Nursing Superintendents (nursing supervisors) – each in charge of a group of wards or departments (medical, surgical, OT, ICU, OPD and emergency) and of night supervision.
  4. Senior Nursing Officers (ward in-charges or ward sisters) – manage individual wards and units.
  5. Nursing Officers (staff nurses) – give direct patient care.
  6. Nursing students, multipurpose workers and ward attendants – work under nursing supervision. - Staff (advisory) positions – infection control nurse, nurse educator (in-service education cell), quality and patient-safety nurse, nurse informatics coordinator.

Functions of the nursing department

  • Patient care – planning and providing safe, high-quality nursing care in all units.
  • Personnel management – recruitment, deployment, rosters, appraisal, welfare and discipline of nursing staff.
  • Education – orientation, in-service and continuing education; clinical experience for students.
  • Material management – equipment, linen and supplies in nursing units.
  • Quality and safety – standards, audits, infection control, incident reporting, accreditation.
  • Records and reports – census, nursing reports, statistics.
  • Research and evidence-based practice.
  • Coordination with medical, paramedical and support departments.
  • Budgeting for nursing needs.

Committees of the nursing department – nursing procedure committee, nursing quality committee, nursing education committee, uniform and welfare committee; nurses are also members of hospital committees (infection control, pharmacy and therapeutics, ethics, safety).

Nursing importance A clear structure tells every nurse whom she reports to, what authority she has and where to seek help; it prevents duplication and gaps, speeds communication in emergencies and supports accountability. A poorly organised department leads to confusion, conflict and unsafe care.

Conclusion Organising establishes a structure of roles, authority and relationships guided by principles such as unity of command, span of control, scalar chain, delegation and coordination. Structures may be line, line and staff, functional, matrix or committee-based, shown by organisational charts. In the hospital, the nursing department is organised in a hierarchy from the Chief Nursing Officer to nursing officers, supported by staff specialists and committees, to provide safe and coordinated nursing care.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain delegation – its principles, process, the five rights of delegation and barriers.
answer_html:
Definition Delegation is the process by which a manager assigns a task, together with the authority needed to perform it, to a competent subordinate, while the manager retains accountability for the outcome.

  • Responsibility – the obligation to perform the task; authority – the right to act and make decisions; accountability – being answerable for the results.

Principles

  1. Delegation by results expected – the delegatee must know clearly what is to be achieved.
  2. Parity of authority and responsibility – enough authority must be given to carry out the responsibility.
  3. Absoluteness of accountability – the delegator remains accountable; delegation does not remove it.
  4. Unity of command – the delegatee reports to one person for the task.
  5. Competence – tasks are delegated only to persons trained and legally permitted to do them.
  6. Scalar principle – a clear line of authority so the delegatee knows whom to approach.

Process (steps)

  1. Assess the task, the patient's condition and the skills required.
  2. Select a competent delegatee within his or her legal scope of practice and job description.
  3. Communicate clearly – what, when, how, expected results and when to report.
  4. Grant authority and resources needed.
  5. Supervise and monitor at the appropriate level.
  6. Evaluate and give feedback, and recognise good performance.

Five rights of delegation

  1. Right task – one that can be delegated (routine, predictable, with standard procedures).
  2. Right circumstance – a stable patient and a suitable setting.
  3. Right person – a delegatee with the necessary knowledge, skill and legal authority.
  4. Right direction and communication – clear, specific instructions and limits.
  5. Right supervision and evaluation – monitoring, intervention when needed and feedback.

What a nurse should not delegate – nursing assessment and diagnosis, care planning, evaluation of care, nursing judgement, care of unstable patients, and tasks such as IV medication administration to personnel who are not licensed or trained for them.

Barriers

  • Delegator – fear of losing control, lack of trust, belief that "I can do it better myself", perfectionism, poor communication.
  • Delegatee – lack of competence or confidence, fear of criticism, overload, unclear instructions.
  • Organisation – unclear job descriptions, staff shortage, lack of policies.

Benefits – frees the manager for higher-level work, develops staff skills and confidence, increases job satisfaction, speeds decisions and improves efficiency.

Conclusion Delegation transfers tasks and matching authority to competent staff while accountability stays with the delegator. Following its principles, a systematic process and the five rights, and overcoming barriers, helps nurse managers use their teams effectively and safely.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain the nursing care delivery systems (methods of assigning patient care).
answer_html:
Introduction A nursing care delivery system is the method by which nursing work is organised and assigned to staff so that patients receive care. The choice depends on the number and skill mix of staff, the type of patients and the philosophy of the unit.

1. Case method (total patient care)

  • One nurse is responsible for all the care of one or a few patients during a shift; the oldest method, used in ICUs and private duty nursing.
  • Merits – holistic, continuous care during the shift; high patient satisfaction.
  • Demerits – needs many qualified nurses; costly; continuity may be lost between shifts.

2. Functional nursing

  • Work is divided by tasks – one nurse gives all medicines, another does dressings, another records vital signs; the in-charge coordinates.
  • Merits – efficient and economical when staff are few; each nurse becomes skilled in her task.
  • Demerits – fragmented, task-oriented care; patients deal with many nurses; nobody has an overall picture; low job satisfaction.

3. Team nursing

  • Introduced by Eleanor Lambertsen in the 1950s. A team led by a registered nurse (team leader), with other nurses and auxiliaries, provides care to a group of patients; the team leader plans care and assigns members according to their abilities, and team conferences are held.
  • Merits – uses different skill levels; better coordination and supervision; staff learn from each other.
  • Demerits – depends on the leadership skill of the team leader; time needed for conferences; may become "small functional nursing".

4. Primary nursing

  • Developed by Marie Manthey (1969, USA). A primary nurse is responsible and accountable 24 hours a day for the care of a small group of patients from admission to discharge; associate nurses follow her care plan on other shifts.
  • Merits – continuity, accountability and a close nurse–patient relationship; high patient and nurse satisfaction.
  • Demerits – requires many experienced nurses; difficult when staff rotate frequently.

5. Modular nursing – a modification of team and primary nursing in which a small team stays with patients in one geographical area (module) of the ward.

6. Case management

  • A nurse case manager coordinates care for patients with complex or long-term conditions across settings and time, using clinical pathways, to achieve quality outcomes at controlled cost and length of stay.
Method Basis of assignment Main advantage Main disadvantage
Case method Patients Holistic care Costly
Functional Tasks Economical Fragmented care
Team Group of patients and team Uses skill mix Depends on team leader
Primary Patients, 24-hour accountability Continuity Needs many qualified nurses

Conclusion Nursing care may be organised by the case, functional, team, primary, modular or case-management method. The nurse manager selects or combines methods according to staff numbers, skill mix and patient needs, aiming for safe, continuous and patient-centred care.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain coordination – its importance, principles and techniques in the nursing service.
answer_html:
Definition Coordination is "the orderly arrangement of group effort to provide unity of action in the pursuit of a common purpose" (Mooney and Reiley). It is often called the essence of management, because every function – planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling – requires it.

Importance in nursing

  • Patient care involves many professionals and departments – doctors, nurses, pharmacy, laboratory, radiology, dietary, CSSD, housekeeping, maintenance, billing.
  • Coordination ensures unity of purpose, avoids duplication, gaps and delays (for example, a patient waiting for a missing investigation report before surgery), uses resources efficiently, improves patient safety and satisfaction and builds team spirit.

Types

  • Internal (within the nursing department) and external (with other departments and outside agencies).
  • Vertical (between levels of the hierarchy) and horizontal (between units at the same level, such as wards and OT).

Principles (Mary Parker Follett)

  1. Direct contact – coordination is best achieved through direct personal contact between the people concerned.
  2. Early stages – it should begin at the planning stage.
  3. Reciprocal relationships – all factors in a situation influence one another.
  4. Continuity – coordination is a continuous process. - Also clarity of objectives, effective communication and sound organisation with clear authority.

Techniques

  • Clear organisational structure, job descriptions and policies that define roles.
  • Communication – handover reports, nursing rounds, notice boards, circulars, telephone and electronic systems.
  • Meetings and conferences – staff meetings, team conferences, interdepartmental meetings.
  • Committees – infection control, pharmacy and therapeutics, quality, disaster committees.
  • Liaison persons – for example, a nurse coordinator for the OT or a discharge coordinator.
  • Standard procedures and checklists – surgical safety checklist, transfer checklist.
  • Hospital information systems for orders, results and bed management.
  • Leadership and good interpersonal relationships.

Barriers – poor communication, unclear authority, departmental rivalry, staff shortage, conflicting goals and lack of information systems.

Role of the nurse manager – coordinate care between shifts and team members; arrange investigations, diet, medicines and transfers; liaise with doctors and support departments; organise family meetings and discharge planning; and resolve inter-departmental problems promptly.

Conclusion Coordination brings the efforts of individuals and departments together for a common goal. Using direct contact, early and continuous coordination, clear structure, communication, meetings, committees and information systems, the nurse manager ensures smooth, safe and timely patient care.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain organisational climate, organisational effectiveness and organisational development in relation to the nursing service.
answer_html:
1. Organisational climate

  • Definition – the relatively enduring quality of the internal environment of an organisation as experienced by its members; it is how staff perceive their workplace ("how it feels to work here").
  • Dimensions (Litwin and Stringer) – structure (rules, red tape), responsibility (freedom to make decisions), reward (recognition and fairness), risk, warmth (friendliness), support (help from superiors and colleagues), standards (expectations of performance), conflict (how it is handled) and identity (sense of belonging).
  • Types – an open, supportive climate (trust, participation, recognition) or a closed, defensive climate (fear, rigid control, blame).
  • Factors influencing it – leadership style, communication, workload and staffing, policies, pay and recognition, opportunities for growth, physical working conditions and relationships with other professionals.
  • Effects – a positive climate improves job satisfaction, morale, retention, teamwork and patient outcomes; a negative climate leads to stress, absenteeism, turnover and errors.
  • Assessment – staff climate or engagement surveys, exit interviews, turnover and absenteeism rates.

2. Organisational effectiveness

  • Definition – the degree to which an organisation achieves its goals while using resources efficiently and satisfying its members and clients.
  • Approaches to measuring it
    • Goal attainment – are objectives achieved?
    • System resource – does the organisation obtain the resources it needs?
    • Internal process – are internal processes smooth, with good communication and low conflict?
    • Strategic constituencies – are patients, staff, government and the community satisfied?
  • Indicators in nursing – patient outcomes (falls, pressure injuries, infections, mortality), patient satisfaction, staff satisfaction and turnover, efficiency (length of stay, cost), quality audit scores and accreditation status.

3. Organisational development (OD)

  • Definition – a planned, organisation-wide, long-term effort, managed from the top, to increase organisational effectiveness and health through planned interventions using behavioural science knowledge.
  • Interventions – team building, survey feedback (collecting staff views and acting on them), process consultation, leadership development, job redesign, conflict resolution workshops and quality improvement programmes.
  • Steps – diagnosis, planning interventions, implementation and evaluation, often following Lewin's change model.

Role of the nurse manager – create an open, supportive climate through participation, fair treatment, recognition and good communication; monitor effectiveness indicators; and lead development activities such as team building and staff surveys.

Conclusion Organisational climate is how staff experience their workplace, organisational effectiveness is how well the organisation achieves its goals, and organisational development is the planned effort to improve both. A positive climate and continuous development are essential for an effective nursing service.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is span of control?
answer_html:
• Span of control (span of management) is the number of subordinates that one manager can supervise effectively.
  • A narrow span (few subordinates) allows close supervision but creates more levels (tall structure); a wide span gives more autonomy and fewer levels (flat structure).
  • Factors – complexity and variety of work, competence of staff, physical distance, availability of standard procedures and the manager's ability; for example, a ward in-charge of an ICU can supervise fewer staff closely than the in-charge of a stable general ward.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is unity of command?
answer_html:
• Unity of command is the principle (Henri Fayol) that each employee should receive orders from, and be accountable to, only one superior.
  • It avoids confusion, conflicting instructions and divided loyalty, and makes accountability clear.

  • Nursing example – a nursing officer takes instructions about nursing duties from her ward in-charge, and the ward in-charge from the Assistant Nursing Superintendent; doctors' treatment orders relate to patient care and are carried out within this nursing line of authority.

  • It is violated in functional and matrix structures, where a nurse may receive orders from several bosses; in such cases roles and reporting lines must be written down clearly.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Differentiate between centralisation and decentralisation.
answer_html:
Centralisation Decentralisation
Decision-making authority is concentrated at the top of the organisation Authority is distributed to lower levels, close to where work is done
Uniform policies and control; suits small organisations and emergencies Faster decisions, initiative and development of managers; suits large organisations
May overload top managers and slow decisions Needs competent managers and good coordination
Example: central purchase of equipment by the nursing department Example: ward in-charge decides daily patient assignment and duty roster
  • Most nursing departments use a balance – policies, budget and recruitment are centralised, while day-to-day decisions about patient care are decentralised to the wards.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: (a) Define staffing and state its objectives and principles. (4 marks) (b) Explain the staffing process – recruitment, selection, orientation, placement and retention of nursing personnel. (6 marks) (c) Explain the staffing norms and the calculation of nursing staff for a ward. (5 marks)

diagram.caption: The staffing process in nursing
labels: job specification) → recruitment → selection → appointment → orientation/induction → placement → in-service education and development → performance appraisal → promotion

answer_html:
(a) Definition, objectives and principles of staffing (4 marks)

Definitions
