  • Staffing is "filling and keeping filled the positions in the organisation structure" through identifying workforce requirements, inventorying the people available, recruitment, selection, placement, promotion, appraisal, compensation and training (Koontz and Weihrich).
  • Nursing staffing means providing the right number and the right kind of nursing personnel, at the right place and at the right time, to give safe and effective care round the clock.

Objectives

  1. To ensure adequate numbers and the right skill mix of nursing staff in every unit and every shift.
  2. To provide safe, high-quality and continuous patient care.
  3. To use staff economically, avoiding both understaffing and overstaffing.
  4. To promote job satisfaction, development and retention of nurses.
  5. To comply with norms, laws and accreditation standards.

Principles

  • Staffing is based on the philosophy and objectives of the nursing service and the needs (acuity) of patients, not only on the number of beds.
  • Qualified and competent personnel are placed according to their education and skills; specialised units receive trained staff.
  • Provision of a leave reserve (commonly about 30%) for weekly offs, holidays, leave and training.
  • Fair and consistent policies for recruitment, rosters, promotion and transfer.
  • Flexibility – float pool, on-call arrangements and redeployment during peaks or emergencies.
  • Continuity of care, with reasonable stability of staff in each unit.
  • Staffing decisions are reviewed regularly using workload and outcome data.

(b) The staffing process (6 marks)

1. Human resource (manpower) planning

  • Estimate the number and categories of staff required (from norms, workload and planned expansion), take an inventory of existing staff and identify the gap to be filled, considering expected retirements and resignations.

2. Job analysis – a systematic study of each job, which produces the job description (duties and responsibilities) and the job specification (qualifications, experience, skills and personal qualities needed).

3. Recruitment

  • Definition – the process of searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply for jobs.
  • Internal sources – promotion, transfer, re-employment of former staff, references from present staff.
  • External sources – advertisements in newspapers and online portals, campus recruitment from nursing colleges, employment exchanges, recruitment agencies, walk-in interviews, and common recruitment examinations such as the AIIMS Nursing Officer Recruitment Common Eligibility Test (NORCET) and State public service commission examinations for government posts.

4. Selection

  • Definition – the process of choosing the most suitable candidates from those who have applied.
  • Steps – screening of applications; written test; skill or practical test; interview (structured, by a panel); reference checks; verification of qualifications and registration with the State Nursing Council (through NRTS); medical examination; final selection and appointment letter stating the post, pay, probation period and conditions of service.

5. Orientation (induction)

  • A planned programme introducing the new employee to the organisation, its philosophy, policies, procedures, people and the work unit.
  • Includes general orientation (hospital tour, rules, fire safety, infection control, emergency codes) and unit orientation with a preceptor or "buddy" and a competency checklist.

6. Placement

  • Assigning the employee to a unit and post that suit his or her qualification, experience and aptitude – for example, a nurse with critical care training to the ICU – usually with a probation period during which performance is assessed before confirmation.

7. Development and retention

  • In-service education, performance appraisal, promotion and career development.
  • Retention strategies – fair salary and allowances; safe staffing; fair and flexible rosters; recognition and awards; opportunities for further study and CNE; supportive leadership and participation in decisions; safe working environment and protection from violence; housing, transport and childcare facilities; career ladders; exit interviews to understand why nurses leave.

8. Separation – resignation, transfer, termination and superannuation, handled according to service rules.

(c) Staffing norms and calculation of nursing staff (5 marks)

A. Staffing norms

  1. Staff Inspection Unit (SIU) norms (1991–92) – followed in Central Government hospitals:
    • General wards – one staff nurse/nursing sister for every 6 beds (1:6).
    • Special wards (paediatrics, burns, neurosurgery, cardiothoracic, neuromedicine) – 1:4.
    • Intensive care units – 1:1.
    • Labour room – one nurse for every labour table; major operation theatre – two nurses for every functional table.
  2. Indian Nursing Council norms (1985, with TNAI) – based on beds:
    • Chief Nursing Officer – 1 for 500 beds; Nursing Superintendent – 1 for 400 beds; Deputy Nursing Superintendent – 1 for 300 beds and one more for every additional 200 beds; Assistant Nursing Superintendent – 1 for 100–150 beds or 3–4 wards; ward sister – 1 for 25–30 beds or one per ward.
    • Staff nurses – 1:3 in teaching hospitals and 1:5 in non-teaching hospitals in general wards, and 1:1 in ICUs, each with a 30% leave reserve; one infection control nurse for every 250 beds.
    • (These ratios are for round-the-clock coverage – for example, 1:3 means 10 staff nurses for a 30-bed ward across all shifts, plus leave reserve.)
  3. Other guidance – Indian Public Health Standards for public facilities, accreditation (NABH) requirements, and WHO's Workload Indicators of Staffing Need (WISN) method.

B. Methods of calculating staff

  • Ratio (norms) method – staff = beds ÷ ratio, plus leave reserve.
  • Workload method – based on hours of nursing care required per patient per day, estimated using a patient classification system.

C. Worked example (workload method)

  • A 30-bed medical ward with an average bed occupancy of 80% = 24 patients.
  • Average nursing care needed (by patient classification) = 3 hours per patient per day.
  • Total nursing care hours per day = 24 × 3 = 72 hours.
  • With 8-hour shifts, nurse-shifts needed per day = 72 ÷ 8 = 9 (distributed, for example, as 4 in the morning, 3 in the evening and 2 at night).
  • Nurse-shifts per week = 9 × 7 = 63; each nurse works 6 shifts a week, so nurses needed = 63 ÷ 6 = 10.5.
  • Add a 30% leave reserve: 10.5 × 1.3 = 13.65 ≈ 14 nursing officers, plus one senior nursing officer (ward in-charge) on day duty.
  • Check with norms – INC norm 1:3 for a teaching hospital gives 30 ÷ 3 = 10, plus 30% = 13 – close to the workload estimate.

Skill mix and shift distribution – a suitable proportion of senior and junior nurses and of nursing and auxiliary staff in every shift; more staff during the morning when procedures, rounds and admissions are most frequent.

Nursing importance Adequate and well-matched staffing is strongly linked with fewer errors, infections, falls and deaths and with nurses' job satisfaction. Nurse managers who know the norms and can calculate requirements from workload can justify posts to administrators and protect patients and staff.

Conclusion Staffing provides the right number and kind of nursing personnel at the right time and place. It follows principles of patient-need-based, competent, fair and flexible staffing and proceeds through planning, job analysis, recruitment, selection, orientation, placement, development and retention. Staff requirements are calculated from SIU and INC norms or, more accurately, from workload using patient classification, with a leave reserve of about 30%.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain the patient classification system and its use in nurse staffing.
tags: hours of nursing care per patient per day
answer_html:
Definition A patient classification system (PCS) is a method of grouping patients according to the amount and complexity of nursing care they require (acuity), in order to determine the nursing staff needed and to distribute workload fairly.

Purposes

  • To estimate nursing care hours and the number and skill mix of staff for each shift and unit.
  • To make acuity-based patient assignments.
  • To justify posts and prepare the nursing budget; to compare workload between units and over time.

Types

  1. Prototype evaluation (descriptive) system – patients are placed in broad categories according to a description of typical patients in each category.
  2. Factor evaluation (critical indicator) system – specific care elements (vital signs frequency, mobility, feeding, medications, wound care, IV therapy, teaching, emotional support) are scored, and the total score decides the category and care hours.

Example of categories (care hours vary between hospitals)

  • Category I – self-care (minimal care) – ambulatory, independent, needs little assistance; about 1–2 hours of nursing care in 24 hours.
  • Category II – intermediate (moderate) care – needs some help with activities, regular medications and observations; about 3–4 hours.
  • Category III – extensive (modified intensive) care – largely dependent, frequent monitoring and treatments; about 5–6 hours.
  • Category IV – intensive care – critically ill, needing continuous observation and care; 7 hours or more, often one nurse per patient.

Steps in use

  1. Classify each patient at a fixed time each day or shift, using the agreed tool.
  2. Multiply the number of patients in each category by its care hours to obtain total required hours.
  3. Convert hours into nurse-shifts and compare with staff available.
  4. Adjust staffing – redeploy float staff, call in extra staff, or reduce staff where workload is low; record the data for monthly analysis.

Advantages – objective basis for staffing, fair workload, safer care, better planning and budgeting.

Limitations – subjectivity in rating, time needed to classify, need for validation and regular updating, and it may not capture psychosocial needs or teaching time.

Conclusion A patient classification system groups patients by their nursing care needs so that staffing reflects actual workload rather than just the number of beds. Used regularly, it supports safe staffing, fair assignments and convincing budget proposals.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain job description and job specification, with the job description of a nursing officer (staff nurse).
answer_html:
1. Job description

  • Definition – a written statement of the duties, responsibilities, relationships and working conditions of a particular job, obtained from job analysis.
  • Components – job title and code; department; reports to (immediate superior); supervises; job summary; detailed duties and responsibilities; relationships with others; working conditions (shifts); performance standards; date of preparation and review.

2. Job specification

  • Definition – a statement of the minimum qualifications and personal qualities a person must have to perform the job well – education, registration, experience, skills, knowledge, physical and mental fitness and personal attributes.

Uses – recruitment and selection, orientation, clarity of roles and avoidance of duplication, performance appraisal against duties, training needs, fixing pay and grades, and legal protection in disputes.

3. Job description of a Nursing Officer (Staff Nurse) – an example

  • Job title – Nursing Officer (Staff Nurse); Department – Nursing; Reports to – Senior Nursing Officer (ward in-charge); Supervises – nursing students, multipurpose workers and ward attendants assigned to her.
  • Job summary – provides comprehensive, safe nursing care to assigned patients according to the nursing process, hospital policies and professional standards.
  • Duties and responsibilities
    1. Patient care – admits and assesses patients, plans and gives nursing care, administers medicines and treatments as prescribed, monitors vital signs and condition, recognises and reports changes, and responds to emergencies (basic life support).
    2. Documentation – maintains accurate nursing records, charts, intake–output and medication records; gives and receives handover.
    3. Communication – with patients, families, doctors and other departments; carries out doctors' orders and clarifies doubtful orders.
    4. Infection control and safety – hand hygiene, aseptic techniques, biomedical waste segregation, patient identification, fall and pressure-injury prevention, incident reporting.
    5. Health education – teaches patients and families, including discharge teaching.
    6. Supervision and teaching – guides students and auxiliary staff assigned to her.
    7. Equipment and supplies – uses and maintains equipment, checks emergency trolley, prevents wastage.
    8. Professional development – attends in-service education, participates in audits and quality activities, follows the code of ethics.
  • Working conditions – rotating shifts including nights, weekends and holidays.

4. Job specification (Nursing Officer)

  • Education – B.Sc. Nursing or Diploma in General Nursing and Midwifery from an INC-recognised institution.
  • Registration – registered nurse and midwife with the State Nursing Council (valid, renewed).
  • Experience – as required for the post (for example, one to two years for specialised units).
  • Skills – clinical skills, basic life support certification, communication and basic computer skills.
  • Personal qualities – physical fitness, compassion, honesty, teamwork and emotional stability.

Conclusion The job description states what a job involves, while the job specification states what kind of person is needed for it. Clear, up-to-date job descriptions and specifications, such as those for nursing officers, guide recruitment, orientation, supervision and appraisal and prevent role confusion.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain staff turnover and absenteeism among nurses – causes, effects and measures to reduce them.
answer_html:
1. Definitions and measurement

  • Staff turnover is the rate at which employees leave an organisation and are replaced during a period.
    • Turnover rate (%) = (number of staff who left during the year ÷ average number of staff during the year) × 100.
    • Example – if 12 nurses leave in a year from an average staff of 100, the turnover rate is 12%.
  • Absenteeism is the failure of employees to report for scheduled work, without or with notice (excluding approved leave).
    • Absenteeism rate (%) = (person-days lost through absence ÷ total person-days scheduled) × 100.

2. Causes

  • Job-related – heavy workload and understaffing, frequent night and double shifts, non-nursing duties, lack of equipment.
  • Pay and security – low salary (especially in small private hospitals), contractual posts, delayed payments.
  • Management factors – autocratic or unfair supervision, favouritism in rosters, lack of recognition, poor communication, no participation in decisions.
  • Career factors – no opportunity for further study, promotion or specialisation; migration abroad or to better-paying hospitals.
  • Personal and health factors – illness, stress and burnout, family responsibilities, marriage, transport problems, unsafe night travel.
  • Workplace safety – violence by patients' relatives, exposure to infections, poor facilities for rest.

3. Effects

  • Understaffing and increased workload on remaining nurses, leading to a vicious cycle of further absence and resignation.
  • Poorer patient care – missed care, errors, falls and infections.
  • Cost – recruiting, orienting and training replacements; overtime payments.
  • Loss of experienced staff and reduced continuity; low morale and team spirit.

4. Measures to reduce them

  • Safe staffing and fair, transparent, flexible rosters (considering requests, limiting consecutive nights).
  • Competitive pay, allowances and job security; timely salaries.
  • Supportive leadership – recognition, appreciation, participation in decisions, prompt grievance redressal.
  • Career development – in-service education, sponsorship for higher studies, career ladders and promotion policies.
  • Staff welfare – housing or transport, canteen, creche, health check-ups, counselling and wellness programmes.
  • Safe workplace – security, measures against violence, protection from occupational hazards.
  • Attendance management – clear leave policies, monitoring absence patterns, return-to-work interviews after absence, counselling for frequent absentees.
  • Exit interviews to understand why nurses leave, and action on the findings.

Conclusion High turnover and absenteeism reduce staffing, raise costs and endanger patients. They are caused mainly by workload, pay, management style, lack of growth, stress and safety problems, and they are reduced by safe staffing, fair rosters, supportive leadership, career development, welfare measures and attention to the reasons staff give for leaving.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain discipline and grievance handling among nursing personnel.
answer_html:
A. Discipline

  • Definition – discipline is the orderly conduct of employees according to the rules, standards and expectations of the organisation; it also means training that corrects and strengthens behaviour.
  • Types
    • Positive (self-) discipline – staff follow rules willingly because they understand and accept them; built through good leadership, clear policies, motivation and example.
    • Negative (punitive) discipline – enforced through penalties when rules are broken.
  • Common causes of indiscipline – unclear or unfair rules, poor supervision, favouritism, work overload, personal problems, low morale and lack of recognition.
  • Principles (McGregor's "hot stove rule") – discipline should be like touching a hot stove: there is advance warning (rules are known), the response is immediate, consistent (same for everyone, every time) and impersonal (directed at the act, not the person).
  • Progressive discipline
    1. Counselling and oral warning, recorded.
    2. Written warning.
    3. Suspension or other penalty (stopping increments, recovery of loss).
    4. Termination for serious or repeated misconduct.
  • Procedure and natural justice – a show-cause notice stating the charge, an opportunity for the employee to explain, an inquiry where required, a decision with reasons and a right of appeal, as per the service conduct rules (such as the Central Civil Services rules in government service).
  • Role of the nurse manager – communicate rules clearly, set an example, deal with problems early and privately, document facts, be fair and consistent, and help the employee improve.

B. Grievance handling

  • Definition – a grievance is any dissatisfaction or feeling of injustice that an employee has about his or her employment, whether expressed or not.
  • Common causes – unfair rosters or leave refusal, pay and allowance problems, promotion and transfer decisions, unsafe working conditions, harassment, poor relationships with superiors or colleagues.
  • Grievance procedure (step-ladder)
    1. The employee raises the grievance with the immediate supervisor (ward in-charge), who tries to resolve it within a fixed time.
    2. If unresolved, it goes to the Assistant or Deputy Nursing Superintendent.
    3. Then to the grievance redressal committee or the head of the department.
    4. Then to the hospital management, and finally appeal or conciliation.
  • Complaints of sexual harassment are dealt with by the Internal Committee under the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013.
  • Principles – an open-door approach, prompt action, careful listening, confidentiality, fairness, no victimisation, written records and feedback to the employee.

Conclusion Discipline maintains orderly conduct and is best achieved through positive self-discipline, supported by fair, consistent and progressive corrective action following natural justice. Grievances should be handled promptly through a clear procedure. Both require fair and approachable nurse managers and help maintain morale and good care.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain staff welfare and the policies for promotion, transfer, termination and superannuation of nursing personnel.
answer_html:
A. Staff welfare

  • Definition – all efforts made by the employer to improve the physical, mental, social and economic well-being of employees, beyond wages.
  • Statutory measures (required by law) – safe and healthy working conditions, drinking water, rest rooms, maternity benefit (26 weeks of paid maternity leave under labour law; 180 days for Central Government employees), creche facilities, social security (provident fund or pension, gratuity, employees' state insurance), compensation for work-related injury; these are now covered by the labour codes that came into force in November 2025.
  • Non-statutory (voluntary) measures
    • Housing or nurses' hostel, transport (especially for night duty), canteen.
    • Uniform and washing allowance, nursing and risk allowances.
    • Free medical care and immunisation (hepatitis B), health check-ups, counselling and wellness programmes.
    • Recreation, staff clubs, celebration of Nurses' Day.
    • Support for higher studies and CNE, library.
    • Recognition and awards – best nurse awards, and nationally the National Florence Nightingale Awards presented by the President of India.

B. Promotion

  • Definition – advancement of an employee to a higher post with greater responsibility, status and usually pay.
  • Bases – seniority, merit, or seniority-cum-merit (most common in government service), assessed by a departmental promotion committee using service records and appraisal reports.
  • Career ladder in nursing service – Nursing Officer → Senior Nursing Officer → Assistant Nursing Superintendent → Deputy Nursing Superintendent → Nursing Superintendent → Chief Nursing Officer; clinical specialist and educator tracks are also developing.
  • A good promotion policy is written, fair, known to all, based on clear criteria and linked with training.

C. Transfer

  • Definition – movement of an employee from one job, unit or place to another, usually without change in pay or status.
  • Types – production (to meet staffing needs), replacement, rotation (to broaden experience), remedial (for unsuitable placement or conflict), on request (family or health reasons) and penal transfers.
  • Transfer policy – clear criteria, advance notice, consideration of personal circumstances, retention of trained nurses in specialised units for a reasonable period.

D. Termination and separation

  • Resignation – voluntary, with the required notice period.
  • Termination/dismissal – for misconduct or unsatisfactory performance after due inquiry following service rules; discharge or retrenchment when posts are abolished, with notice and compensation as per law.
  • Exit procedures – handing over charge, clearance, exit interview, relieving and experience certificates.

E. Superannuation

  • Retirement on reaching the age fixed by the employer (commonly 60 years for nursing staff in government service; the INC has allowed nursing faculty to continue up to 70 years).
  • Benefits – pension (or National Pension System), gratuity, leave encashment; pre-retirement counselling.

Conclusion Welfare measures, both statutory and voluntary, improve nurses' well-being and retention. Fair, written policies for promotion, transfer, termination and superannuation, applied consistently, maintain morale, protect employees' rights and keep the nursing service stable and effective.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is credentialing?
answer_html:
• Credentialing is the process of verifying a health professional's qualifications, registration, training, experience and competence before allowing him or her to practise, especially in specialised areas (ICU, dialysis, OT, chemotherapy).
  • It includes primary-source verification of certificates and State Nursing Council registration, review of experience, competency assessment and granting of specific clinical privileges.

  • It is repeated periodically (re-credentialing) and is required by accreditation bodies such as NABH, ensuring that only competent nurses perform high-risk procedures.

  • Records of credentialing are kept in each nurse's personal file and reviewed when she is transferred to a new specialised unit.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Differentiate between recruitment and selection.
answer_html:
Recruitment Selection
Process of searching for and attracting suitable candidates to apply Process of choosing the most suitable candidates from the applicants
A positive process – increases the number of applicants A negative process – rejects unsuitable applicants
Comes first Follows recruitment
Methods – advertisements, campus recruitment, portals, employment exchanges Methods – screening, tests, interviews, verification, medical examination
Ends when applications are received Ends with the offer of appointment
  • Both are steps of the staffing process: good recruitment gives a large pool of suitable applicants, and careful selection from that pool ensures that competent, registered nurses are appointed.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: State the nurse–patient ratios recommended by the Staff Inspection Unit (SIU).
answer_html:
The Staff Inspection Unit (SIU) norms of 1991–92, followed in Central Government hospitals, recommend:

  • General wards – one staff nurse/nursing sister for every 6 beds (1:6).
  • Special wards (paediatrics, burns, neurosurgery, cardiothoracic, neuromedicine) – 1:4.
  • Intensive care units – 1:1.
  • Labour room – one nurse per labour table; major operation theatre – two nurses per functional operating table.

  • These are calculated for round-the-clock care and are now considered outdated by many experts, who recommend workload-based staffing.

  • A leave reserve must be added to these numbers to cover weekly offs, holidays and leave.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Define in-service education. Explain its need, objectives and types. Describe the planning, organisation and evaluation of an in-service education programme for nurses.

diagram.caption: Planning cycle of in-service education
labels: results) → follow-up and records → back to needs assessment

answer_html:
Definition In-service education is a planned programme of learning activities provided by the employing organisation, within the work setting, to help its staff maintain and improve their competence in their present jobs and prepare for new responsibilities.

Related terms

  • Orientation (induction) – introduction of new employees to the organisation and their job.
  • In-service education – job-related learning for employees after orientation.
  • Continuing education – broader, planned learning for professional growth beyond the basic qualification, often outside the organisation, which earns CNE credits for renewal of registration.
  • Staff development – the umbrella term for all of these.

Need for in-service education

  1. Rapid advances in medicine, technology and nursing – new drugs, equipment (infusion pumps, ventilators), procedures and evidence.
  2. Changing policies and standards – national guidelines, accreditation requirements, legal changes.
  3. New staff and high turnover – new nurses need to reach the expected level quickly.
  4. Gaps in performance found in audits, incident reports and patient complaints.
  5. Patient safety and quality – prevention of errors, infections and falls.
  6. New roles and units – critical care, dialysis, oncology, nurse practitioners.
  7. Professional requirement – CNE hours for renewal of registration.
  8. Job satisfaction, motivation and retention – learning opportunities make nurses feel valued.

Objectives

  • To orient new staff to the organisation, policies and their duties.
  • To update knowledge and skills and maintain competence.
  • To improve the quality and safety of patient care.
  • To prepare staff for new equipment, procedures and roles.
  • To develop leadership, management, communication and teaching skills.
  • To promote evidence-based practice and research.
  • To develop positive attitudes, teamwork and professional values.

Types

  1. Induction/orientation training – for newly appointed nurses.
  2. On-the-job (job-specific) training – skill training at the bedside or unit, such as use of a new monitor.
  3. Refresher courses – periodic updating in routine skills (injection safety, documentation).
  4. Mandatory training – basic and advanced life support, fire safety, infection control, biomedical waste management, patient safety, prevention of sexual harassment.
  5. Specialty training – critical care, neonatal care, dialysis, chemotherapy, emergency nursing.
  6. Remedial training – to correct specific deficiencies.
  7. Leadership and management development – for ward in-charges and supervisors.
  8. Preparation for promotion and new roles; cross-training to work in other units.

Methods – lectures with discussion, demonstration and return demonstration, workshops, seminars and conferences, case presentations, simulation and skills laboratories, e-learning and online modules, journal clubs, bedside teaching and nursing rounds, role play, self-learning packages, mentoring and coaching.

Planning an in-service education programme

  1. Training needs assessment (TNA) – identify learning needs from surveys of staff, observation of practice, audit and incident reports, appraisal reports, patient feedback, new equipment and policy changes.
  2. Set priorities – urgent needs related to patient safety first.
  3. Write objectives – specific and measurable ("At the end of the session, participants will correctly programme the infusion pump").
  4. Select content according to objectives and level of participants.
  5. Select methods, teaching aids and resources.
  6. Select resource persons – senior nurses, nurse educators, doctors, biomedical engineers, external experts.
  7. Schedule – date, time, duration and venue, convenient for different shifts; repeat sessions so that all staff can attend without leaving wards unattended; prepare an annual training calendar.
  8. Budget – materials, refreshments, honoraria, equipment.
  9. Publicise and nominate participants; arrange release from duty.
  10. Implement the programme as planned.
  11. Evaluate and follow up in the wards.

Organisation

  • An in-service education cell (department) headed by a Deputy Nursing Superintendent (Education) or nurse educator, with clinical instructors.
  • An in-service education committee – nurse educator, representatives of nursing administration and ward in-charges, infection control nurse and other specialists – identifies needs, approves the calendar and reviews outcomes.
  • Facilities – classroom, skills laboratory and simulation equipment, audio-visual aids, library and e-learning access.
  • Records – attendance registers, training hours of each nurse, certificates, evaluation reports; programmes may be approved by the State Nursing Council for CNE credits.
  • Coordination with nursing colleges, professional bodies and equipment suppliers.

Evaluation – Kirkpatrick's four levels

  1. Reaction – participants' satisfaction (feedback forms).
  2. Learning – gain in knowledge and skill (pre-test and post-test, skill checklists).
  3. Behaviour – application of learning on the job (observation, audits a few weeks later).
  4. Results – impact on outcomes (fewer infections, errors or falls, better patient satisfaction). - Also evaluate the organisation of the programme (timing, venue, resource persons) and its cost.

Role of the nurse manager – identify needs in her unit, release staff to attend, encourage participation, conduct sessions, supervise the application of new skills and give feedback to the in-service cell.

Principles of in-service education

  • It should be based on identified needs of staff and patients, not on convenience.
  • It must be continuous and planned, with an annual calendar, rather than occasional.
  • Participation of staff in planning increases interest and attendance.
  • Learning should be practical and job-related, using adult learning principles – building on experience, active participation and immediate application.
  • It should be available to all categories and all shifts, including night staff.
  • Every programme should be evaluated and followed up in practice.

Example – a one-day programme on prevention of medication errors

  • Need identified – three medication errors reported in a month in the surgical wards.
  • Objectives – participants will state the "rights" of medication administration, identify high-alert medicines, use the double-check procedure and report errors through the incident reporting system.
  • Sessions – causes and types of medication errors (lecture–discussion); high-alert medicines and look-alike, sound-alike drugs (case studies); calculation of doses and infusion rates (exercise); demonstration and return demonstration of the double-check and barcode procedures; incident reporting and a just culture (discussion); post-test and feedback.
  • Follow-up – audit of medication charts and observation of administration after four weeks; comparison of error reports before and after the programme.

Problems and solutions

  • Staff cannot be released because of shortage – hold short, repeated sessions in the unit and use e-learning.
  • Lack of interest – link attendance with CNE credits, appraisal and recognition, and make sessions interactive.
  • Lack of resources – share facilities with the nursing college and use low-cost simulation.
  • No follow-up – make ward in-charges responsible for supervising the application of new skills.

Nursing importance Health care changes too quickly for basic education to last a lifetime. Planned in-service education keeps nurses competent, confident and safe, reduces errors and helps hospitals meet accreditation and legal requirements, while giving nurses opportunities for growth.

Conclusion In-service education is planned, job-related learning provided by the employer to maintain and improve the competence of staff. It is needed because of advances in care, new staff, performance gaps and professional requirements, and it includes induction, on-the-job, refresher, mandatory, specialty, remedial and leadership training. It is planned from a training needs assessment, organised through an in-service education cell and committee, and evaluated at the levels of reaction, learning, behaviour and results.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: (a) Define material management and state its objectives and principles. (4 marks) (b) Explain the procurement, storage, issue and inventory control of equipment and supplies. (7 marks) (c) Explain the maintenance, auditing and condemnation of equipment, and the role of the nurse manager. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Material management cycle
labels: estimation of requirements → specifications → procurement (purchase committee
GeM) → receiving and inspection → storage (FIFO/FEFO) → issue against indent → use → maintenance → stock verification and audit → condemnation and disposal → replacement planning

answer_html:
(a) Definition, objectives and principles (4 marks)

Definition Material management is the planning, procurement, storage, distribution, control and disposal of materials – equipment, instruments, drugs, linen and consumables – so that the right materials are available in the right quantity, of the right quality, at the right time and place, at the right cost.

Objectives

  • Uninterrupted availability of supplies and working equipment for patient care.
  • Economy – minimum investment in stock, avoiding both shortage and overstocking.
  • Quality – materials that meet specifications and safety standards.
  • Prevention of wastage, pilferage, damage and expiry.
  • Efficient record keeping and accountability.
  • Proper maintenance and safe disposal of equipment.

Principles

  1. Five rights of purchasing – right quality, right quantity, right time, right source and right price.
  2. Standardisation – using a limited range of standard items makes purchase, use and maintenance easier.
  3. Proper specifications – clear technical specifications for every item.
  4. Economy – value for money, considering running and maintenance costs, not only purchase price.
  5. Accountability – every item is recorded from receipt to disposal.
  6. Safety – equipment must be safe for patients and staff, with training in its use.
  7. Transparency and fairness in procurement, following financial rules.

(b) Procurement, storage, issue and inventory control (7 marks)

1. Procurement

  • Estimation of requirement – based on past consumption, patient load, new services and stock in hand; prepared by each unit and consolidated by the nursing department.
  • Specifications – prepared by users (nurses) with technical experts.
  • Methods of purchase – small purchases, purchase through a purchase committee, and tenders (open, limited or single) for larger values, according to the financial rules; government institutions use the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) portal.
  • Trials and evaluation of samples, especially for new equipment, with nursing participation.
  • Purchase order and follow-up for timely supply.

2. Receiving and inspection – check the items against the purchase order for quantity, quality, specifications, batch number, expiry date and damage; enter in the stock register; report shortages or defects.

3. Storage

  • Clean, dry, well-ventilated, pest-free and secure store with shelves and labelling.
  • Arrangement by category; heavy items low; cold-chain storage for vaccines and certain drugs; separate locked storage for controlled drugs; fire safety.
  • FIFO (first in, first out) and FEFO (first expiry, first out) to avoid expiry.

4. Issue

  • Items are issued to wards against indents (requisitions) signed by the ward in-charge, at fixed times; emergency issues as required.
  • Ward stock is kept at a level fixed for each unit (imprest or par-level system).

5. Inventory control

  • Definition – the scientific control of stock so that materials are available when needed at minimum cost.
  • ABC analysis (by annual consumption value) – A items (about 10–20% of items, about 70% of value) are tightly controlled; B items moderately; C items (many items, small value) loosely.
  • VED analysis (by criticality) – Vital (stock-out cannot be tolerated – emergency drugs, oxygen, defibrillator), Essential and Desirable.
  • ABC–VED matrix – Category I (AV, AE, AD, BV, CV) needs the closest control; Category II (BE, CE, BD); Category III (CD) the least.
  • FSN analysis (fast-, slow- and non-moving items), SDE analysis (scarce, difficult, easily available) and HML analysis (high, medium, low unit cost).
  • Economic order quantity (EOQ) – the order size that minimises total ordering and carrying costs: EOQ = √(2AO ÷ C), where A is annual demand, O is the cost of placing one order and C is the carrying cost per unit per year.
  • Reorder level – the stock level at which a new order is placed: reorder level = (average daily consumption × lead time in days) + buffer stock. Example: if 50 IV sets are used daily, the supplier takes 10 days and the buffer stock is 200, the reorder level is 50 × 10 + 200 = 700 sets.
  • Buffer (safety) stock protects against delays and sudden increases in use; lead time is the time between placing an order and receiving it.

(c) Maintenance, auditing, condemnation and the nurse manager's role (4 marks)

Maintenance

  • Preventive maintenance – regular cleaning, calibration and servicing according to a schedule, to prevent breakdown.
  • Breakdown (corrective) maintenance – repair after failure; defects are reported promptly in writing to the biomedical engineering department.
  • Annual maintenance contracts (AMC) or comprehensive maintenance contracts (CMC) for costly equipment.
  • Equipment history card (log book) for each major item – date of purchase, supplier, warranty, repairs and maintenance.

Auditing

  • Physical stock verification at least once a year by a committee, comparing actual stock with registers; checking indent books, issue records and expiry dates; explaining and writing off shortages according to rules.

Condemnation and disposal

  • Equipment that is beyond economical repair, obsolete or unsafe is examined by a condemnation committee, recorded in the condemnation register, written off with approval and disposed of according to rules – auction, buy-back, e-waste rules for electronic items and biomedical waste rules for contaminated items.

Role of the nurse manager

  • Estimate requirements accurately and indent in time; participate in preparing specifications and in purchase and trial committees.
  • Receive and check items; store them correctly (FEFO, labelling, security).
  • Maintain records – stock register, indent book, equipment inventory, breakage and condemnation registers, crash-cart checklist.
  • Check emergency equipment and drugs daily.
  • Ensure preventive maintenance, report defects promptly and follow up repairs.
  • Train staff in the correct use and care of equipment; prevent wastage and pilferage; promote cost-consciousness.

Records used in material management

  • Stock (inventory) register for consumables and a separate equipment (dead-stock) register for non-consumable items.
  • Indent book (requisitions), issue and receipt vouchers.
  • Breakage and loss register, with reports of the circumstances.
  • Condemnation register and write-off orders.
  • Equipment history cards, maintenance logs and AMC records.
  • Expiry register for drugs and sterile supplies; daily crash-cart checklist.

Common problems and their remedies

  • Frequent stock-outs – realistic estimation, reorder levels, buffer stock for vital items.
  • Overstocking and expiry – FEFO, monitoring of slow-moving items, transfer of near-expiry items to units that use them.
  • Equipment lying idle because of minor faults – preventive maintenance and prompt reporting.
  • Pilferage and wastage – proper locking, accountability of the in-charge, regular stock checks and staff education on cost-consciousness.

Care of linen and consumables at ward level – linen is counted at exchange, soiled and infected linen are bagged separately, and torn linen is sent for repair or condemnation; consumables are kept at par levels, opened only when needed and checked daily for expiry, so that the ward neither runs short nor wastes stock.

Nursing importance Patient care stops when a ventilator fails, oxygen runs out or emergency drugs have expired. Nurses use most of the equipment and supplies in a hospital, so their skill in material management directly affects safety, quality and cost.

Conclusion Material management ensures the right materials of the right quality and quantity at the right time and cost. It includes estimation, procurement, receiving, storage (FIFO/FEFO), issue, scientific inventory control using ABC, VED, EOQ and reorder levels, maintenance, auditing and condemnation. The nurse manager plays a key role at every step, from indent to disposal.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is ABC analysis?
answer_html:
• ABC analysis is an inventory control technique that classifies items according to their annual consumption value (unit cost × annual quantity used), based on the Pareto principle.
  • A items – about 10–20% of items accounting for about 70% of the value; need strict control, frequent ordering in small quantities, close monitoring.
  • B items – about 20–30% of items and about 20% of the value; moderate control.
  • C items – about 60–70% of items but only about 10% of the value; simple control, bulk ordering.
  • It helps the nurse manager concentrate effort and money where they matter most.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is VED analysis?
answer_html:
• VED analysis classifies items according to their criticality for patient care:
    • Vital – items without which patient care stops or life is endangered (emergency drugs, oxygen, IV fluids, defibrillator, suction apparatus); stock-out cannot be tolerated.
    • Essential – items whose short absence can be tolerated (most routine drugs and dressings).
    • Desirable – items whose absence does not affect care seriously.
  • Vital items are kept with an adequate buffer stock; combined with ABC analysis it forms the ABC–VED matrix for setting control priorities.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is an induction (orientation) programme?
answer_html:
• An induction (orientation) programme is a planned introduction of a newly appointed employee to the organisation, its philosophy, policies, procedures, people and the job.
  • It includes general orientation (hospital tour, rules, fire safety, infection control, emergency codes, patients' rights) and unit orientation under a preceptor or "buddy", with a competency checklist to be completed before the nurse works independently.

  • It reduces anxiety, errors and early resignation, and helps new nurses become productive and safe quickly.

  • Its duration and content depend on the unit; specialised areas such as ICUs need longer orientation.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is training needs assessment?
answer_html:
• Training needs assessment (TNA) is the systematic process of identifying the gap between the knowledge and skills staff have and those they need for their jobs, so that training can be planned.
  • Sources and methods – staff surveys and interviews, observation of practice, audit and incident reports, performance appraisals, patient complaints, introduction of new equipment, procedures or policies, and accreditation requirements.
  • It is the first step in planning in-service education and ensures that training is relevant, prioritised and cost-effective.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: (a) Define directing and explain its principles and elements. (5 marks) (b) Define supervision. Explain the principles and techniques of supervision and the qualities of a good nursing supervisor. (10 marks)

diagram.caption: Elements of directing
labels: feedback) – coordination – guidance and counselling – discipline; all directed towards the objectives of the nursing service

answer_html:
(a) Directing – definition, principles and elements (5 marks)

Definition

  • Directing is "the interpersonal aspect of managing by which subordinates are led to understand and contribute effectively and efficiently to the attainment of enterprise objectives" (Koontz and O'Donnell).
  • It is the function that puts plans into action – guiding, supervising, motivating, communicating with and leading people.

Characteristics

  • Initiates action – plans and organisation remain on paper until people are directed.
  • Continuous – it goes on throughout the life of the organisation.
  • Pervasive – performed by every manager at every level.
  • Flows from top to bottom through the chain of command.
  • Deals with the human element, and therefore requires understanding of behaviour.

Principles of directing

  1. Harmony of objectives – individual goals of staff should be in harmony with the goals of the organisation.
  2. Maximum individual contribution – direction should bring out the best from each person.
  3. Unity of command – instructions should come from one superior.
  4. Unity of direction – one plan and one direction for one set of activities.
  5. Direct supervision – personal contact between superior and subordinates increases effectiveness.
  6. Effective communication – clear, complete, two-way communication.
  7. Appropriate leadership and motivation suited to the situation.
  8. Use of the informal organisation – understanding informal groups to support goals.
  9. Follow-up – checking that instructions have been carried out and giving feedback.

Elements of directing

  1. Supervision – overseeing and guiding the work of subordinates.
  2. Motivation – stimulating people to work willingly and enthusiastically.
  3. Leadership – influencing people to achieve goals.
  4. Communication – issuing orders and instructions, receiving feedback.
  5. Coordination – harmonising the efforts of individuals and units.
  6. Also guidance and counselling, delegation and discipline.

Characteristics of good orders and instructions – clear and complete, reasonable and feasible, consistent with objectives and policies, given to the right person with the necessary authority, in writing when important, in a courteous tone, and followed up.

(b) Supervision (10 marks)

Definition

  • Supervision is the process of guiding, helping, teaching and evaluating the work of subordinates so that the objectives of the organisation are achieved and the subordinates grow in competence.
  • Nursing supervision is "a process of guiding, helping, encouraging and stimulating nursing personnel to improve their performance so that they can give efficient nursing care to patients."
  • In the hospital, supervision is done by the ward in-charge (of nursing officers and students), the Assistant Nursing Superintendent (of ward in-charges and a group of units) and the night supervisor.

Objectives

  • To ensure safe, high-quality care according to standards and policies.
  • To help staff develop knowledge, skill and confidence.
  • To identify problems early and solve them.
  • To maintain good working relationships and morale.
  • To ensure the economical use of resources.
  • To evaluate performance fairly and provide information for appraisal.

Principles of supervision

  1. Based on objectives and standards – supervision is directed towards clearly stated goals.
  2. Democratic and cooperative – staff participate in planning their work and solving problems.
  3. Respect for the individual – personality, dignity and abilities of each worker are respected.
  4. Constructive and creative, not fault-finding – it builds on strengths and encourages initiative.
  5. Planned, continuous and systematic, not occasional or only during crises.
  6. Flexible – adapted to the needs of each person and situation.
  7. Teaching-oriented – every supervisory contact is an opportunity to teach.
  8. Objective and fair evaluation, based on facts and recorded observations.
  9. Uses scientific methods – data, audits and evidence.
  10. Promotes self-direction – the ultimate aim is that staff become able to supervise themselves.

Techniques (methods) of supervision

  1. Observation – direct observation of nursing procedures, patient care and staff behaviour; indirect observation through patient outcomes and records.
  2. Supervisory (nursing) rounds – planned rounds to see patients, check care, equipment and records, and discuss problems with staff.
  3. Conferences
    • Individual conferences – private discussion with a nurse about her work, problems and progress.
    • Group conferences – team conferences, staff meetings and case discussions.
  4. Demonstration of correct procedures and of new equipment.
  5. Review of records and reports – nursing notes, care plans, medication charts, incident reports, registers.
  6. Written instructions – procedure manuals, checklists, circulars and job descriptions.
  7. In-service education to correct deficiencies identified.
  8. Evaluation and feedback – performance appraisal, praise for good work, guidance for improvement.
  9. Counselling for personal or professional difficulties.
  10. Delegation with follow-up to develop staff.

Types of supervision

  • Autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire supervision, according to the style of leadership.
  • Corrective supervision – concentrates on finding and correcting faults; preventive supervision – anticipates mistakes and prevents them; constructive supervision – helps staff improve their work; creative supervision – encourages new ideas and initiative (the most desirable).
  • Clinical supervision – a structured, reflective discussion of practice with an experienced practitioner, widely used in mental health and other specialties.

Qualities of a good nursing supervisor

  • Professional knowledge and clinical competence – sound knowledge of nursing, policies and current practice; ability to demonstrate skills.
  • Leadership ability – able to guide, inspire and set an example.
  • Communication skills – listens actively, gives clear instructions and constructive feedback.
  • Human relations – tactful, approachable, understanding, empathetic and respectful.
  • Fairness and impartiality – no favouritism; consistent decisions.
  • Emotional stability and patience – calm in emergencies and conflicts.
  • Decision-making and problem-solving ability.
  • Teaching ability – interest in developing others.
  • Integrity and honesty; punctuality and discipline.
  • Open-mindedness – accepts new ideas and suggestions.
  • Good health, energy and a sense of humour.

Functions of the nursing supervisor (Assistant Nursing Superintendent)

  • Plans and organises nursing work in her area; prepares or approves rosters; deploys staff according to workload.
  • Guides, teaches and evaluates ward in-charges and staff; maintains standards of care.
  • Coordinates with doctors and other departments; solves problems and handles emergencies.
  • Checks equipment, supplies and records; reports to the Nursing Superintendent.
  • Conducts night supervision – rounds of all units, management of emergencies, admissions and staffing problems at night.

Problems in supervision and remedies

  • Fault-finding and fear – adopt a supportive, constructive approach.
  • Too many subordinates – appropriate span of control and delegation.
  • Lack of time because of administrative work – plan supervisory time; delegate clerical tasks.
  • Lack of preparation of supervisors – training in supervision and leadership.

Nursing importance Good directing and supervision convert plans into safe care at the bedside. Supportive supervisors reduce errors, help new nurses grow, maintain standards and morale, and are a major reason why nurses stay in an organisation.

Conclusion Directing is the interpersonal function of guiding and leading staff, based on principles such as harmony of objectives, maximum individual contribution, unity of command, communication and follow-up; its elements are supervision, motivation, leadership, communication and coordination. Supervision in nursing is a democratic, constructive, planned and teaching-oriented process using observation, rounds, conferences, demonstration, review of records and evaluation, and it requires supervisors with knowledge, leadership, fairness, communication skills and emotional stability.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain management by objectives (MBO) and its application in nursing.
answer_html:
Definition Management by objectives (MBO), introduced by Peter Drucker (1954), is a management approach in which superiors and subordinates jointly set clear, measurable objectives for each person, plan how to achieve them, review progress periodically and evaluate performance against the agreed objectives.

Features

  • Emphasis on results, not activities.
  • Participation of subordinates in setting their own objectives.
  • Objectives are SMART – specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
  • Links individual objectives with departmental and organisational goals.
  • Periodic review and feedback; appraisal based on results.

Steps of MBO

  1. Setting organisational goals – by top management (for example, "improve patient safety").
  2. Setting departmental objectives – the nursing department sets objectives in line with these goals.
  3. Setting individual objectives jointly – each manager and subordinate agree on objectives and standards.
  4. Developing action plans – activities, resources and time schedules.
  5. Implementation with the necessary authority and support.
  6. Periodic review – progress meetings, solving problems, adjusting objectives if conditions change.
  7. Final appraisal – comparison of results with objectives, feedback, recognition and setting of new objectives.

Example in nursing

  • Hospital goal – reduce patient harm.
  • Nursing department objective – reduce patient falls in all wards by 30% within one year.
  • Ward in-charge's objective (agreed with the Assistant Nursing Superintendent) – reduce falls in the orthopaedic ward from six to four per quarter within six months by fall-risk assessment of every patient on admission, bed alarms for high-risk patients, hourly rounding and staff training.
  • Nursing officer's objective – complete the fall-risk assessment for every patient she admits within one hour of admission.
  • Monthly review of fall data and compliance; appraisal at six months.

Advantages

  • Clear direction and focus on results; better planning.
  • Motivation and commitment through participation.
  • Objective basis for performance appraisal.
  • Improved communication between levels; development of managers.

Limitations

  • Time-consuming to set and review objectives.
  • Difficulty in setting measurable objectives for some nursing activities (such as emotional care).
  • Danger of emphasising short-term, measurable goals and ignoring others.
  • Needs support of top management and a culture of trust.

Conclusion MBO is a participative, results-oriented approach in which objectives are jointly set, regularly reviewed and used for appraisal. In nursing, it aligns the work of every nurse with the goals of the department and the hospital and improves motivation and accountability.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain participatory management in nursing, including quality circles and shared governance.
answer_html:
Definition Participatory management is a style of management in which employees are involved in decision-making, problem-solving and planning that affect their work, rather than decisions being made only by top managers.

Principles

  • Staff who do the work know its problems best.
  • Participation increases commitment, acceptance and morale.
  • Mutual trust, open communication and sharing of information are essential.
  • Responsibility and authority are shared, while accountability remains clear.

Forms of participation

  1. Consultation – managers seek staff opinions before decisions (for example, on a new roster pattern).
  2. Staff meetings and team conferences – regular forums for discussion.
  3. Joint committees – procedure, uniform, welfare and quality committees with representatives of all levels.
  4. Suggestion schemes – suggestion boxes or digital platforms, with recognition for useful ideas.
  5. Quality circles
    • Started by Kaoru Ishikawa in Japan in the early 1960s.
    • A small group (about 6–12) of employees from the same work area who meet voluntarily and regularly to identify, analyse and solve work-related problems, under a trained leader, and present solutions to management.
    • Nursing example – a quality circle in the OT reduces delays in starting the first case of the day.
  6. Shared governance
    • A structure in which nurses share authority with managers for decisions about practice, quality, education and research, usually through unit practice councils and a hospital-wide nursing council.
  7. Self-managed (self-directed) teams – teams that plan their own work and schedules.
  8. Self-scheduling of duty rosters within agreed rules.

Advantages

  • Better decisions, because more ideas and practical knowledge are used.
  • Greater acceptance of change and commitment to decisions.
  • Higher job satisfaction, morale and retention.
  • Development of leadership among staff; improved quality and safety.

Barriers

  • Autocratic attitudes and fear of losing control among managers.
  • Lack of time, staff shortage and heavy workload.
  • Lack of skills in group problem-solving; mistrust; token participation without real influence.

Role of the nurse manager – create a climate of trust, share information, invite and act on suggestions, train staff in problem-solving methods, support quality circles and councils, and give recognition.

Conclusion Participatory management involves nurses in decisions through consultation, meetings, committees, suggestion schemes, quality circles, shared governance and self-managed teams. It improves decisions, commitment, morale and quality, provided managers genuinely share influence and support staff.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain inter-sectoral coordination and inter-professional collaboration in health care, with the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
A. Inter-sectoral coordination

  • Definition – joint action between the health sector and other sectors (education, water and sanitation, agriculture and food, women and child development, rural development, social welfare, police, industry, media) to improve health; it was emphasised as a principle of primary health care in the Alma-Ata Declaration (1978).
  • Why it is needed – most determinants of health – nutrition, water, sanitation, housing, education, income, gender and safety – lie outside the health sector.
  • Examples
    • School health programmes with the education department (screening, deworming, iron–folic acid supplementation, life-skills education).
    • Nutrition – Anganwadi services and POSHAN Abhiyaan with the Department of Women and Child Development.
    • Water and sanitation – Swachh Bharat Mission and Jal Jeevan Mission.
    • Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Committees of the panchayat.
    • TB elimination – nutrition support under Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana and community support.
    • Medico-legal care and violence – coordination with police, One Stop Centres and child welfare committees.
    • Disasters and epidemics – coordination with district administration, revenue, police and NGOs.

B. Inter-professional collaboration

  • Definition (WHO) – collaborative practice happens when multiple health workers from different professional backgrounds work together with patients, families, carers and communities to deliver the highest quality of care.
  • Core competencies – shared values and ethics, understanding of each other's roles and responsibilities, inter-professional communication, and teamwork.
  • Strategies
    • Multidisciplinary ward rounds, case conferences and discharge-planning meetings.
    • Structured communication tools such as SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) and standard handover formats.
    • Shared care plans, clinical pathways and electronic records accessible to all.
    • Joint training and simulation (for example, obstetric emergency drills).
    • Mutual respect and clear role definitions.
  • Barriers – professional hierarchy, role ambiguity, poor communication, stereotypes, lack of time and separate education of professions.
  • Benefits – fewer errors, better outcomes, shorter stays, higher patient and staff satisfaction.

Role of the nurse

  • Acts as the link between the patient, family and all members of the team, because she is present round the clock.
  • Communicates observations clearly (SBAR), participates in rounds and case conferences, coordinates investigations, therapies, diet and discharge.
  • In the community, works with Anganwadi workers, teachers, panchayat members, ASHAs and NGOs in programmes.
  • Advocates for patients' needs across departments and sectors.

Conclusion Inter-sectoral coordination links health with other sectors that influence health, while inter-professional collaboration brings different health professionals together around the patient. Nurses, through their continuous presence and community links, play a central role in both.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain the principles and methods of preparing a duty roster for nursing staff, including rotation of staff.
answer_html:
Definition A duty roster is a written plan showing the duty hours, shifts, offs and leave of each member of staff of a unit for a given period (a week, fortnight or month).

Purposes – ensures adequate and competent staff in every shift, continuity of care, fair distribution of work and offs, and planning of leave and training; it is also an official record of attendance.

Principles

  1. Based on patient needs and workload – more staff when activity is high (mornings, operation days).
  2. Skill mix in every shift – at least one senior, experienced nurse in charge of each shift, including nights.
  3. Fairness and equity – rotation of nights, weekends and holidays among all staff; no favouritism.
  4. Compliance with rules – working hours, weekly off, holidays and leave as per service rules; adequate rest between shifts.
  5. Advance posting – prepared and displayed at least one to two weeks in advance.
  6. Consideration of staff requests as far as possible (studies, family needs, health).
  7. Continuity – nurses work consecutive days in the same unit to know their patients.
  8. Limits on consecutive night duties and avoidance of a night duty immediately followed by a morning shift.
  9. Students and auxiliaries are rostered separately and never counted as replacements for qualified nurses.
  10. Changes only with the approval of the in-charge, recorded on the roster.

Types of scheduling

  • Centralised – prepared by the nursing office for all units (uniform, but less sensitive to unit needs).
  • Decentralised – prepared by each ward in-charge (responsive to unit needs).
  • Self-scheduling – staff choose their shifts within agreed rules; improves satisfaction.
  • Cyclical scheduling – a fixed pattern of shifts and offs repeats every few weeks; staff can plan their lives.
  • Fixed shifts (permanent mornings or nights) versus rotating shifts.

Steps in preparing a roster

  1. List all staff, their categories, leave sanctioned and training dates.
  2. Calculate the number of staff needed for each shift from workload and norms.
  3. Allocate the in-charge for each shift and distribute senior and junior staff.
  4. Assign weekly offs and nights fairly.
  5. Check for gaps, overlaps and fairness; adjust.
  6. Obtain approval, display the roster and keep a copy as a record.

Rotation of staff between units

  • Merits – broadens experience, develops versatility, provides relief from stressful units and helps staff replace one another.
  • Demerits – frequent rotation reduces continuity and expertise, especially in specialised units; staff need orientation in each new unit.
  • Policy – planned rotation at reasonable intervals, while retaining trained nurses in specialised units such as ICU and NICU for longer periods.

Conclusion A good duty roster provides competent staff in every shift with a fair distribution of nights, weekends and offs, prepared in advance according to rules and patient workload. Planned rotation develops staff while preserving continuity and expertise.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Differentiate between supervision and inspection.
answer_html:
Supervision Inspection
A continuous process of guiding, helping and teaching staff A periodic, often unannounced examination of work, facilities or records
Democratic, supportive and constructive Often authoritarian and fault-finding
Aims at improvement and growth of staff Aims at checking compliance with rules and standards
Involves a relationship of mutual trust Little personal relationship
Example: ward in-charge guiding a new nurse during a procedure Example: a council or accreditation inspection of the hospital
  • Modern nursing management prefers supportive supervision; inspections are still needed for statutory and accreditation purposes, and good supervision prepares a unit to meet them.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is a quality circle?
answer_html:
• A quality circle is a small group of about 6–12 employees from the same work area who meet voluntarily and regularly (for example, for an hour a week) to identify, analyse and solve problems related to their work, and present solutions to management.
  • The concept was developed by Kaoru Ishikawa in Japan in the early 1960s.
  • The group uses simple quality tools – brainstorming, cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagrams, check sheets and Pareto charts.
  • Nursing example – nurses of the dialysis unit form a quality circle to reduce delays in starting dialysis sessions.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is shared governance in nursing?
answer_html:
• Shared governance is a professional practice model in which staff nurses and nurse managers share authority and accountability for decisions about nursing practice, quality, education and research.
  • It works through unit practice councils and a hospital-wide nursing council in which staff nurses take part.

  • It is based on partnership, equity, accountability and ownership, and is associated with higher job satisfaction, retention and quality of care, as seen in "magnet" hospitals.

  • Example – a unit practice council of staff nurses reviews the pressure-injury prevention protocol, pilots changes and recommends them to the nursing council for adoption across the hospital.

question: (a) Define leadership and state the qualities of a nurse leader. (4 marks) (b) Explain the theories of leadership. (7 marks) (c) Explain the styles of leadership, with their merits and demerits. (4 marks)
