answer_html:
(a) Definition of leadership and qualities of a nurse leader (4 marks)

Definitions

  • Leadership is "the art or process of influencing people so that they will strive willingly and enthusiastically towards the achievement of group goals" (Koontz and Weihrich).
  • In nursing, leadership is the process of influencing nurses and the health team to provide safe, high-quality care and to improve nursing practice.

Leadership and management

  • Management is concerned with planning, organising, controlling and efficiency – "doing things right"; it relies on positional authority.
  • Leadership is concerned with vision, inspiration, influence and change – "doing the right things"; it may come from any position.
  • An effective nurse manager must also be a leader.

Qualities of a nurse leader

  1. Vision – a clear picture of better care and the ability to share it.
  2. Professional competence – sound knowledge and clinical expertise that earns respect.
  3. Integrity and honesty – ethical conduct that builds trust.
  4. Communication skills – listening, clarity, feedback and assertiveness.
  5. Emotional intelligence – self-awareness, self-control, empathy and social skills.
  6. Decision-making and problem-solving ability, including under pressure.
  7. Self-confidence and courage – to take responsibility and stand up for patients and staff.
  8. Fairness and respect for all team members.
  9. Ability to inspire and motivate, recognising others' contributions.
  10. Flexibility and openness to change; willingness to learn continuously.
  11. Team-building and delegation skills.
  12. Accountability – accepts responsibility for outcomes.

(b) Theories of leadership (7 marks)

1. Great man and trait theories

  • The great man theory held that leaders are born, not made – certain people are destined to lead.
  • Trait theory (studied by Stogdill and others) tried to identify personal traits of leaders – intelligence, initiative, self-confidence, dominance, sociability, energy and integrity.
  • Limitation – no consistent set of traits predicts leadership in all situations; traits alone do not explain effectiveness.

2. Behavioural theories – focus on what leaders do, implying that leadership can be learned.

  • Lewin, Lippitt and White (1939) – described autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire styles; democratic groups showed better morale and originality.
  • Ohio State studies – two dimensions of leader behaviour: initiating structure (task orientation – defining roles and standards) and consideration (relationship orientation – trust, respect, concern for staff); leaders high in both were most effective.
  • University of Michigan studies – job-centred versus employee-centred leaders; employee-centred leaders had more productive groups.
  • Managerial grid (Blake and Mouton, 1964) – plots concern for production against concern for people on a 9 × 9 grid: 1,1 impoverished, 1,9 country club, 9,1 authority–compliance (task), 5,5 middle-of-the-road and 9,9 team management – the ideal, with high concern for both.

3. Contingency and situational theories – the best style depends on the situation.

  • Fiedler's contingency model (1967) – effectiveness depends on matching the leader's style (task- or relationship-oriented, measured by the "least preferred co-worker" scale) with the situation – leader–member relations, task structure and position power. Task-oriented leaders do best in very favourable or very unfavourable situations; relationship-oriented leaders in moderately favourable ones.
  • Hersey and Blanchard's situational leadership – the leader adapts to the readiness (competence and commitment) of followers:
    • S1 Telling (directing) – for followers who are unable and unwilling or insecure (a new graduate in the ICU).
    • S2 Selling (coaching) – for followers who are willing but not yet able.
    • S3 Participating (supporting) – for followers who are able but lack confidence or motivation.
    • S4 Delegating – for followers who are able and willing (an experienced senior nurse).
  • House's path–goal theory (1971) – the leader helps followers achieve goals by clarifying the path and removing obstacles, using directive, supportive, participative or achievement-oriented behaviour according to the followers and the task.

4. Contemporary theories

  • Transactional leadership – based on an exchange: rewards for performance and correction of deviations ("management by exception"); maintains routine efficiency.
  • Transformational leadership (Burns, 1978; Bass) – the leader inspires followers to rise above self-interest for a shared vision through the "four Is" – idealised influence (role model), inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation and individualised consideration; associated with high staff satisfaction, retention and quality of care.
  • Servant leadership (Greenleaf) – the leader's first aim is to serve and develop others.
  • Authentic leadership – leaders who are self-aware, genuine, transparent and ethical.
  • Emotional intelligence and leadership (Goleman) – effective leaders use emotional intelligence and choose among styles such as visionary, coaching, affiliative, democratic, pacesetting and commanding.

(c) Styles of leadership (4 marks)

1. Autocratic (authoritarian)

  • The leader makes decisions alone, gives orders and expects obedience; close control.
  • Merits – quick decisions; useful in emergencies (cardiac arrest, disaster) and with inexperienced staff.
  • Demerits – low morale and creativity, dependence, resentment and high turnover.

2. Democratic (participative)

  • The leader involves staff in decisions, shares information and encourages suggestions, while retaining final responsibility.
  • Merits – high morale, commitment, creativity and acceptance of change; develops staff.
  • Demerits – slower decisions; not suitable in emergencies; may be seen as indecisive.

3. Laissez-faire (free-rein)

  • The leader gives minimum direction and leaves decisions to the group.
  • Merits – suits highly competent, self-motivated experts (a research team).
  • Demerits – confusion, lack of direction and poor productivity with ordinary groups.

4. Bureaucratic – the leader follows rules and procedures strictly. Merits: consistency and fairness. Demerits: rigidity and slowness.

5. Paternalistic – the leader acts like a parent, caring for staff but making decisions for them. Merits: loyalty and security. Demerits: dependence and lack of growth.

6. Situational – the leader uses the style appropriate to the situation and the followers – the most effective approach in nursing.

Choosing a leadership style in nursing – examples

  • During a cardiac arrest, the team leader uses a directive (autocratic) style – giving short, clear commands to named people – because speed and coordination save life.
  • When planning a new duty-roster pattern, the ward in-charge uses a democratic style, inviting all nurses to suggest and vote on options, because their acceptance determines success.
  • With an experienced specialist nurse running a wound-care clinic, the manager delegates – agreeing on goals and leaving the methods to the nurse.
  • With a newly joined graduate in the ICU, the in-charge uses telling and then selling (coaching) – close guidance, demonstration and explanation – and moves towards supporting and delegating as competence and confidence grow.

Developing as a leader – nurses become better leaders by seeking feedback, reflecting on their own behaviour, learning from role models and mentors, taking responsibility for small projects and committees, and continuing their education in management and leadership.

Nursing importance Leadership determines the climate of a ward – whether nurses feel supported, speak up about safety, accept change and stay in their jobs. Understanding leadership theories helps nurses choose the right approach for each situation and grow into effective leaders at every level.

Conclusion Leadership is the process of influencing people to work willingly towards goals, and nurse leaders need vision, competence, integrity, communication, emotional intelligence and fairness. Leadership has been explained by trait, behavioural (including the managerial grid), contingency and situational (Fiedler, Hersey–Blanchard, path–goal) and contemporary theories (transactional, transformational, servant and authentic leadership). Autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire and other styles each have merits and demerits, and the effective nurse leader adapts her style to the situation.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain conflict management in nursing – its sources, types, stages and strategies.
answer_html:
Definition Conflict is a disagreement between two or more people or groups arising from perceived incompatible goals, values, interests or actions. It is unavoidable in busy health-care settings and can be constructive (stimulating improvement) or destructive (harming teamwork and care).

Sources of conflict in nursing

  • Scarce resources – staff, beds, equipment, budget, leave.
  • Role ambiguity or overlap – unclear duties between nurses, doctors and other staff.
  • Communication failures – incomplete handover, misunderstanding of orders.
  • Differences in values, goals and priorities – for example, between patient safety and speed of discharge.
  • Work overload, stress and fatigue.
  • Unfair rosters, assignments or promotion decisions.
  • Hierarchy and power differences (nurse–doctor, senior–junior).
  • Personality differences and resistance to change.

Types

  • Intrapersonal – within a person (conflict between duty and family needs).
  • Interpersonal – between two people.
  • Intragroup – within a team.
  • Intergroup – between groups or departments (nursing and housekeeping).
  • Organisational – between staff and the organisation (policies, pay).
  • Functional (constructive) versus dysfunctional (destructive) conflict.

Stages (Pondy)

  1. Latent conflict – conditions that could lead to conflict exist (shortage of staff).
  2. Perceived conflict – people become aware of the problem.
  3. Felt conflict – emotions such as anger and anxiety develop.
  4. Manifest conflict – open behaviour – arguments, complaints, withdrawal.
  5. Conflict aftermath – the outcome, which may resolve the issue or leave resentment that leads to future conflict.

Strategies (Thomas–Kilmann modes)

  1. Competing (forcing) – one party wins, the other loses; useful in emergencies or when safety rules must be enforced.
  2. Accommodating (smoothing) – one party gives in to preserve harmony; useful when the issue matters more to the other party.
  3. Avoiding (withdrawing) – postponing or ignoring the issue; useful for trivial matters or to allow cooling down.
  4. Compromising – each side gives up something; useful when time is short.
  5. Collaborating (problem-solving) – both sides work together to find a win–win solution; best for important issues and long-term relationships. - Other approaches – negotiation, mediation by a neutral third person, and arbitration.

Steps in resolving a conflict

  1. Recognise the conflict early.
  2. Meet the parties privately and listen to each side.
  3. Gather facts; focus on the issue, not the person.
  4. Identify common goals and generate options together.
  5. Agree on a solution and responsibilities.
  6. Implement, follow up and evaluate.

Role of the nurse manager – prevent conflict through clear roles, fair policies, good communication and adequate resources; recognise conflict early; act as a mediator; model respectful behaviour; and use conflict constructively to improve systems.

Conclusion Conflict arises from scarce resources, unclear roles, poor communication, differing values and workload. It passes through latent, perceived, felt, manifest and aftermath stages and can be handled by competing, accommodating, avoiding, compromising or collaborating. Skilled nurse managers manage conflict early and constructively, preferring collaborative, win–win solutions.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain decision-making – its types, steps and techniques, with the role of the nurse manager.
answer_html:
Definition Decision-making is the process of identifying a problem or opportunity and choosing a course of action from among alternatives to achieve a desired goal. It is at the heart of all managerial functions.

Types of decisions

  • Programmed – routine, repetitive decisions guided by policies and procedures (indenting weekly supplies).
  • Non-programmed – new, complex or unique decisions requiring judgement (managing a sudden outbreak in the ward).
  • Individual and group decisions.
  • Strategic (top level, long-term), tactical (middle level) and operational (daily, first-line) decisions.
  • Decisions under certainty, risk (probabilities known) and uncertainty (outcomes unknown).

Steps of decision-making

  1. Identify and define the problem clearly.
  2. Gather information – facts, data, opinions, evidence and resources available.
  3. Generate alternatives – as many possible solutions as practical.
  4. Evaluate alternatives – advantages, disadvantages, costs, risks, feasibility, ethical and legal aspects.
  5. Select the best alternative.
  6. Implement the decision – communicate it, assign responsibilities, provide resources.
  7. Evaluate the results and modify if necessary.

Techniques and tools

  • Decision tree – a diagram showing alternatives, possible outcomes and their probabilities.
  • Decision grid (matrix) – alternatives are scored against weighted criteria.
  • SWOT analysis, cost–benefit analysis and PERT/Gantt charts for planning decisions.
  • Group techniques
    • Brainstorming – free generation of ideas without criticism.
    • Nominal group technique – individuals write ideas silently, share them in turn, discuss and vote.
    • Delphi technique – experts give opinions anonymously in repeated rounds until consensus is reached.
    • Consensus decision-making.
  • Evidence-based practice and critical thinking.

Barriers – inadequate or wrong information, time pressure, personal bias and emotions, fear of risk, habit, pressure from superiors, and groupthink in groups.

Role of the nurse manager

  • Make sound, timely decisions about patient care, staffing, resources and safety.
  • Involve staff in decisions that affect them; use group techniques for complex problems.
  • Base decisions on evidence, policies and ethics; document them.
  • Accept responsibility for decisions and evaluate their outcomes.

Conclusion Decision-making is choosing the best course of action among alternatives through a systematic process of defining the problem, gathering information, generating and evaluating alternatives, selecting, implementing and evaluating. Tools such as decision trees, grids, brainstorming, nominal group and Delphi techniques help nurse managers make better, more acceptable decisions.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain planned change in nursing, with reference to Lewin's change theory and the management of resistance to change.
answer_html:
Definition

  • Change is the process of making something different from what it was.
  • Planned change is a deliberate, systematic and collaborative effort to bring about an improvement, managed by a change agent (often a nurse leader).
  • Examples – introducing bedside handover, electronic nursing records, a new care delivery system or a fall-prevention programme.

Lewin's change theory (Kurt Lewin, 1951)

  • Force field analysis – any situation is held in balance by driving forces (pushing for change – evidence, administrative support, patient complaints) and restraining forces (resisting change – fear, extra work, lack of skills). Change occurs when driving forces are strengthened or restraining forces are weakened. 1. Unfreezing – creating awareness of the need for change: sharing data (such as errors during handover), explaining benefits, reducing fears and building support. 2. Moving (changing) – implementing the change: planning, training, providing resources, involving staff, piloting and giving support and feedback. 3. Refreezing – stabilising the change so that it becomes the new norm: revising policies and procedures, continued monitoring, reinforcement and recognition.

Other models (in brief)

  • Lippitt's phases of change – diagnosing the problem, assessing motivation and capacity for change, assessing the change agent's resources, setting progressive objectives, choosing the change agent's role, maintaining the change and ending the helping relationship.
  • Rogers' diffusion of innovations – people adopt change at different rates: innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority and laggards; early adopters can be used as champions.

Resistance to change

  • Causes – fear of the unknown, loss of status or security, habit and comfort with the old way, lack of information, extra workload, lack of trust in management, poor timing and peer pressure.
  • Ways of overcoming resistance (Kotter and Schlesinger)
    1. Education and communication – explain the reasons and benefits.
    2. Participation and involvement – involve staff in planning.
    3. Facilitation and support – training, resources and emotional support.
    4. Negotiation and agreement – offer incentives or adjustments.
    5. Manipulation and co-optation – giving key resisters a role (used carefully).
    6. Explicit or implicit coercion – only as a last resort, for example when safety demands it.

Example – introducing bedside handover

  • Unfreezing – share incidents caused by poor handover, show evidence that bedside handover improves safety and involves patients.
  • Moving – form a working group, develop a structured format (such as SBAR), train staff, pilot in one ward, address concerns about time and confidentiality.
  • Refreezing – include it in the nursing procedure manual, audit compliance, recognise good practice and extend it to other wards.

Role of the nurse leader as change agent – identify the need for change, gather evidence, build a coalition of supporters, plan and communicate, manage resistance with empathy, provide training and resources, monitor and sustain the change.

Conclusion Planned change is a deliberate, systematic process best understood through Lewin's unfreezing, moving and refreezing stages and force field analysis. Resistance is natural and is reduced by education, participation, support and negotiation, enabling nurse leaders to introduce lasting improvements.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain power and empowerment in nursing.
answer_html:
1. Power

  • Definition – power is the ability to influence the behaviour of others to achieve desired outcomes.
  • Authority is the legitimate right to give orders that comes with a position; power may exist with or without formal authority.
  • Sources (bases) of power – French and Raven
    1. Legitimate power – from one's position (Nursing Superintendent, ward in-charge).
    2. Reward power – ability to give rewards (good rosters, recommendations, recognition).
    3. Coercive power – ability to punish (warnings, disciplinary action).
    4. Expert power – from knowledge and skill (a respected critical-care nurse).
    5. Referent power – from personal qualities that make others admire and identify with the person.
    6. Later additions – information power (access to valuable information) and connection power (links with influential people).
  • Expert and referent power produce the most willing cooperation; over-use of coercive power produces fear and resentment.

2. Politics

  • Organisational politics – activities by which people acquire, develop and use power to obtain preferred outcomes – networking, forming coalitions, negotiating and lobbying.
  • Positive use in nursing – influencing hospital decisions on staffing and resources, advocating for patients, and participating in health policy through professional organisations; it must remain ethical, transparent and patient-centred, avoiding manipulation.

3. Empowerment

  • Definition – the process of giving people the authority, resources, information and support to make decisions and act, and of building their confidence to use them.
  • Structural empowerment (Kanter) – access to information, support, resources and opportunities to learn and grow within the organisation.
  • Psychological empowerment – the person's sense of meaning in work, competence, self-determination (autonomy) and impact.
  • Strategies to empower nurses
    • Education and continuous professional development.
    • Participatory management and shared governance; representation on hospital committees.
    • Autonomy in nursing practice – nurse-led protocols, clear scope of practice.
    • Access to information and resources; supportive leadership and mentoring.
    • Recognition and fair rewards; strong professional organisations.
  • Benefits – higher job satisfaction and commitment, less burnout and turnover, more innovation, better patient outcomes and a stronger professional voice.

Conclusion Power is the ability to influence others and arises from legitimate, reward, coercive, expert, referent, information and connection bases. Used ethically, power and politics allow nurses to advocate for patients and staff. Empowerment gives nurses the structures and confidence to act, improving both their work life and the quality of care.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain negotiation – its types, principles and process, with examples from nursing.
answer_html:
Definition Negotiation is a process in which two or more parties with different needs or views discuss an issue in order to reach a mutually acceptable agreement.

Types

  • Distributive (win–lose) negotiation – the parties compete to divide a fixed amount (a fixed budget); one gains what the other loses.
  • Integrative (win–win) negotiation – the parties work together to find solutions that satisfy the interests of both; preferred in health care because relationships continue.

Principled negotiation (Fisher and Ury)

  1. Separate the people from the problem – deal with emotions and relationships respectfully, and attack the problem, not the person.
  2. Focus on interests, not positions – find out why each party wants something.
  3. Invent options for mutual gain – brainstorm several solutions before deciding.
  4. Insist on objective criteria – use norms, data, policies and evidence.
  5. Know your BATNA – the "best alternative to a negotiated agreement", which tells you when to walk away.

Process (stages)

  1. Preparation – collect facts and data, define objectives and priorities, decide the minimum acceptable outcome, understand the other party's interests and choose the time and place.
  2. Opening and exchange of information – state the issue and interests calmly; listen to the other side.
  3. Bargaining – present proposals, discuss options, make and request concessions, and look for common ground.
  4. Closing – agree on the solution and put it in writing.
  5. Implementation and follow-up – carry out the agreement and review it.

Skills needed – active listening, clear and assertive communication, emotional control, patience, flexibility, persuasion using evidence and respect for the other party.

Examples in nursing

  • A Nursing Superintendent negotiates with the hospital administration for additional nurses for a new ICU, using workload data and norms.
  • A ward in-charge negotiates with a nurse about leave during a period of shortage, agreeing on alternative dates.
  • Nurses and doctors negotiate a nurse-initiated protocol for early removal of urinary catheters.
  • Negotiating with suppliers on the price and maintenance terms of equipment.

Conclusion Negotiation is reaching agreement between parties with different interests. Using integrative, principled negotiation – separating people from the problem, focusing on interests, creating options, using objective criteria and knowing the BATNA – nurse managers can resolve problems and obtain resources while preserving relationships.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain leadership development in nursing, including leadership competencies, mentorship and succession planning.
answer_html:
Introduction Leaders are developed, not only born. Because nurse leaders are needed at every level – from shift in-charge to Chief Nursing Officer – organisations must deliberately prepare nurses for leadership.

Leadership competencies for nurse leaders

  • Communication and relationship management – building trust, teamwork and collaboration with other professionals.
  • Knowledge of the health-care environment – clinical practice, patient safety, quality, health policy and regulation.
  • Leadership skills – vision, decision-making, change management, conflict resolution, delegation.
  • Professionalism – ethics, accountability, advocacy and lifelong learning.
  • Business skills – financial management, human resource management, use of information technology and data.

Methods of leadership development

  1. Formal education – post-graduate programmes in nursing administration, hospital or health management.
  2. Leadership and management training – workshops on supervision, communication, rostering, budgeting, quality improvement.
  3. Mentorship – a long-term relationship in which an experienced leader (mentor) guides, advises and supports a less experienced nurse (mentee) in career and leadership growth.
  4. Coaching – focused, short-term help to improve specific skills, such as conducting meetings or giving feedback.
  5. Preceptorship – one-to-one support of newly appointed nurses by experienced nurses during their transition, which also develops the preceptor's leadership skills.
  6. Job rotation and acting assignments – giving nurses temporary charge of a shift or ward, membership of committees and responsibility for projects.
  7. 360-degree feedback and reflective practice to identify strengths and development needs.
  8. Self-development – reading, professional associations, conferences and research.

Succession planning

  • Definition – a planned process of identifying and developing staff with potential to fill key leadership positions in the future, so that the organisation is not left without leaders when senior nurses retire or leave.
  • Steps – identify critical positions, identify high-potential staff, assess their development needs, provide training, mentoring and acting opportunities, and review progress regularly.

Role of senior nurse leaders – act as role models and mentors, identify and encourage potential leaders, create opportunities for responsibility, provide feedback, and support further education.

Conclusion Leadership development prepares nurses with communication, clinical and health-care knowledge, leadership, professionalism and business competencies through education, training, mentorship, coaching, preceptorship, acting assignments and feedback. Succession planning ensures a continuous supply of capable nurse leaders.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is transformational leadership?
answer_html:
• Transformational leadership, described by James MacGregor Burns (1978) and developed by Bernard Bass, is a style in which the leader inspires and motivates followers to achieve a shared vision and to perform beyond their own expectations.
  • Four components ("four Is") – idealised influence (acting as a trusted role model), inspirational motivation (communicating a compelling vision), intellectual stimulation (encouraging new ideas) and individualised consideration (attention to each person's needs and growth).
  • In nursing it is associated with higher job satisfaction, retention, teamwork and quality of care; it contrasts with transactional leadership, which is based on rewards and corrections.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: List the bases of power described by French and Raven.
answer_html:
French and Raven (1959) described five bases of power, later extended:

  1. Legitimate power – from position or formal authority.
  2. Reward power – from the ability to give rewards.
  3. Coercive power – from the ability to punish.
  4. Expert power – from special knowledge and skill.
  5. Referent power – from personal qualities that make others admire and identify with the person. - Later additions – information power (Raven) and connection power (links with influential people). - Expert and referent power are the most effective for nurse leaders because they produce willing cooperation.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is the managerial grid?
answer_html:
• The managerial grid, developed by Robert Blake and Jane Mouton (1964), describes leadership styles according to two dimensions – concern for production (tasks) and concern for people – each rated from 1 to 9.
  • Main styles – 1,1 impoverished (low concern for both); 1,9 country club (high people, low task); 9,1 authority–compliance (high task, low people); 5,5 middle-of-the-road (moderate balance); 9,9 team management (high concern for both).
  • The 9,9 team management style is considered the most effective, as it achieves goals through committed, involved staff.

question: (a) Define controlling and explain the steps of the control process. (5 marks) (b) Explain the techniques of control used in the nursing service. (4 marks) (c) Define nursing audit and explain its types, method and uses. (6 marks)

revised procedures) or revise standards → feedback to planning

answer_html:
(a) Controlling – definition and steps of the control process (5 marks)

Definition

  • Controlling is "the measurement and correction of performance in order to make sure that enterprise objectives and the plans devised to attain them are accomplished" (Koontz and O'Donnell).
  • In nursing, control ensures that nursing care and the use of resources conform to the standards and plans of the nursing service.

Characteristics

  • Closely linked with planning – plans provide the standards; control shows whether plans are being achieved and feeds back into new plans.
  • Continuous and pervasive – every manager controls, at every level.
  • Forward-looking – the aim is to correct and prevent, not merely to find fault.
  • Action-oriented – control is incomplete without corrective action.

Steps of the control process

  1. Establishing standards
    • Standards are criteria against which performance is measured; they may be quantitative (nurse–patient ratio, hand-hygiene compliance of at least 90%, zero wrong-patient errors) or qualitative (dignity and courtesy to patients).
    • Structure standards (staff, equipment, facilities), process standards (procedures, documentation) and outcome standards (infection rates, falls, patient satisfaction).
    • Sources – INC and professional standards, accreditation (NABH, National Quality Assurance Standards), hospital policies and procedure manuals, evidence-based guidelines.
  2. Measuring actual performance
    • By personal observation, rounds, review of records and reports, audits, quality indicators, incident reports, patient feedback and appraisal.
    • Measurement must be accurate, timely and objective, at critical control points.
  3. Comparing performance with standards
    • Identify deviations and their causes; minor variations within acceptable limits need no action.
    • Management by exception – managers concentrate on significant deviations rather than on everything.
  4. Taking corrective action
    • Remove the causes – training, supervision, additional staff or equipment, revised procedures, motivation or discipline.
    • If standards are unrealistic, revise the standards or the plan.

Types of control according to timing

  • Feedforward (preventive) control – before the activity: checking equipment, competency of staff, availability of supplies.
  • Concurrent control – during the activity: supervision, checklists such as the surgical safety checklist.
  • Feedback control – after the activity: audits, analysis of incidents and patient satisfaction surveys.

(b) Techniques of control in the nursing service (4 marks)

  1. Personal observation and supervision – the oldest and most direct technique.
  2. Nursing rounds – by ward in-charges and supervisors to check care, environment, equipment and records.
  3. Policies, procedures, protocols and checklists – standing plans that guide and control practice.
  4. Records and reports – census, nursing reports, incident reports, registers and statistics (bed occupancy, infection rates).
  5. Budgetary control – comparing actual expenditure with the budget and analysing variances.
  6. Nursing audit and quality indicators – falls, pressure injuries, medication errors, catheter- and line-associated infections, displayed on dashboards.
  7. Performance appraisal of staff.
  8. Patient satisfaction surveys and complaint analysis.
  9. Incident reporting and root cause analysis of serious events.
  10. Network techniques – PERT and CPM for projects; Gantt charts.
  11. Management information systems – computerised data for monitoring.
  12. Inventory control – ABC, VED and stock verification.

(c) Nursing audit (6 marks)

Definition

  • Nursing audit is a systematic, formal process of evaluating the quality of nursing care by reviewing patients' records and care against pre-determined criteria and standards, in order to identify deficiencies and improve care.
  • Maria Phaneuf defined it as "the evaluation of the quality of clinical nursing as reflected in the patient-care records for discharged patients".

Purposes

  • To evaluate the quality of nursing care and documentation.
  • To identify strengths and deficiencies and their causes.
  • To provide a basis for improvement, in-service education and policy changes.
  • To promote accountability and professional standards; to support accreditation and legal defence.

Types

  1. Retrospective audit – evaluation after the patient is discharged, mainly by reviewing records (for example, Phaneuf's nursing audit method).
    • Advantages – easy to organise, covers many records. Limitation – depends on the quality of documentation; deficiencies are found after the event.
  2. Concurrent audit – evaluation while the patient is receiving care, through observation of care, interviews with patients and staff, and review of records (for example, the Quality Patient Care Scale and the Slater Nursing Competencies Rating Scale).
    • Advantage – allows immediate correction. Limitation – time-consuming; staff may change behaviour when observed.
  3. Internal (by the institution's own staff, often peer review) and external (by outside agencies, such as accreditation assessors) audits.

Phaneuf's nursing audit method

  • Fifty items grouped under seven functions of nursing – (1) application and execution of the physician's legal orders; (2) observation of symptoms and reactions; (3) supervision of the patient; (4) supervision of those participating in care; (5) reporting and recording; (6) application and execution of nursing procedures and techniques; (7) promotion of physical and emotional health by direction and teaching.
  • Each item is scored from the record, and the total score (0–200) is rated as excellent (161–200), good (121–160), incomplete (81–120), poor (41–80) or unsafe (0–40).

Method – the audit cycle

  1. Form an audit committee – senior nurses, nurse educator, quality nurse and representatives of wards.
  2. Select the topic – high-risk, high-volume or problem-prone areas (medication administration, pressure-injury prevention, pre-operative care, documentation).
  3. Set criteria and standards – measurable, based on evidence and policies (for example, "fall-risk assessment documented within 4 hours of admission in 100% of patients").
  4. Prepare the audit tool – checklist or scale; decide the sample (number of records or patients) and period.
  5. Collect data – review records, observe care, interview patients.
  6. Analyse and compare results with standards; identify gaps and causes.
  7. Report and discuss findings with staff in a non-punitive manner.
  8. Implement changes – training, revised procedures, resources.
  9. Re-audit after an interval to see whether care has improved – "closing the loop".

Uses

  • Improves the quality and safety of care and of documentation.
  • Identifies training needs for in-service education.
  • Provides data for performance appraisal, staffing and budget proposals.
  • Supports accreditation, research and evidence-based practice.
  • Encourages professional accountability and peer review.

Limitations – depends on complete and honest records; time-consuming; staff may feel threatened; good documentation does not always mean good care.

Characteristics of an effective control system – it is accurate and timely, focused on critical points, understandable to staff, economical, flexible enough for changing conditions, acceptable to the people controlled and, above all, it leads to corrective action; it emphasises learning rather than blame, so that staff report problems openly.

Nursing importance Without control, standards remain only on paper. Regular measurement, nursing audit and timely corrective action allow nurse managers to detect problems early, prove the quality of nursing care and continuously improve it.

Conclusion Controlling is the measurement and correction of performance to ensure that objectives are achieved; it involves setting standards, measuring performance, comparing it with standards and taking corrective action, using feedforward, concurrent and feedback controls. Techniques include observation, rounds, records, budgets, audits, indicators, appraisal, patient surveys, incident reporting and network methods. Nursing audit – retrospective or concurrent, such as Phaneuf's method – systematically evaluates care against standards through an audit cycle that ends with re-audit.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain performance appraisal of nursing personnel – its purposes, methods, process and common errors.
answer_html:
Definition Performance appraisal is the systematic evaluation of an employee's performance and potential against the requirements of the job, carried out periodically by the superior (and others), for decisions about development, rewards and placement.

Purposes

  • To give staff feedback on their strengths and weaknesses.
  • To identify training and development needs.
  • To provide a basis for promotion, confirmation, increments, transfer and rewards.
  • To improve performance and motivation; to set future goals.
  • To validate selection and training methods; to maintain records.

Methods

  1. Traditional methods
    • Confidential reports – the annual report by the superior; in government service, the Annual Performance Assessment Report (APAR), with a self-appraisal section.
    • Graphic rating scale – rating of traits and work qualities (knowledge, skill, punctuality, initiative) on a scale.
    • Checklist – a list of behaviours marked "yes" or "no".
    • Ranking, paired comparison and forced distribution – comparing employees with one another.
    • Critical incident method – recording examples of very good or poor behaviour during the period.
    • Essay (narrative) method – a written description of performance.
  2. Modern methods
    • Management by objectives – appraisal against jointly set objectives.
    • Behaviourally anchored rating scales (BARS) – rating points described by specific behaviours.
    • 360-degree feedback – from superiors, peers, subordinates, self and patients.
    • Self-appraisal and assessment centres.

Process

  1. Establish performance standards from the job description and communicate them in advance.
  2. Observe and collect data throughout the period (anecdotal records, audits, incident reports).
  3. Evaluate performance against standards using the chosen tool.
  4. Conduct an appraisal interview – private, two-way discussion; begin with strengths; discuss areas for improvement with facts; listen to the employee.
  5. Agree on a development plan and goals for the next period.
  6. Follow up with support and review.

Common errors (biases)

  • Halo effect – one good trait influences the rating of all others; horn effect – one poor trait lowers all ratings.
  • Leniency (rating everyone high) and strictness (rating everyone low).
  • Central tendency – rating everyone average.
  • Recency effect – judging only on recent events.
  • Personal bias – favouritism, prejudice, similarity to the rater.

Essentials of a good appraisal system – clear, job-related criteria; trained, fair appraisers; regular, documented observation; employee participation; confidentiality; and use of results for development, not only for control.

Conclusion Performance appraisal systematically evaluates staff performance for feedback, development and personnel decisions, using traditional methods such as APAR, rating scales and critical incidents and modern methods such as MBO, BARS and 360-degree feedback. A fair process with good appraisal interviews and awareness of rating errors makes appraisal a tool for growth rather than fear.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain PERT and CPM as tools of planning and control, with an example.
answer_html:
Introduction Network techniques show a project as a network of activities and events, making clear the sequence, dependence and time of each activity. The two main techniques are PERT and CPM.

1. PERT (Programme Evaluation and Review Technique)

  • Developed in 1958 for the US Navy's Polaris missile project.
  • Event-oriented and used when activity times are uncertain.
  • Uses three time estimates for each activity – optimistic (a), most likely (m) and pessimistic (b) – and calculates the expected time: tₑ = (a + 4m + b) ÷ 6.
  • Example – purchase of ICU equipment: a = 8, m = 10, b = 14 weeks, so tₑ = (8 + 40 + 14) ÷ 6 ≈ 10.3 weeks.

2. CPM (Critical Path Method)

  • Developed in 1957 by DuPont for construction and maintenance projects.
  • Activity-oriented, used when times are known with reasonable certainty; it also considers cost–time trade-offs (spending more to shorten an activity).
  • The critical path is the longest path through the network; activities on it have no slack (float), so any delay in them delays the whole project.

Steps (common to both)

  1. List all activities of the project.
  2. Determine their sequence and dependencies (which must be completed before others can start).
  3. Draw the network diagram – arrows for activities, circles (nodes) for events.
  4. Estimate time for each activity.
  5. Identify the critical path and calculate slack for other activities.
  6. Monitor progress, giving priority to critical activities, and update the network.

Example – commissioning a new 10-bed ICU

  • A – administrative approval and budget: 4 weeks.
  • B – civil and electrical work (after A): 8 weeks.
  • C – purchase of equipment (after A): 10 weeks.
  • D – recruitment of nurses (after A): 6 weeks.
  • E – training of nurses (after D): 4 weeks.
  • F – installation of equipment (after B and C): 2 weeks.
  • G – commissioning and mock drill (after E and F): 1 week.
  • Paths – A–B–F–G = 15 weeks; A–C–F–G = 17 weeks; A–D–E–G = 15 weeks.
  • The critical path is A–C–F–G (17 weeks); the nurse manager must closely monitor equipment purchase, while recruitment and training have two weeks of slack.

Uses in nursing – planning new units, shifting a hospital, accreditation preparation, conferences and CNE programmes, research projects, mass vaccination campaigns and disaster drills.

Advantages – clear picture of the whole project and interdependence; identification of critical activities; better use of time and resources; useful for control and reporting.

Limitations – time estimates may be inaccurate; complex for very large projects; needs updating and skill.

Conclusion PERT and CPM are network techniques that plan and control projects by showing activities, their sequence and time. PERT uses three time estimates for uncertain activities, while CPM identifies the critical path of known activities, helping nurse managers complete projects on time.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain the measurement of patient satisfaction and its use in improving nursing care.
tags: factors influencing patient satisfaction with nursing
answer_html:
Definition Patient satisfaction is the patient's evaluation of the care received in relation to his or her expectations. It is an important outcome indicator of the quality of care, alongside clinical outcomes.

Importance

  • Reflects the patient's experience of nursing care – communication, respect, comfort and responsiveness.
  • Satisfied patients are more likely to follow treatment advice, return for follow-up and recommend the hospital.
  • Dissatisfaction is an early warning of problems and a common cause of complaints and legal action.
  • Required by accreditation and quality programmes (NABH, National Quality Assurance Standards).

Factors influencing satisfaction with nursing

  • Nurses' communication and courtesy; responsiveness to call bells and requests.
  • Pain management and comfort; information about care, medicines and discharge.
  • Respect, privacy and dignity; involvement in decisions.
  • Cleanliness, food, noise, waiting time and cost.

Methods of measurement

  1. Questionnaires/surveys – usually with a Likert scale, given at discharge or by telephone after discharge; standard tools such as the Newcastle Satisfaction with Nursing Scales.
  2. Exit interviews of patients and attendants.
  3. Electronic feedback – the Ministry of Health's "Mera Aspataal" (My Hospital) initiative (2016) collects feedback from patients of public hospitals through SMS, outbound calls, a mobile application and a web portal.
  4. Suggestion boxes and complaint registers; analysis of complaints and compliments.
  5. Focus group discussions and patient advisory groups.
  6. Patient rounds by nurse managers – talking to patients during rounds.
  7. Online reviews and social media monitoring.

Steps in a satisfaction survey

  • Decide objectives; select or develop a valid, reliable tool in the local language; choose the sample; administer the tool confidentially; analyse results; report them to staff; plan and implement improvements; repeat the survey.

Use of results to improve nursing care

  • Identify specific problem areas (for example, poor explanation of medicines at discharge) and plan action – training, discharge-teaching checklists, changes in routines.
  • Give feedback to staff and recognise units and nurses praised by patients.
  • Track trends over time and link them with quality indicators.

Limitations – patients may hesitate to criticise; high expectations or illiteracy affect responses; surveys may be biased if handled by the same staff; satisfaction does not always reflect clinical quality.

Conclusion Patient satisfaction is the patient's evaluation of care against expectations and is a key outcome of nursing quality. It is measured through surveys, interviews, electronic feedback such as Mera Aspataal, complaints and rounds, and the results are used to improve nursing practice and recognise good care.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain nursing rounds as a tool of supervision and control.
answer_html:
Definition A nursing round (supervisory round) is a planned visit by a nurse manager to patients and units to observe and evaluate nursing care, the environment, staff, equipment and records, to guide staff and to solve problems.

Purposes

  • To ensure that patients receive safe, high-quality care according to standards.
  • To supervise, guide and support staff and students.
  • To identify problems in staffing, supplies, equipment and environment.
  • To maintain communication between management, staff and patients.
  • To check records, safety measures and infection control.

Types

  • Daily rounds by the ward in-charge – at the beginning of the shift and at intervals.
  • Supervisory rounds by Assistant/Deputy Nursing Superintendents and the Nursing Superintendent.
  • Night rounds by the night supervisor.
  • Special rounds – infection-control rounds, patient-safety (leadership) walk rounds, fire-safety rounds, documentation rounds.
  • Intentional (hourly) rounding by nurses – regular visits to each patient to check pain, position, toilet needs and that possessions and the call bell are within reach, which reduces falls and call-bell use.

Planning a round

  • Set objectives for the round; prepare a checklist (patient care, records, equipment, environment, staff); choose a suitable time (and occasionally an unannounced time); review previous reports and pending problems.

Conduct of the round

  1. Greet staff and receive a brief report from the in-charge.
  2. Visit patients – observe their condition, comfort and safety; talk to them and their attendants about their care.
  3. Observe care and procedures; check emergency equipment, drugs, supplies and cleanliness.
  4. Review records – nursing notes, medication charts, care plans, incident reports.
  5. Discuss problems with staff, offer guidance and teach on the spot.
  6. Appreciate good work publicly; correct mistakes privately and tactfully.
  7. Record findings and decisions in the round book or report; assign responsibility and dates for follow-up.

Follow-up – act on problems found (indents, repairs, staffing changes, training) and check at the next round that they have been resolved.

Benefits – early detection of problems, better standards and accountability, support for staff, improved patient satisfaction and safety, and visible leadership.

Problems – rounds that are only fault-finding create fear; hurried or irregular rounds miss problems; lack of follow-up reduces credibility.

Conclusion Nursing rounds are planned visits by nurse managers to observe care, guide staff and solve problems. Well-planned rounds with checklists, respectful conduct, documentation and follow-up are among the most effective tools of supervision and control.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is 360-degree feedback?
answer_html:
• 360-degree feedback is a method of performance appraisal in which an employee receives feedback from all directions – superiors, peers, subordinates, self-appraisal and sometimes patients – rather than only from the immediate superior.
  • Advantages – a more complete and balanced picture of performance, especially of communication, teamwork and leadership; useful for leadership development.

  • Limitations – time-consuming, needs anonymity and trust, and raters may be biased; it is best used for development rather than for pay or promotion decisions.

  • In nursing it is increasingly used for ward in-charges and supervisors, whose leadership is best judged by the people they lead and work with.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is the halo effect in performance appraisal?
answer_html:
• The halo effect is a rating error in which one outstanding quality of an employee influences the appraiser to rate all other qualities highly, regardless of actual performance – for example, a pleasant, well-dressed nurse being rated high on clinical skills she has not shown.
  • The opposite is the horn effect, where one poor trait lowers all ratings.

  • Prevention – rate each quality separately against clear criteria, record specific observations through the year, use several raters and train appraisers.

  • It reduces the fairness and usefulness of appraisal, because real weaknesses are not identified for training.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is the critical path?
answer_html:
• The critical path is the longest sequence of dependent activities in a project network, which determines the minimum time needed to complete the project.
  • Activities on the critical path have zero slack (float) – any delay in them delays the whole project – whereas other activities can be delayed within their slack.

  • Identifying the critical path helps the nurse manager give priority and close monitoring to these activities, for example the purchase of equipment when setting up a new ICU.

  • The project can be shortened only by reducing the time of critical activities (for example, by paying for faster delivery), not of non-critical ones.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: (a) Define group and group dynamics. (2 marks) (b) Explain the stages of group development and the factors that influence group behaviour. (6 marks) (c) Explain committees – their types and functions – and the conduct of an effective meeting. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Tuckman's stages of group development
labels: dependent on leader) → storming (conflict over roles and ideas) → norming (agreement on norms and roles
group disbands); leader's style shifts from directing to coaching to supporting to delegating

answer_html:
(a) Definitions (2 marks)

  • A group is two or more persons who interact, depend on one another and work together to achieve common goals, and who see themselves as members of the group – for example, the nursing team of a ward.
  • Group dynamics (a term popularised by Kurt Lewin) refers to the forces, processes and interactions operating within a group – communication, roles, norms, cohesion, leadership and conflict – that influence its behaviour and performance.
  • Types of groups – formal groups created by the organisation (command groups such as the ward team; task groups such as committees) and informal groups formed by members themselves (friendship and interest groups); also primary and secondary groups.

(b) Stages of group development and factors influencing group behaviour (6 marks)

Stages (Bruce Tuckman, 1965; adjourning added in 1977)

  1. Forming – members come together and get to know one another; they are polite, uncertain and dependent on the leader; goals and roles are not yet clear.
    • Leader's role – give clear direction, explain the purpose, set ground rules, introduce members.
  2. Storming – conflicts arise over roles, ideas, leadership and methods; members may resist the task.
    • Leader's role – manage conflict openly, encourage listening, clarify roles and keep the focus on goals.
  3. Norming – members agree on norms, roles and ways of working; trust and cohesion develop.
    • Leader's role – encourage participation, recognise contributions, share leadership.
  4. Performing – the group works productively and interdependently, solving problems and achieving goals.
    • Leader's role – delegate, support and remove obstacles.
  5. Adjourning – the task is completed and the group disbands (for example, a committee set up to plan Nurses' Day); members may feel loss.
    • Leader's role – evaluate achievements, recognise members and close formally.

Factors influencing group behaviour (group dynamics)

  1. Size – small groups (5–7) allow participation; large groups need more structure and may split into sub-groups.
  2. Composition – mix of skills, experience, age and personalities; diversity brings ideas but may increase conflict.
  3. Goals – clear, shared and accepted goals unite the group.
  4. Norms – the unwritten rules of behaviour accepted by members (punctuality, helping one another).
  5. Roles (Benne and Sheats)
    • Task roles – initiator, information seeker, coordinator, evaluator.
    • Maintenance roles – encourager, harmoniser, gatekeeper, compromiser.
    • Self-serving (individual) roles that harm the group – aggressor, blocker, dominator, recognition seeker.
  6. Status – differences in status affect participation and communication.
  7. Cohesiveness – the degree to which members are attracted to the group and want to stay in it; increased by frequent interaction, shared goals, success, small size and outside threats. High cohesion improves performance when group norms support organisational goals.
  8. Leadership and communication patterns.
  9. Environment and organisational support – workload, time, rewards and physical setting.
  10. Group problems – groupthink (pressure for agreement suppresses critical thinking) and social loafing (some members put in less effort in a group).

Characteristics of an effective group – clear goals, open communication, mutual trust and respect, shared leadership, constructive handling of conflict, decisions by participation, regular evaluation of its own working, and high commitment.

(c) Committees and the conduct of an effective meeting (7 marks)

Definition – a committee is a group of persons appointed or elected to consider, discuss, decide, recommend or report on matters referred to it.

Types

  1. Standing (permanent) committees – continue indefinitely and meet regularly, such as the infection control committee, pharmacy and therapeutics committee, quality and patient-safety committee, nursing procedure committee and purchase committee.
  2. Ad hoc (special) committees – formed for a specific purpose and dissolved when it is achieved, such as an inquiry committee or a committee to plan an accreditation visit.
  3. Executive (line) committees – have authority to make decisions.
  4. Advisory (staff) committees – only recommend.
  5. Formal and informal committees; sub-committees for parts of a task.

Functions

  • Advisory – giving expert advice; decision-making; coordination between departments; communication and sharing of information; problem-solving; review and recommendation of policies; inquiry into incidents.

Advantages – pooled knowledge and judgement, coordination, participation and representation of different groups, greater acceptance of decisions and training of members.

Disadvantages – time-consuming and costly, delays, compromise decisions, divided responsibility and domination by a few members.

Committees with nursing participation – infection control, pharmacy and therapeutics, ethics, quality and patient safety, disaster management, purchase and condemnation, grievance, Internal Committee (prevention of sexual harassment), nursing procedure, nursing education and welfare committees.

Conduct of an effective meeting

  1. Before the meeting
    • Clarify the purpose; decide date, time and venue.
    • Prepare and circulate the agenda and relevant papers in advance.
    • Ensure members are informed and that a quorum (minimum number required) will be present.
  2. During the meeting
    • The chairperson begins on time, welcomes members, and confirms the minutes of the previous meeting and the action taken.
    • Discussion follows the agenda; the chairperson encourages all members to speak, keeps to the topic and the time limit, manages disagreements and avoids domination by individuals.
    • Decisions are summarised clearly with responsibilities and deadlines; other matters are taken up with the chairperson's permission.
  3. After the meeting
    • The secretary (convenor) prepares the minutes – date, time, venue, members present and absent, items discussed, decisions taken, persons responsible and time limits – gets them approved by the chairperson and circulates them.
    • Follow-up of decisions and an action-taken report at the next meeting.

Roles

  • Chairperson – leads the meeting, ensures order and fair participation, and sums up decisions.
  • Secretary (convenor) – prepares the agenda, notices and minutes, keeps records and follows up actions.
  • Members – come prepared, participate constructively, respect others and carry out assigned tasks.

Building an effective ward team – practical measures for the nurse manager

  • Hold a short team meeting at the start of each shift to share the plan, high-risk patients and expected admissions.
  • Clarify roles – who is in charge, who covers which patients, who responds to emergencies – and rotate leadership roles so that everyone grows.
  • Agree on team norms – punctuality, helping one another during peaks, respectful communication, speaking up about safety.
  • Recognise team achievements (for example, a month without falls) as well as individual work.
  • Deal with conflicts early and privately, focusing on the issue.
  • Involve the team in solving unit problems through brief huddles, suggestion schemes or quality circles.
  • Include new staff and students warmly and assign them a buddy.

Example of the stages in a ward – when a new dialysis unit opens with nurses drawn from different wards, the in-charge guides them closely at first (forming), helps them settle disagreements over routines (storming), agrees on standard procedures and rosters with them (norming) and, once the unit runs smoothly, delegates responsibilities and concentrates on improvement (performing).

Nursing importance Nurses work in teams and on committees every day. Understanding how groups develop and behave helps nurse managers build cohesive, productive teams, and skill in conducting meetings and serving on committees gives nurses a stronger voice in hospital decisions.

Conclusion A group is two or more interdependent people working towards common goals, and group dynamics are the forces operating within it. Groups pass through forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning, and their behaviour is influenced by size, composition, goals, norms, roles, status, cohesiveness, leadership and communication. Committees – standing or ad hoc, advisory or executive – advise, decide, coordinate and review; effective meetings need preparation, a clear agenda, skilled chairing, minutes and follow-up.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain organisational behaviour – its concept, levels, models and importance for nurse managers.
answer_html:
Definition Organisational behaviour (OB) is "a field of study that investigates the impact that individuals, groups and structure have on behaviour within organisations, for the purpose of applying such knowledge towards improving an organisation's effectiveness" (Stephen Robbins).

Contributing disciplines – psychology (individual behaviour, motivation, learning), sociology (groups, roles, culture), social psychology (attitudes, change), anthropology (culture and values) and political science (power and conflict).

Levels of organisational behaviour

  1. Individual level – perception, attitudes, values, personality, learning, motivation, emotions, job satisfaction and stress of each nurse.
  2. Group level – communication, group dynamics, teamwork, leadership, power, conflict and negotiation within teams.
  3. Organisational (system) level – structure, policies, organisational culture and climate, technology and change.

Models of organisational behaviour (Keith Davis)

  1. Autocratic model – based on power and authority; employees obey; result – minimum performance and dependence on the boss.
  2. Custodial model – based on economic resources (pay, benefits, security); employees are loyal and secure but not strongly motivated.
  3. Supportive model – based on leadership and support; managers help employees grow; result – participation and higher motivation.
  4. Collegial model – based on partnership and teamwork; employees are responsible and self-disciplined; result – enthusiasm and commitment. Modern nursing management moves towards supportive and collegial models.

Importance for nurse managers

  • Understanding why nurses behave as they do – reasons for absenteeism, resistance, conflict or high performance.
  • Improving motivation, job satisfaction and morale, and reducing turnover and burnout.
  • Building effective teams and inter-professional collaboration.
  • Choosing suitable leadership styles and managing conflict and change.
  • Creating a positive organisational culture of safety, learning and respect.
  • Ultimately improving the quality and safety of patient care.

Applications in the ward – understanding individual differences when assigning work, recognising signs of stress and burnout, using group norms to support safe practices, choosing a leadership style suited to the team, and shaping a culture in which nurses report errors without fear.

  • It also helps the manager to understand informal groups and the grapevine, and to use them to spread accurate information.

Conclusion Organisational behaviour studies how individuals, groups and structures influence behaviour at work. With knowledge of the individual, group and organisational levels and of autocratic, custodial, supportive and collegial models, nurse managers can motivate staff, build teams and create a culture that supports excellent care.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y and Ouchi's Theory Z, with their application in nursing management.
answer_html:
1. McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y Douglas McGregor, in The Human Side of Enterprise (1960), described two opposite sets of assumptions that managers hold about people.

Theory X (traditional view)

  • The average person dislikes work and avoids it if possible.
  • People must be coerced, controlled, directed or threatened with punishment to work.
  • They avoid responsibility, have little ambition and want security above all.
  • Management implications – autocratic leadership, close supervision, detailed rules, rewards and punishments.

Theory Y (modern view)

  • Work is as natural as play or rest.
  • People exercise self-direction and self-control towards goals to which they are committed.
  • Commitment depends on rewards, especially satisfaction of esteem and self-actualisation needs.
  • People not only accept but seek responsibility.
  • Creativity and ingenuity are widely distributed, and the potential of most people is only partly used.
  • Management implications – participative management, delegation, job enrichment, self-evaluation and opportunities for growth.

2. Ouchi's Theory Z William Ouchi (1981) described Theory Z, combining features of Japanese and American management:

  • Long-term (often lifelong) employment and job security.
  • Collective (consensus) decision-making, with individual responsibility for results.
  • Slow evaluation and promotion, based on long-term performance.
  • Informal, implicit control together with formal measures.
  • Moderately specialised career paths (job rotation).
  • Holistic concern for the employee and his or her family; strong organisational culture and loyalty.

3. Application in nursing management

  • Most nurses respond best to Theory Y and Z approaches – involvement in decisions (shared governance, quality circles), self-scheduling, delegation of responsibility, recognition and praise, opportunities for further study, career ladders and support for family needs (childcare, flexible rosters).
  • Job security and long-term development of staff (Theory Z) build loyalty and reduce turnover.
  • Theory X methods – close supervision and firm rules – may still be needed briefly for new, inexperienced staff or in cases of persistent indiscipline, but should not be the general approach.
  • A manager's assumptions tend to become self-fulfilling – treating nurses as responsible professionals encourages responsible behaviour.

Conclusion Theory X assumes people dislike work and need control, Theory Y assumes they are self-directed and seek responsibility, and Theory Z emphasises long-term employment, consensus decisions and holistic concern. Nurse managers who apply Theory Y and Z principles foster commitment, initiative and retention among nursing staff.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain morale – the indicators of high and low morale and the measures to build morale among nursing staff.
answer_html:
Definition Morale is the mental and emotional attitude of an individual or a group towards work, the organisation and colleagues; it reflects the degree of enthusiasm, confidence, cooperation and willingness with which people work.

Indicators | High morale | Low morale | |---|---| | Enthusiasm and pride in work | Apathy and indifference | | Cooperation and team spirit | Conflicts, groupism, rumours | | Low absenteeism and turnover | High absenteeism and turnover | | Few grievances and complaints | Frequent grievances, indiscipline | | Initiative and willingness to take responsibility | Resistance to change, avoidance of work | | Good quality of care, few errors | Errors, carelessness, patient complaints |

Factors affecting morale

  • Leadership and supervision – fair, supportive or autocratic, fault-finding.
  • Pay, allowances and job security.
  • Workload and staffing, working hours, night duties.
  • Recognition and appreciation; opportunities for growth.
  • Relationships with colleagues, doctors and patients.
  • Working conditions – safety, rest rooms, equipment.
  • Organisational policies – fairness of rosters, leave, promotion and transfers.
  • Personal factors – health, family situation, personal goals.

Measurement of morale

  • Attitude or staff-satisfaction surveys (anonymous questionnaires).
  • Interviews and informal discussions; exit interviews.
  • Observation of behaviour and team functioning.
  • Records – absenteeism, turnover, grievances, accidents and errors.
  • Suggestion boxes and complaints.

Measures to build morale

  1. Recognition – praise good work, awards, appreciation letters, celebration of achievements.
  2. Participation in decisions – staff meetings, committees, shared governance, self-scheduling.
  3. Fair and transparent policies for rosters, leave, promotion and transfer.
  4. Effective two-way communication – keeping staff informed and listening to them.
  5. Adequate staffing and reasonable workload.
  6. Fair pay and welfare measures – allowances, housing, transport, creche, health care.
  7. Career development – in-service education, sponsorship for higher studies, career ladders.
  8. Supportive supervision and prompt grievance redressal.
  9. Safe and pleasant working environment – protection from violence, adequate equipment and rest facilities.
  10. Team building and social activities – Nurses' Day, sports, cultural programmes.
  11. Job enrichment – more responsibility, variety and autonomy.

Morale and productivity – high morale usually improves productivity and quality of care, but good morale must be combined with good organisation and resources to produce results.

Conclusion Morale is the attitude and spirit of staff towards their work. High morale shows in enthusiasm, cooperation and low absenteeism, while low morale appears as apathy, conflict, absenteeism and errors. Nurse managers build morale through recognition, participation, fair policies, communication, adequate staffing, welfare, career development and a supportive environment.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain public relations in the nursing service and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Definition Public relations (PR) is the planned and sustained effort to establish and maintain goodwill and mutual understanding between an organisation and its publics.

Publics of a hospital – patients and their families, visitors, the community, staff, the media, government and regulatory bodies, referring doctors, insurance agencies and donors.

Objectives

  • To create trust and a good image of the hospital and the nursing service.
  • To provide accurate information about services, facilities and procedures.
  • To understand and respond to public expectations and complaints.
  • To promote health awareness and community participation.
  • To maintain good internal relations among staff.

Principles – truthfulness and transparency; two-way communication; consistency between what is said and what is done; empathy and courtesy; timeliness; respect for confidentiality and privacy.

Methods and tools

  • Public relations or patient relations officer; help desks ("May I help you" counters) at entrances.
  • Clear signage, information boards, display of patients' rights, charges and visiting hours.
  • Brochures, leaflets, website and official social media pages.
  • Newsletters and annual reports; recognition of staff achievements.
  • Health camps, community outreach and health education programmes; celebration of days such as World Health Day and Nurses' Day.
  • Patient feedback systems and prompt grievance redressal.
  • Media relations through press releases and an authorised spokesperson.

Role of the nurse in public relations

  • Nurses are the first and most frequent point of contact for patients and families; their behaviour largely determines the image of the hospital.
  • Courtesy and respect – greeting, introducing oneself, calling patients by name, patience with anxious relatives.
  • Clear communication – explaining procedures, routines and delays; giving information within one's role and referring other questions appropriately.
  • Prompt response to needs and call bells; keeping the environment clean and safe.
  • Handling complaints calmly – listening, apologising where appropriate, solving or referring the problem.
  • Confidentiality – no discussion of patients in public places; no statements to the media or posting on social media about patients or the hospital without authorisation.
  • Participation in health education and community programmes.

Conclusion Public relations builds goodwill and understanding between the hospital and its publics through honest, two-way communication, information, feedback and community programmes. Nurses, through their courtesy, communication, responsiveness and discretion, are the hospital's most important public relations agents.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain professional associations, trade unions and collective bargaining for nurses.
tags: difference between professional association and trade union
answer_html:
1. Professional associations

  • Voluntary organisations of members of a profession that work to advance the profession, maintain standards and promote the welfare of members – for example, the Trained Nurses' Association of India (TNAI), the Student Nurses' Association, specialty nursing societies and, internationally, the International Council of Nurses (ICN).
  • Functions – professional development (conferences, CNE), setting and promoting standards and ethics, publications, research, advocacy on policy, and welfare of members.

2. Trade unions

  • Definition – an organisation of employees formed to protect and promote their economic and social interests, such as wages, working conditions and job security, through collective action.
  • In India, trade unions were registered under the Trade Unions Act, 1926, which, together with the laws on industrial disputes, has been consolidated into the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 (in force from November 2025); the Code also provides for recognition of a negotiating union in an establishment.
  • Nurses in several States have formed unions and federations of government and private-sector nurses.
  • Functions – negotiating pay, allowances, staffing and working hours; protecting members from unfair treatment; grievance handling; welfare activities; representing nurses before employers and government.
Professional association Trade union
Aims at professional development and standards Aims at economic welfare and working conditions
Members of one profession Workers of an industry or establishment
Methods – education, publications, advocacy Methods – collective bargaining, representation, industrial action
Example – TNAI, ICN Example – nurses' unions and federations

3. Collective bargaining

  • Definition (ILO) – negotiations about working conditions and terms of employment between an employer (or employers) and one or more workers' organisations, with a view to reaching an agreement.
  • Features – collective (between groups, not individuals); a continuous, two-way process of give and take; aims at a mutually acceptable written agreement; flexible and voluntary.
  • Process
    1. Preparation – the union collects data on pay, workload and staffing; management prepares its position.
    2. Negotiation – presentation of demands, discussion, proposals and counter-proposals.
    3. Agreement (settlement) – written and signed by both sides.
    4. Implementation and administration – carrying out the agreement and resolving disputes about its interpretation.
  • Types – distributive (win–lose sharing of fixed resources), integrative (win–win problem-solving), productivity bargaining and concessionary bargaining.
  • Advantages – fair working conditions, industrial peace, participation of employees, reduced conflict and better morale.

4. Ethical issues – strikes in health care

  • Health services are essential services, and strikes are regulated by law.
  • Professional ethics require that, even during industrial action, emergency and critical care continue and patients are not abandoned; dialogue and negotiation are preferred to strikes.

Conclusion Professional associations such as TNAI and ICN advance nursing standards and development, while trade unions protect nurses' economic interests through collective bargaining – a structured negotiation between employers and employees' organisations leading to written agreements. Nurses must balance their right to collective action with their ethical duty to patients.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is groupthink?
answer_html:
• Groupthink, described by Irving Janis (1972), is a situation in which a highly cohesive group values agreement so much that members suppress doubts and fail to examine alternatives critically, leading to poor decisions.
  • Symptoms – illusion of invulnerability and unanimity, pressure on dissenters, self-censorship, stereotyping of outsiders.

  • Prevention – the leader encourages open criticism and withholds his or her own view at first, appoints a "devil's advocate", invites outside experts and considers several alternatives before deciding.

  • It can affect committees in hospitals, for example when no one questions a popular but unsafe practice.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is an agenda? What are minutes of a meeting?
answer_html:
• Agenda – a list of items to be discussed at a meeting, in order of priority, circulated to members in advance with the date, time and venue; it usually includes confirmation of previous minutes, action taken, new items and any other business with the chairperson's permission.
  • Minutes – the official written record of a meeting, prepared by the secretary and approved by the chairperson; they include the date, time, venue, members present and absent, items discussed, decisions taken, responsible persons and time limits.
  • Minutes are circulated to members and confirmed at the next meeting; they serve as a legal and administrative record.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: (a) Define budget and state its purposes and principles. (4 marks) (b) Explain the types of budget. (5 marks) (c) Describe the budgetary process and the preparation of a budget proposal for the nursing department. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Budgetary cycle of the nursing department
labels: review objectives and plans → collect data (expenditure
prices) → unit estimates by ward in-charges → departmental budget with justification → submission to budget committee → review
