negotiation and approval → allocation and implementation → monthly monitoring and variance analysis → revised estimates → year-end evaluation and audit → next year's planning

answer_html:
(a) Definition, purposes and principles of budget (4 marks)

Definitions

  • A budget is a plan, expressed in numerical (usually financial) terms, of the expected income and expenditure of an organisation for a specific future period, usually one financial year.
  • Budgeting is "the formulation of plans for a given future period in numerical terms" (Koontz).
  • The nursing budget is the plan of financial resources required by the nursing department – staff, supplies, equipment, education and other needs – to achieve its objectives. In India the financial year runs from 1 April to 31 March.

Purposes

  1. Planning – translates the objectives and plans of the nursing service into financial terms.
  2. Allocation of resources – distributes limited funds according to priorities.
  3. Control – provides standards against which actual expenditure is compared.
  4. Coordination – links the needs of different units with the overall hospital budget.
  5. Communication – informs staff and administration about priorities.
  6. Accountability – managers are responsible for spending within the budget.
  7. Evaluation and motivation – measures performance and encourages economy.
  8. Basis for future planning and justification of new posts and equipment.

Principles

  • Based on objectives and plans, not on guesswork.
  • Realistic and accurate – based on past expenditure, workload data, price trends and new services.
  • Comprehensive – includes all items of income and expenditure.
  • Participatory – unit in-charges are involved in preparing estimates.
  • Flexible – allows adjustment for unforeseen changes (epidemics, price rise).
  • Timely – prepared and submitted before the financial year, according to the hospital's calendar.
  • Balanced and economical – avoids both waste and under-provision.
  • Controlled – regular monitoring and variance analysis.
  • Transparent and accountable, following financial rules.

(b) Types of budget (5 marks)

A. According to content

  1. Operating (revenue or recurring) budget – day-to-day expenses of running the services: salaries, consumables, drugs, linen, utilities, minor repairs.
  2. Capital budget – expenditure on long-lasting, costly assets: major equipment (ventilators, monitors, dialysis machines), buildings, renovation and vehicles; items above a fixed value and with a long life are included here.
  3. Personnel (manpower) budget – salaries, allowances, overtime, new posts and leave reserve; usually the largest part of the nursing budget.
  4. Supplies and expense budget – consumables, stationery, linen, uniforms.
  5. Cash budget – estimates of cash receipts and payments month by month.
  6. Programme or project budget – for a specific activity, such as an in-service education programme, a new unit or a research project.

B. According to approach

  1. Incremental (traditional, line-item) budget – last year's figures are increased by a percentage for each item (line). Merit: simple. Demerit: past inefficiencies continue.
  2. Zero-based budgeting (ZBB) – every activity and item must be justified afresh from zero each year; activities are ranked and funded according to priority. Merit: removes unnecessary expenditure. Demerit: time-consuming.
  3. Performance budgeting – expenditure is linked with activities and outputs, such as cost per patient-day or per procedure.
  4. Programme budgeting (planning–programming–budgeting system) – funds are allocated to programmes according to their objectives and expected results; the Government of India also uses outcome budgets.
  5. Fixed (static) budget – prepared for one fixed level of activity.
  6. Flexible (variable) budget – adjusts with the level of activity (for example, supplies vary with patient-days), giving better control.
  7. Open-ended budget – a list of expenditures without limits; rarely used because it gives no control.

(c) Budgetary process and preparation of a budget proposal (6 marks)

Steps of the budgetary process

  1. Review the objectives and plans of the hospital and nursing department for the coming year – new services, expansion, quality targets.
  2. Collect data – previous years' actual expenditure, patient census and bed occupancy, staffing position and norms, vacancies, price trends and inflation, equipment condition and replacement needs, training needs.
  3. Prepare unit estimates – each ward in-charge estimates the requirements of her unit (staff, supplies, equipment, repairs).
  4. Consolidate the departmental budget – the Nursing Superintendent compiles unit estimates under budget heads, removes duplication and sets priorities.
  5. Write justifications – for new posts (workload calculations, norms), new equipment (need, cost–benefit, safety) and increased expenditure.
  6. Submit the proposal to the hospital budget committee or administration by the deadline.
  7. Review, negotiation and approval – the nursing head presents and defends the proposal; the approved budget may be modified.
  8. Allocation and implementation – funds are allocated to units and spent according to rules.
  9. Monitoring and control – monthly expenditure statements; variance analysis (comparison of budgeted and actual expenditure) and corrective action; revised estimates in mid-year if needed.
  10. Evaluation and audit at the end of the year, providing lessons for the next budget.

Format of a budget proposal for the nursing department

  • Title, name of the department and financial year.
  • Introduction and objectives – services provided, workload statistics, new plans.
  • Budget heads, each showing the actual expenditure of the previous year, the budget of the current year and the proposed budget:
    1. Personnel – salaries and allowances of existing staff; new posts.
    2. Consumables and supplies – dressings, disposables, linen, uniforms.
    3. Equipment – replacement and new items (capital).
    4. Repair and maintenance – annual maintenance contracts.
    5. Education and training – in-service education, CNE, conferences, library.
    6. Staff welfare and miscellaneous.
  • Justification for each increase or new item, with supporting data.
  • Summary of total amount requested, signature and date.
Head Previous year (actual) Current year (budget) Proposed
Personnel ✓ ✓ ✓ with new posts
Consumables and linen ✓ ✓ ✓
Equipment (capital) ✓ ✓ ✓
Maintenance ✓ ✓ ✓
Education and training ✓ ✓ ✓

Role of the nurse manager

  • Participate actively in preparing the budget; obtain accurate data from units.
  • Prepare strong justifications based on workload, norms, patient safety and cost–benefit.
  • Monitor expenditure, control wastage and report variances.
  • Train ward in-charges in budgeting and cost-consciousness.

Example of justification for a new post in a budget proposal

  • Request – eight additional nursing officer posts for the medical ICU.
  • Data – the ICU has 8 beds with an average occupancy of 90% (about 7 patients, most of them ventilated); norms recommend one nurse per ventilated patient per shift; 24 posts are sanctioned at present.
  • Calculation – 7 nurses per shift × 3 shifts = 21 nurse-shifts a day, or 147 a week; at 6 shifts per nurse per week this needs 24.5 nurses, and with a 30% leave reserve about 32 nurses – 8 more than sanctioned.
  • Benefits – compliance with norms, fewer adverse events and less overtime; the cost of the posts is set against the expected reduction in complications and length of stay.
  • Presenting data, norms and patient-safety benefits in this way makes approval more likely.

Common problems in budgeting and their remedies – estimates based on guesswork (use data and trends), non-involvement of unit in-charges (participatory budgeting), late submission (follow the budget calendar), overspending on some heads and lapse of funds on others (monthly monitoring and timely re-appropriation).

Nursing importance The nursing department uses a large share of a hospital's budget, mainly for staff and supplies. Nurse managers who can prepare and defend sound budgets obtain the posts, equipment and training their units need and show administrators that nursing resources are used efficiently.

Conclusion A budget is a financial plan for a future period that serves planning, allocation, control and accountability, and follows principles such as realism, comprehensiveness, participation and flexibility. Budgets may be operating, capital, personnel, supplies, cash or programme budgets and may follow incremental, zero-based, performance, programme, fixed or flexible approaches. The budgetary process moves from reviewing objectives and collecting data, through unit estimates, justification, submission and approval, to implementation, monitoring, variance analysis and evaluation.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain financial management in health care – its objectives, functions, principles and the role of the nurse manager.
answer_html:
Definition Financial management is the planning, organising, directing and controlling of the financial activities of an organisation – obtaining funds and using them effectively – to achieve its objectives.

Objectives in health care

  • Ensure adequate funds for services.
  • Efficient and economical use of resources; cost control.
  • Financial sustainability of the institution.
  • Affordable, quality care for patients.
  • Accountability and transparency in the use of public and private funds.
  • Protection of the organisation's assets.

Functions (elements)

  1. Financial planning and budgeting – estimating requirements and preparing budgets.
  2. Raising funds – government grants, user charges, health insurance and government schemes (such as reimbursement under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana), donations and corporate social responsibility funds.
  3. Allocation of funds among departments and programmes according to priorities.
  4. Accounting and reporting – recording transactions and preparing financial statements.
  5. Cost accounting and cost control – calculating costs (cost per patient-day, cost of a procedure) and finding ways to reduce them.
  6. Revenue management – accurate billing and timely insurance claims.
  7. Auditing – internal and external checks of accounts.
  8. Asset and inventory management.

Principles

  • Economy, efficiency and effectiveness (the "three Es").
  • Equity – fair allocation according to needs.
  • Accountability and transparency; compliance with financial rules (such as the General Financial Rules in government institutions).
  • Prudence – avoiding unnecessary risks and wasteful expenditure.

Scope in nursing

  • Preparing and controlling the nursing budget.
  • Costing nursing services and demonstrating their value.
  • Cost containment – preventing wastage and pilferage, rational use of supplies, preventing complications (infections, pressure injuries) that increase costs, and maintaining equipment.
  • Accurate documentation and charging of nursing procedures and consumables for billing and insurance claims.

Role of the nurse manager

  • Participate in budgeting and justify resources with data.
  • Monitor expenditure against the budget and explain variances.
  • Promote cost-consciousness among staff without compromising safety.
  • Ensure records and documentation support billing and audit.

  • Plan cost-effective improvements using cost–benefit analysis.

  • Example – reducing the use of disposable items that are opened but not used, and preventing one pressure injury, can save more money than many small cuts in other budget heads.

Conclusion Financial management in health care involves planning, obtaining, allocating, accounting for and controlling funds, guided by economy, efficiency, effectiveness, equity and accountability. Nurse managers contribute through sound budgeting, cost control, accurate documentation and demonstrating the value of nursing care.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is zero-based budgeting?
answer_html:
• Zero-based budgeting (ZBB) is a method in which every activity and item of expenditure must be justified afresh from zero for each budget period, instead of increasing the previous year's budget.
  • Each activity is described as a "decision package" with its costs and benefits; packages are ranked by priority, and funds are given to the highest-ranked ones. It was developed by Peter Pyhrr in the 1970s.
  • Advantages – removes unnecessary or outdated expenditure and links spending to priorities. Disadvantages – time-consuming and needs skill and data.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is a financial audit?
answer_html:
• A financial audit is an independent, systematic examination of the financial records, accounts and transactions of an organisation to verify that they are accurate, legal and in accordance with rules.
  • Types – internal audit (continuous checking by the organisation's own auditors), external (statutory) audit (by chartered accountants or, for government institutions, by the Comptroller and Auditor General through the Accountants General) and performance audit (whether funds achieved their purpose economically).
  • The nurse manager's role is to maintain accurate stock registers, indents, vouchers and records and to explain expenditure when required.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain the records and reports maintained by the nursing service department and the responsibilities of the nurse manager.
answer_html:
Introduction Besides patient records kept in the wards, the nursing service department maintains administrative records and reports that are essential for management, planning, legal protection and accreditation. Increasingly these are kept electronically in the hospital management information system (HMIS).

A. Records

  1. Personnel records
    • Personal file of each nurse – appointment, qualifications, State Nursing Council registration and renewal, CNE credits, credentialing, appraisal reports, awards and disciplinary actions.
    • Attendance and leave registers, duty rosters, staff-strength and vacancy statements, records of transfers and promotions.
    • Training and in-service education records.
  2. Patient-related records
    • Daily census (bed-state) reports – patients admitted, discharged, transferred, died, seriously ill.
    • Admission, discharge and transfer registers; medico-legal case register; birth and death registers (labour room and wards).
    • Incident and accident register; infection-surveillance and quality-indicator data (falls, pressure injuries, medication errors).
  3. Material records – indent book, stock register, equipment (dead-stock) register, linen register, breakage and condemnation registers, controlled-drug register.
  4. Administrative records – circulars and orders, policy and procedure files, minutes of meetings, round books and inspection reports, complaint and grievance registers, correspondence.

B. Reports

  • Daily nursing report (day and night report) to the Nursing Superintendent – census, seriously ill patients, deaths, admissions, incidents, staffing position and problems.
  • Monthly reports – statistics (bed occupancy, average length of stay), quality indicators, training conducted, staffing and supplies.
  • Annual report of the nursing department – achievements, statistics, problems and plans.
  • Special reports – incident and investigation reports, reports for accreditation and inspections.

C. Principles of record keeping

  • Accurate, complete, legible, dated and signed; standard formats.
  • Timely entries; corrections made by a single line with signature, never by erasing.
  • Confidential – kept securely; electronic records protected by passwords and access controls.
  • Retention and disposal according to policy and law – patient records are generally kept for at least three years and medico-legal records longer – followed by safe disposal.

D. Uses – communication between shifts and levels, planning and staffing decisions, budgeting, evaluation and audit, legal evidence, research and accreditation.

Responsibilities of the nurse manager

  • Ensure that all required records are maintained correctly and up to date.
  • Check and countersign records during rounds; train staff in documentation.
  • Prepare and submit reports on time; analyse data for decisions.
  • Protect confidentiality; ensure safe storage, retention and disposal; promote electronic record systems.

Conclusion The nursing department maintains personnel, patient-related, material and administrative records and prepares daily, monthly, annual and special reports. Accurate, timely, confidential records support management decisions, quality, legal protection and accreditation, and the nurse manager is responsible for their proper maintenance.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain career planning and career development for nurses.
answer_html:
Definitions

  • A career is the sequence of work-related positions and experiences a person has over a working life.
  • Career planning is the process by which an individual sets career goals and identifies the means to achieve them.
  • Career development includes the activities of the individual and the organisation – education, training, experience, mentoring and promotion – that help a person progress in the career.

Steps of career planning

  1. Self-assessment – identify interests, values, strengths, weaknesses, skills and personal circumstances (a personal SWOT analysis).
  2. Exploring opportunities – learn about career paths in nursing – clinical specialties, nurse practitioner roles, education, administration, community and public health, research, informatics, occupational health, armed forces nursing, entrepreneurship and international careers – and their requirements.
  3. Setting career goals – short-term (for example, a critical care certificate within two years) and long-term (for example, becoming a nursing superintendent or an associate professor), stated as SMART goals.
  4. Preparing an action plan – higher education (post-basic B.Sc., M.Sc., Ph.D.), specialised courses and certifications (life support, infection control), suitable experience, CNE, research and publication, membership of professional organisations, networking and finding a mentor.
  5. Implementation – pursue the plan steadily while balancing work and family.
  6. Review and revision – review progress regularly and adjust goals to new opportunities.

Tools – an up-to-date curriculum vitae, a professional portfolio (certificates, CNE record, achievements, reflections), and records of registration and renewal.

Role of the organisation in career development

  • Career counselling and performance appraisal linked with development plans.
  • Sponsorship and study leave for higher education; in-service education and CNE.
  • Mentoring and coaching; job rotation and acting assignments.
  • Clear career ladders and fair promotion policies.
  • Recognition of specialist and advanced practice roles.

Benefits

  • For the nurse – direction, motivation, job satisfaction and growth.
  • For the organisation – competent, committed staff, better retention and future leaders.
  • For patients – care by skilled and motivated nurses.

Conclusion Career planning is the individual's process of setting and pursuing career goals through self-assessment, exploration of opportunities, goal setting, action plans and review, while career development combines these efforts with organisational support such as education, mentoring and career ladders. Planned careers benefit nurses, organisations and patients.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain the Indian Nursing Council norms and guidelines for establishing a new B.Sc. Nursing college – eligibility of the organisation, essentiality certificate, parent hospital and clinical facilities, physical facilities and faculty – and the steps involved.

diagram.caption: Steps in establishing a B.Sc. Nursing college
labels: eligible organisation with parent hospital and land → Essentiality Certificate/NOC from State Government → application to university for affiliation (consent) → recognition by State Nursing Council after inspection → application to INC → statutory inspection under section 13 → suitability granted → university affiliation → admission of students → periodic inspections and renewal

answer_html:
Introduction A new nursing college must meet the minimum requirements laid down by the Indian Nursing Council (INC) under the INC Act, 1947, together with the requirements of the State Government, the State Nursing (Registration) Council and the affiliating university. These norms ensure that students receive education of a uniform, acceptable standard. (The norms are revised from time to time, so the latest INC regulations must be consulted.)

1. Eligible organisations

  • Central Government, State Government or local bodies.
  • Private or public trusts registered under the law, and societies registered under the Societies Registration Act (including missionary organisations).
  • Companies registered under Section 8 (not-for-profit companies) of the Companies Act, 2013.

2. Essentiality Certificate / No Objection Certificate

  • The organisation must obtain an Essentiality Certificate or No Objection Certificate (NOC) from the State Government, certifying that a nursing college is needed in the area and that the government has no objection to its establishment.

3. Parent hospital and clinical facilities

  • The institution must have its own parent hospital – under the INC guidelines, a hospital of at least 100 beds for a B.Sc. Nursing programme, owned by the same trust or management and located in a single (unitary) building or campus close to the college.
  • The number of seats sanctioned depends on the bed strength of the parent hospital and the teaching facilities – earlier norms permitted up to 60 seats, or up to 100 seats where there was a parent medical college or a hospital of 300 beds or more, and the INC has since allowed larger intakes in suitable institutions.
  • The hospital must provide adequate medical, surgical, obstetric and gynaecological, paediatric and specialty experience, with reasonable bed occupancy and nursing staff as per INC norms.
  • Affiliation with other agencies for experience not available in the parent hospital – a psychiatric hospital or unit, and community health facilities (PHC/CHC and community areas) for community health nursing.

4. Physical facilities

  • A separate college building, near the parent hospital, with:
    • Lecture halls (sufficient for each batch) and an examination hall or multipurpose hall/auditorium.
    • Laboratories – nursing foundations (skills), community health nursing, nutrition, maternal and child health (midwifery and paediatrics), advanced nursing skills/simulation, pre-clinical sciences (anatomy, physiology, microbiology, biochemistry) and a computer laboratory with internet.
    • Library with adequate textbooks, reference books, Indian and international journals, e-resources and a reading room.
    • Rooms for the principal, vice-principal and faculty; office, record room, store, common rooms for students and staff, toilets, drinking water and fire-safety arrangements.
  • Hostel – separate, safe accommodation for students, with a warden, mess, recreation and security.
  • Transport – vehicles for clinical and community postings.
  • Audio-visual and teaching aids, models, manikins and equipment as per INC lists.

5. Faculty

  • Teacher–student ratio of 1:10 (on the sanctioned strength).
  • Typical faculty for an annual intake of 40–60 – one Professor-cum-Principal, one Professor-cum-Vice-Principal, two Associate Professors, three Assistant Professors and 10–18 Tutors, with more for larger intakes.
  • Qualifications (INC norms, broadly) – Principal: M.Sc. Nursing with about 15 years' experience, mostly in teaching in a collegiate programme; Vice-Principal: M.Sc. Nursing with about 12 years' experience including 10 years' teaching; Associate Professor: M.Sc. Nursing with 8 years' experience including 5 years' teaching; Assistant Professor: M.Sc. Nursing with 3 years' teaching experience; Tutor: M.Sc. Nursing, or B.Sc./Post Basic B.Sc. Nursing with 1 year's experience; a Ph.D. is desirable for senior posts. All must be registered nurses and midwives.
  • Non-teaching staff – office superintendent, accountant, clerks, librarian and assistant, laboratory attendants, warden, drivers, security and housekeeping staff.

6. Steps in establishing the college

  1. An eligible organisation with a parent hospital, land and building decides to start the programme.
  2. Obtain the Essentiality Certificate/NOC from the State Government.
  3. Apply to the university for consent of affiliation.
  4. Apply to the State Nursing (Registration) Council for recognition; the Council inspects and grants recognition if norms are met.
  5. Apply to the Indian Nursing Council for statutory inspection under Section 13 of the INC Act (within the prescribed time after State Council recognition); the INC inspects infrastructure, faculty, clinical facilities and records and declares the institution suitable for the programme with a specified number of seats.
  6. Obtain university affiliation for the academic year.
  7. Admit students according to INC eligibility criteria and the State admission process.
  8. Maintain standards – periodic inspections, renewal of recognition and affiliation, and submission of required information.

7. Planning before applying – role of the nurse administrator

  • Feasibility study and project report – need for nurses in the area, availability of students, location, land and building plans, the parent hospital's bed strength and occupancy, clinical affiliations, estimated capital and recurring costs and sources of funds.
  • Building plan prepared with an architect according to INC area requirements, with expansion space.
  • Recruitment of qualified faculty in advance, with verification of qualifications, experience and current registration of every teacher.
  • Procurement of laboratory equipment, models, manikins, library books, journals and computers as per INC lists.
  • Documents – registration of the trust or society, ownership or lease of land, building completion and fire-safety certificates, essentiality certificate, hospital registration and staffing details, affiliation agreements, faculty files and financial statements.

8. Common deficiencies found during inspections and their prevention

  • Inadequate or unqualified faculty, or faculty shown only on paper – appoint and retain qualified teachers and maintain attendance records.
  • Low bed occupancy or lack of specialties in the parent hospital – ensure adequate patient load and formal agreements with other hospitals.
  • Poorly equipped laboratories and libraries – maintain inventories and purchase as per norms.
  • Inadequate hostel, transport or safety arrangements – provide them before admitting students.
  • Incomplete records of students' clinical experience and internal assessment – keep them up to date throughout the year.

9. After establishment – the college must maintain the faculty and facilities on which recognition was granted, inform the councils of changes, renew recognition and affiliation on time, admit only the sanctioned number of students, and develop gradually into a centre for continuing education and research for nurses of the region.

Nursing importance Students can be registered as nurses only if they qualify from institutions that meet these norms. Knowing the norms helps nurse administrators plan new institutions correctly, prepare for inspections and maintain the quality of nursing education.

Conclusion A B.Sc. Nursing college may be established by government, trusts, societies or not-for-profit companies after obtaining an Essentiality Certificate, provided it has a parent hospital of adequate size, clinical affiliations, a separate building with classrooms, laboratories, library and hostel, and qualified faculty in the ratio of 1:10. It must obtain university consent, State Nursing Council recognition and INC suitability through statutory inspection before admitting students, and must continue to meet the norms through periodic inspections.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain the affiliation of a nursing college with the university and the State Nursing Council (examination board), and its coordination with regulatory bodies.
answer_html:
Meaning of affiliation Affiliation is the formal association of a college with a university (or an examination board), by which the college follows the university's regulations and curriculum, and its students appear for the university's examinations and receive its degree.

1. Affiliation with the university (degree programmes)

  • Process – the college applies with the prescribed fees and documents (essentiality certificate, details of land, building, parent hospital, faculty, equipment and finances); the university sends a local inquiry committee to inspect; provisional (temporary) affiliation is granted for an academic year, renewed annually; permanent affiliation may be granted after the college has fulfilled all conditions for a specified period.
  • Functions of the university – adopts the INC curriculum and frames regulations; approves faculty; conducts university examinations, moderates internal assessment and awards degrees; inspects colleges; promotes research.

2. State Nursing (Registration) Council and examination boards

  • The State Nursing Council recognises institutions in the State, inspects them, registers nurses and midwives after they qualify, renews registration and maintains standards of practice.
  • For diploma programmes (ANM, GNM), a State Board of Nursing Examination (or the Council itself) conducts examinations and awards diplomas.

3. Coordination with regulatory and other bodies

  • Indian Nursing Council – suitability for programmes and seats, statutory inspections, compliance with norms and curriculum, timely submission of information and data.
  • State Government – health or medical education department (essentiality certificate, fees, admission process, government seats and scholarships).
  • University – academic calendar, examinations, results and faculty approval.
  • Accreditation bodies – such as NAAC for quality assessment of colleges.
  • Clinical agencies – memoranda of understanding with the parent hospital, psychiatric hospital, community health centres and other institutions for clinical experience.
  • Other authorities – fire, pollution control and local bodies for building and safety approvals.

Role of the principal

  • Ensure that all applications, renewals, fees and returns are submitted on time.
  • Prepare the college for inspections and act on their recommendations.
  • Maintain records required by each body; communicate changes in faculty or facilities.
  • Maintain cordial, professional relationships with all agencies.

Conclusion Affiliation links a nursing college with a university or examination board that conducts examinations and awards qualifications, while the State Nursing Council recognises the institution and registers its graduates. Continuous coordination with the INC, State Government, university, accreditation bodies and clinical agencies is essential to run a recognised, good-quality nursing programme.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain the inspection and accreditation of nursing educational institutions.
answer_html:
1. Inspection

  • Definition – an official examination of an institution by a competent authority to verify that it meets prescribed norms of infrastructure, faculty, clinical facilities, curriculum and administration.
  • Types
    • Statutory inspection by the Indian Nursing Council (under Section 13 of the INC Act) – to grant or continue suitability of programmes, since only qualifications from institutions meeting INC standards are recognised.
    • Inspection by the State Nursing (Registration) Council – for recognition and its renewal.
    • University inspections (local inquiry committees) for affiliation.
    • Periodic and surprise inspections, and inspections following complaints.
  • Process
    1. The institution submits an application and required information and documents.
    2. An inspection team visits; it verifies documents (land, building, essentiality certificate, faculty appointments and registrations), inspects classrooms, laboratories, library, hostel and the parent hospital and affiliated clinical facilities, checks records (attendance, clinical experience, internal assessment) and interacts with faculty and students.
    3. The team submits a report with deficiencies and recommendations.
    4. The authority grants, continues, reduces or withdraws recognition or seats; the institution must correct deficiencies within a given time.

2. Accreditation

  • Definition – a voluntary or mandated process of external quality review in which an institution is evaluated against pre-set standards and, if it meets them, is formally recognised (accredited) for a period.
  • Examples – the National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC) for colleges and universities, through a self-study report, a peer team visit and a grade or accredited status; hospitals used for clinical teaching may be accredited by NABH. The National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act, 2023 provides for a Nursing and Midwifery Assessment and Rating Board to assess and rate institutions.
  • Benefits – continuous quality improvement, public confidence, better students and faculty, eligibility for grants and collaborations.

3. Preparation for inspection or accreditation

  • Keep records and documents updated throughout the year, not just before the visit.
  • Prepare a self-assessment against the norms; conduct mock inspections; correct deficiencies.
  • Ensure faculty files, registration renewals, clinical affiliation agreements, laboratory inventories and student records are complete.
  • Brief faculty and students; present facts honestly.

Conclusion Inspections by the INC, State Nursing Council and university verify that nursing institutions meet minimum standards, while accreditation is an external quality review that recognises institutions achieving defined standards. Regular self-assessment and good records make both processes tools for improving nursing education.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is an essentiality certificate?
answer_html:
• An essentiality certificate (or no objection certificate) is a document issued by the State Government certifying that the establishment of a proposed nursing institution or programme is desirable and needed in the area and that the government has no objection to it.
  • It is one of the first requirements for starting a new nursing college or programme and must be submitted to the university, the State Nursing Council and the Indian Nursing Council along with other documents.
  • It usually confirms the name of the organisation, the programme, the number of seats and the location.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: What is the teacher–student ratio prescribed by the INC? Why is it important?
answer_html:
• The Indian Nursing Council prescribes a teacher–student ratio of 1:10 for nursing programmes, calculated on the sanctioned student strength of the institution.
  • Importance – nursing education includes extensive clinical teaching and supervision in wards and the community, which requires small groups; an adequate ratio ensures individual guidance, safe patient care by students, proper evaluation and quality of education.

  • Institutions that do not maintain the ratio may have their seats reduced or recognition withdrawn.

  • Additional faculty are needed when an institution runs several programmes, such as GNM and post-graduate courses.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
unit_title: Planning and Organising a Nursing College
question: (a) Write the philosophy and objectives of a college of nursing. (4 marks) (b) Draw and explain the organisational structure of a college of nursing. (4 marks) (c) Explain the preparation of the master plan, time table and clinical rotation plan for the B.Sc. Nursing programme. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Organisational structure of a college of nursing
labels: management/governing body – Principal – Vice-Principal – Heads of departments (Nursing Foundations
Mental Health) – Associate Professors – Assistant Professors – Tutors/clinical instructors – students; administrative office (office superintendent
hostel warden; committees; coordination with Medical Superintendent and Nursing Superintendent of the parent hospital

answer_html:
(a) Philosophy and objectives of a college of nursing (4 marks)

Philosophy – a statement of the beliefs and values of the faculty that guide all activities of the college. Example: "The faculty of the College of Nursing believe that:

  • health is a fundamental right of every individual, and nursing is a profession that helps individuals, families and communities to promote health, prevent illness, recover and live with dignity;
  • nursing education should be based on the INC curriculum, integrate theory with practice, and prepare competent, compassionate and ethical nurses who can work in hospitals and communities;
  • each student is a unique adult learner with potential for growth, who learns best through active participation, guidance and good role models;
  • faculty are facilitators of learning, clinical experts and researchers committed to their own continuous development;
  • learning is a lifelong process, and research and evidence-based practice improve nursing care;
  • the college has a responsibility to the community it serves."

Objectives of the college

  1. To prepare competent professional nurses and midwives who can provide safe, evidence-based care in hospitals and communities, as per INC standards.
  2. To develop critical thinking, communication, leadership and management skills in students.
  3. To inculcate ethical values, professionalism and respect for patients' rights.
  4. To promote research, publications and evidence-based practice among faculty and students.
  5. To provide continuing education for nurses and to serve the community through health programmes.
  6. To develop students' personality through co-curricular activities and the Student Nurses' Association.

(b) Organisational structure of a college of nursing (4 marks)

  • Management / governing body – the trust, society, company or government department that owns the college; it frames broad policies, provides funds and appoints senior staff.
  • Principal – the academic and administrative head; responsible for planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling all activities, liaison with the university, INC, State Council and hospital.
  • Vice-Principal – assists the principal and acts in her absence; often coordinates academic programmes and examinations.
  • Heads of departments (Professors) – Nursing Foundations, Medical-Surgical Nursing, Child Health Nursing, Obstetrics and Gynaecology (Midwifery), Community Health Nursing and Mental Health Nursing; they plan and supervise teaching in their subjects.
  • Associate Professors, Assistant Professors and Tutors (clinical instructors) – classroom and clinical teaching, evaluation, guidance of students.
  • Students – organised in batches, with class representatives and the Student Nurses' Association.
  • Supporting staff – office superintendent, accountant and clerks (administration and accounts); librarian; laboratory staff; hostel warden; drivers and others.
  • Committees – curriculum, examination, admission, discipline, anti-ragging, grievance, library, hostel and others.
  • Coordination with the parent hospital – through a coordination committee with the Medical Superintendent and Nursing Superintendent for clinical postings, facilities and joint appointments.

(c) Master plan, time table and clinical rotation plan (7 marks)

1. Master plan

  • Definition – an overall plan for the entire programme (four years, eight semesters) showing the distribution of courses, theory and practical hours, clinical experience, examinations, vacations and internship in each semester.
  • Preparation
    1. Study the INC curriculum, university regulations and academic calendar.
    2. Calculate the working weeks in each semester after excluding vacations, holidays and examinations.
    3. Distribute the courses of each semester with their theory, laboratory and clinical hours as prescribed.
    4. Fix the periods for internal assessment, university examinations and internship.
    5. Prepare an academic calendar with dates of commencement, examinations, vacations and important events.
  • Uses – ensures that all prescribed hours are covered, guides faculty and students, and helps plan staff, rooms and clinical facilities.

2. Time table

  • Definition – a weekly schedule showing the time, subject, teacher and place of each class and practical session.
  • Types – master (college) time table, class time table for each batch, teacher's individual time table, and laboratory and clinical schedules.
  • Principles
    • Hours as per the curriculum and master plan; correlation of theory with clinical practice.
    • Difficult subjects at times of maximum alertness; variety to avoid fatigue; breaks between sessions.
    • Fair distribution of workload among faculty; no clash of teachers, rooms or laboratories.
    • Provision for library, tutorials, co-curricular activities and remedial classes.
    • Flexibility, approval by the principal and display in advance.

3. Clinical rotation plan

  • Definition – a plan showing which group of students is posted to which clinical area, for how long and under whose supervision, so that every student obtains the required clinical experience.
  • Preparation
    1. Identify the clinical requirements of each course (areas, weeks, procedures, case studies).
    2. List the available clinical areas in the parent and affiliated hospitals and community, with their patient load.
    3. Divide students into small groups (to avoid overcrowding in wards).
    4. Rotate groups through all areas in sequence, correlated with theory being taught.
    5. Assign a clinical teacher to each group; prepare clinical objectives and assignments for each area.
    6. Consult the Nursing Superintendent and ward in-charges so that patient care is not disturbed and wards can accommodate students.
    7. Display the plan and maintain clinical experience records (logbooks).
  • Principles – adequate variety and number of patients, safe supervision, continuity in each area for a reasonable period, community and specialty experience, and no use of students as substitutes for staff.

Example – clinical rotation of a group of students in a semester with medical-surgical nursing

  • Students are divided into groups of about 8–10.
  • Group A – medical ward for four weeks, then surgical ward for four weeks, then operation theatre for two weeks.
  • Group B – surgical ward, then medical ward, then intensive care observation, in the same weeks.
  • Each group has a named clinical teacher, a list of clinical objectives (for example, admission of a patient, preparation and administration of medicines under supervision, pre- and post-operative care, a nursing care plan and a case presentation) and a logbook.
  • Theory classes on the related topics are timed to come just before or during the posting, so that students can apply what they learn.

Problems in academic planning and their solutions

  • Shortage of clinical areas or overcrowding of students – spread postings over several hospitals and shifts, and use simulation laboratories.
  • Faculty shortage – share teaching across departments and appoint visiting faculty for specialised topics.
  • Disruption by holidays or unforeseen events – keep reserve periods in the master plan and remedial classes in the time table.
  • Poor correlation between theory and practice – joint planning by classroom and clinical teachers.

Nursing importance A clear philosophy, sound structure and careful academic planning ensure that students receive all the theory and clinical experience prescribed by the INC, in the right sequence, under adequate supervision – the foundation for producing competent nurses.

Conclusion The philosophy states the beliefs of the faculty about health, nursing, education, students and faculty, and the objectives state what the college aims to achieve. The organisational structure runs from the governing body and principal through heads of departments and faculty to students, supported by administrative staff and committees and coordinated with the parent hospital. The master plan distributes the whole programme, the time table organises weekly teaching, and the clinical rotation plan schedules students' clinical experience.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
unit_title: Planning and Organising a Nursing College
question: Explain the committees of a college of nursing and their functions.
answer_html:
Introduction Committees allow participation of faculty, students and others in the management of the college, share responsibility and ensure that decisions are fair and well considered.

Important committees and their functions

  1. Curriculum committee – plans the master plan and time tables, reviews implementation of the INC curriculum, recommends changes and evaluates the programme.
  2. Admission committee – conducts admissions according to INC eligibility and State rules; verifies documents; ensures transparency.
  3. Examination committee – plans internal assessment and college examinations, maintains confidentiality, coordinates university examinations and results.
  4. Discipline committee – frames rules of conduct, inquires into indiscipline and recommends action.
  5. Anti-ragging committee and squad – mandatory under the UGC regulations on curbing the menace of ragging; prevents ragging, conducts surprise checks, obtains undertakings and acts on complaints.
  6. Internal Committee – under the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013, inquires into complaints of sexual harassment.
  7. Grievance redressal committee – resolves grievances of students and staff.
  8. Library committee – selects books and journals, frames library rules and plans its budget.
  9. Hostel committee – manages hostel admission, rules, mess, safety and welfare.
  10. Student welfare / guidance and counselling committee – scholarships, health care, counselling and mentoring of students.
  11. Research and ethics committees – review and guide research projects of faculty and students and ensure ethical standards.
  12. Faculty development / CNE committee – plans workshops, CNE programmes and faculty training.
  13. Purchase committee – approves the purchase of equipment, books and supplies according to rules.
  14. Internal Quality Assurance Cell (IQAC) – in accredited colleges, plans and monitors quality improvement.
  15. Sports, cultural and magazine committees; the Student Nurses' Association unit; alumni association.

General principles – each committee has a defined composition (chairperson, member-secretary, faculty members and student representatives where appropriate), clear terms of reference, regular meetings, minutes and reports to the principal.

  • Example – the anti-ragging committee, chaired by the principal with faculty, parents' and students' representatives, displays anti-ragging rules, obtains undertakings from students and parents at admission, makes surprise visits to the hostel and acts immediately on any complaint.
  • Committees are reconstituted periodically, and their decisions are recorded and implemented through the principal.

Conclusion Committees such as curriculum, admission, examination, discipline, anti-ragging, internal complaints, grievance, library, hostel, welfare, research, faculty development, purchase and quality assurance share the work of managing a nursing college, encourage participation and ensure fair, transparent decisions.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
unit_title: Planning and Organising a Nursing College
question: Explain the planning and organisation of the library of a college of nursing.
answer_html:
Objectives

  • To provide learning resources that support the curriculum, research and continuing education of students and faculty.
  • To develop self-learning and reading habits and information-searching skills.

Physical planning

  • Location – central, quiet and easily accessible, away from noise; with expansion space.
  • Areas – reading room for students (with adequate seats), separate faculty reading area, stack area for books, periodicals section, reference section, digital library (computers with internet and access to e-journals and databases), audio-visual section, librarian's office, issue counter and photocopying area.
  • Furniture and environment – shelves, catalogue terminals, reading tables and chairs, good natural and artificial lighting, ventilation, fire extinguishers and security (CCTV, exit control).

Collection development

  • Textbooks in adequate numbers and editions for each subject, reference books, Indian and international nursing journals, newspapers and magazines, e-books and e-journals, theses and research reports, audio-visual materials and models.
  • Selection based on the curriculum and recommendations of faculty through the library committee; regular addition of new editions and weeding of outdated material.

Technical organisation

  • Classification of books by a standard system such as the Dewey Decimal Classification.
  • Cataloguing using library software with an online public access catalogue (OPAC), barcodes or RFID for issue and return.
  • Accession register, issue records and periodical registers.

Staff – a qualified librarian with library assistants and attendants.

Services – lending of books; reference and information services; internet and database searching; orientation of new students; current awareness (display of new arrivals); inter-library loans; photocopying within copyright rules.

Rules and management – working hours (including extended hours before examinations), borrowing limits and periods, fines, care of books, silence and discipline; annual budget; annual stock verification; the library committee reviews needs and performance.

  • Modern trends – access to e-journals and databases through university or consortium subscriptions, remote access for students, plagiarism-checking software for research work, and training of students in searching literature for evidence-based practice.
  • The library should meet the INC requirements for the number of books and journals in relation to the number of students, and its use should be encouraged through assignments that require reading.

Conclusion A well-planned library – centrally located, with adequate space, an up-to-date collection of print and electronic resources, systematic classification and cataloguing, qualified staff, useful services and clear rules – is essential for learning, research and continuing education in a college of nursing.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
unit_title: Planning and Organising a Nursing College
question: Explain the records and reports maintained in a college of nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Records and reports are the memory of the institution. They are required for academic management, student guidance, evaluation, inspections by regulatory bodies and legal purposes.

1. Student records

  • Admission records – application, eligibility documents, admission order, fee receipts.
  • Cumulative record – a continuous record of each student's academic, clinical, health and personal development throughout the programme.
  • Attendance registers – theory, laboratory and clinical attendance (important for eligibility to appear in examinations).
  • Internal assessment records – marks of tests, assignments, practical and clinical evaluations.
  • Clinical experience records – logbooks, procedure records, case studies and rotation records.
  • Health records – medical examination, immunisation (including hepatitis B) and illness records.
  • Leave, conduct and disciplinary records, scholarship records, hostel records and progress reports to parents.

2. Faculty and staff records

  • Personal files – appointment orders, qualifications, registration and renewal, experience, approval by university or council.
  • Attendance and leave records, workload (teaching and clinical hours), CNE and faculty development, publications and research, performance appraisal.

3. Academic and administrative records

  • Curriculum documents, master plan, time tables, clinical rotation plans, lesson plans.
  • Minutes of committees and staff meetings; circulars and orders.
  • Question papers, answer books (as per rules), results and university correspondence.
  • Inventory registers of laboratories, library and equipment; purchase and condemnation records.
  • Accounts – fees, salaries, budget and audit reports.
  • Affiliation, recognition and inspection documents; essentiality certificate; agreements with clinical agencies.
  • Annual report of the college.

Principles – accurate, complete, up to date, legible and signed; in standard formats; stored securely (with computerised backups); confidential; retained and disposed of according to rules.

Uses – evaluation and guidance of students, certificates and references, eligibility for examinations, evidence for inspections and accreditation, planning and budgeting, research and legal protection.

Computerisation of records – college management software for admissions, attendance (including biometric attendance), internal assessment and fees; digital archives with regular backup; controlled access with passwords; and electronic submission of data to regulatory bodies.

Responsibility – the principal is responsible overall; class coordinators, clinical teachers, the librarian, the warden and office staff maintain the records of their areas, and records are checked periodically against an inspection checklist.

Conclusion A nursing college maintains student, faculty, academic and administrative records and prepares regular reports. Well-kept records support academic management, student development and successful inspections.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
unit_title: Planning and Organising a Nursing College
question: What is a cumulative record?
answer_html:
• A cumulative record is a continuous, comprehensive record of a student's progress maintained by the institution from admission to completion of the programme.
  • Contents – personal and family details, academic performance (marks of each semester), clinical performance and experience, attendance, health and immunisation records, co-curricular activities, special achievements, conduct and counselling notes.

  • Uses – guidance and counselling, identification of students needing help, writing references and certificates, and evidence for inspections; it must be kept confidential.

  • It is kept up to date by the class coordinator and reviewed at the end of each semester.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
unit_title: Planning and Organising a Nursing College
question: What is an academic calendar?
answer_html:
• An academic calendar is a schedule of the important academic events of an institution for the academic year, prepared before the year begins.
  • It shows the dates of commencement of each semester, teaching periods, internal assessments, university examinations, vacations, holidays, clinical postings and important events (orientation, Nurses' Day, sports, CNE).

  • It is prepared from the university calendar and master plan, approved by the principal and circulated to faculty and students, helping everyone plan their work in advance.

  • Changes made during the year are notified to all concerned in writing.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: (a) Explain the process of recruitment, selection and placement of faculty in a college of nursing. (6 marks) (b) Write the job description of the Principal of a college of nursing. (5 marks) (c) Explain faculty development and faculty welfare. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Faculty recruitment and selection in a college of nursing
labels: INC ratio 1:10) → job analysis and eligibility (INC and university norms) → advertisement → scrutiny of applications → selection committee (interview
experience and registration → appointment and university approval → orientation → placement in department → probation and confirmation → development and retention

answer_html:
(a) Recruitment, selection and placement of faculty (6 marks)

1. Manpower planning

  • Calculate the number and categories of faculty required from the programmes offered (B.Sc., Post Basic B.Sc., M.Sc., GNM), the sanctioned intake and the INC teacher–student ratio of 1:10, with the prescribed numbers of professors, associate and assistant professors and tutors.
  • Identify vacancies, expected retirements and specialty requirements (Medical-Surgical, Child Health, OBG, Community Health, Mental Health and Nursing Foundations).

2. Job analysis and eligibility

  • Prepare job descriptions and specifications for each post according to INC and university norms – qualifications (M.Sc. or B.Sc. Nursing), teaching and clinical experience, registration with the State Nursing Council, and desirable qualifications such as a Ph.D. or publications.

3. Recruitment

  • Advertisement in newspapers, the college and university websites and professional journals, stating posts, qualifications, pay, last date and method of application; government and aided colleges follow reservation rules and recruitment through public service commissions or designated bodies.
  • Internal promotion of eligible faculty where rules permit.

4. Selection

  • Scrutiny of applications and shortlisting of eligible candidates.
  • Selection committee – usually the principal, a management representative, subject experts and a university nominee (as per university rules), with representation required by government rules.
  • Selection methods – personal interview, demonstration lecture or teaching session to assess teaching ability, and sometimes a clinical or written test.
  • Verification of certificates, experience, current registration and references.
  • Appointment order stating designation, pay, probation, duties and conditions of service; approval of the appointment by the university where required.

5. Orientation (induction)

  • Introduction to the philosophy, objectives, rules and organisation of the college and parent hospital; the curriculum and academic calendar; teaching–learning and evaluation methods; record keeping; clinical areas and staff; a senior faculty member as mentor.

6. Placement

  • Posting to the department matching the faculty member's specialty (for example, an M.Sc. in Child Health Nursing to the Child Health department), with defined teaching and clinical responsibilities and a fair workload.
  • Probation with periodic appraisal, followed by confirmation.

7. Retention – fair pay and promotion, supportive leadership, opportunities for development and research, a reasonable workload and a good working environment.

(b) Job description of the Principal (5 marks)

  • Job title – Principal (Professor-cum-Principal), College of Nursing.
  • Reports to – the governing body or management, and academically to the university.
  • Supervises – all teaching and non-teaching staff and students.
  • Job summary – the academic and administrative head of the college, responsible for planning, organising, directing and controlling all its activities so that the programmes meet the standards of the INC, State Nursing Council and university.

Duties and responsibilities

  1. Planning – formulates the philosophy, objectives and development plans; prepares the academic calendar, master plan and budget; plans new programmes.
  2. Organising – organises departments and committees, time tables, clinical rotations and physical facilities; delegates responsibilities.
  3. Staffing – recruitment and selection of faculty and staff, orientation, workload allocation, faculty development and performance appraisal.
  4. Directing – provides leadership, motivation, guidance and supervision of faculty and students; conducts staff meetings; maintains discipline.
  5. Controlling – monitors curriculum implementation, teaching and clinical experience, examinations and results; conducts academic audits and programme evaluation.
  6. Student affairs – admissions as per rules, student welfare, guidance and counselling, hostel, scholarships, anti-ragging measures, Student Nurses' Association activities.
  7. Liaison and coordination – with the university, INC, State Nursing Council, State Government, parent hospital and community agencies; coordination with the Medical and Nursing Superintendents for clinical facilities.
  8. Financial management – preparation and control of the college budget, purchase procedures, accounts and audits.
  9. Records and reports – maintains all academic and administrative records and submits reports and returns.
  10. Accreditation and inspections – prepares the college for inspections and accreditation and acts on recommendations.
  11. Research and continuing education – promotes research and publications; organises CNE programmes and workshops.
  12. Teaching – teaches her specialty and nursing management to students.
  13. Public relations and professional leadership – represents the college, maintains good relations with the community and professional organisations.

Job specification – M.Sc. Nursing with the experience prescribed by INC norms (about 15 years, mostly in teaching in a collegiate programme), Ph.D. desirable, registered nurse and midwife, with leadership, administrative, communication and financial skills.

(c) Faculty development and faculty welfare (4 marks)

Faculty development

  • Definition – planned activities that improve the knowledge, teaching skills, clinical competence, research ability and leadership of faculty.
  • Need – changes in curriculum (such as the competency-based B.Sc. curriculum), new teaching and evaluation methods, advances in nursing and technology, research expectations and career growth.
  • Methods
    • Induction programme and mentoring of new faculty.
    • Workshops on curriculum, teaching methods, simulation, clinical teaching and evaluation (OSCE, rubrics).
    • CNE programmes, conferences and seminars; online courses.
    • Higher studies (Ph.D.) with study leave or sponsorship.
    • Research projects and publications; journal clubs.
    • Clinical practice updates in the parent hospital.
    • Peer observation of teaching and feedback; exchange visits to other institutions.

Faculty welfare

  • Pay and allowances as per norms; timely salaries; fair promotion policy.
  • Leave – casual, earned, medical, maternity and study leave.
  • Housing or transport, health care and insurance, childcare facilities.
  • Reasonable workload and support staff; safe working environment.
  • Recognition and awards for teaching and research; financial support for conferences and publications.
  • Grievance redressal and participation in decision-making; retirement benefits.

Problems in recruiting and retaining nursing faculty, and solutions

  • Shortage of post-graduate and doctoral nurses, especially in specialties and in rural areas – sponsor in-service nurses for M.Sc. and Ph.D. programmes, offer study leave and bonds, and develop joint appointments with the parent hospital.
  • Movement of faculty to better-paying institutions or abroad – competitive pay, transparent promotions, recognition and a positive work culture.
  • Heavy workload of teaching, clinical supervision and administration – fair distribution of duties, adequate support staff and use of technology.
  • Limited opportunities for research – seed grants, research committees and time allotted for research.

Workload and placement – each faculty member's workload should balance classroom teaching, clinical supervision, evaluation, mentoring, committee work and research; senior faculty take more planning and supervisory responsibilities, while tutors spend more time in clinical teaching under their guidance.

  • Faculty should also be released periodically for clinical updating so that their teaching remains close to current practice.

Nursing importance The quality of a nursing college depends above all on its teachers. Careful recruitment, a principal who leads effectively, continuous faculty development and attention to welfare attract and retain competent faculty who produce competent nurses.

Conclusion Faculty are recruited through manpower planning, job analysis, advertisement, selection by a committee with interviews and demonstration lectures, verification, appointment, orientation and placement according to specialty. The Principal plans, organises, staffs, directs and controls all academic and administrative activities and coordinates with regulatory bodies and the hospital. Continuous faculty development and good welfare measures keep faculty competent and motivated.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain the recruitment, selection and admission of students to the B.Sc. Nursing programme.
answer_html:
1. Recruitment of students

  • Publicity through the prospectus, website, advertisements, career guidance in schools and information through the State admission authority, so that suitable candidates apply.

2. Eligibility criteria (INC norms for B.Sc. Nursing)

  • Minimum age of 17 years on or before 31 December of the year of admission.
  • 10+2 (or equivalent) with Physics, Chemistry, Biology and English, with a minimum of 45% aggregate marks in Physics, Chemistry and Biology; relaxation of marks for reserved categories as per INC and government rules.
  • Candidates who passed 10+2 science through the National Institute of Open Schooling with the required marks are eligible.
  • The student must be medically fit; admission is made once a year.

3. Selection

  • Through an entrance examination conducted by the State, the university or a designated authority (such as a State common entrance test), followed by a merit list and centralised counselling for allotment of seats.
  • Reservation of seats according to government rules; management or institutional quotas where permitted.
  • Verification of documents (mark sheets, age, category and domicile certificates), medical examination (including immunisation status) and payment of fees.
  • Issue of the admission order and enrolment with the university.

4. Orientation of new students

  • Introduction to the college, parent hospital, rules and regulations, curriculum, library and hostel; the nursing profession and its ethics; anti-ragging rules and undertakings by students and parents; introduction to the Student Nurses' Association; assignment of a faculty mentor.

5. Student welfare and clinical placement

  • Welfare – hostel, health care and immunisation (hepatitis B), scholarships, guidance and counselling, grievance redressal, co-curricular activities.

  • Clinical placement – posting according to the clinical rotation plan, in small groups under clinical teachers, with clinical objectives and logbooks, in the parent and affiliated hospitals and the community.

  • Records at admission – admission register, personal file, cumulative record, health record and fee records are opened for every student.

Conclusion Students are admitted to the B.Sc. Nursing programme according to INC eligibility criteria – minimum age 17 years, 10+2 science with English and 45% in PCB (with relaxation for reserved categories), and medical fitness – through entrance examinations, merit lists and counselling, followed by verification, orientation, welfare measures and planned clinical placement.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Explain the performance appraisal of nursing faculty.
answer_html:
Purposes

  • To evaluate and improve the quality of teaching and other academic work.
  • To identify development needs of faculty.
  • To provide a fair basis for confirmation, promotion, increments and awards.
  • To ensure accountability to students, the university and regulatory bodies.

Areas of appraisal

  1. Teaching – preparation (lesson plans), use of appropriate methods and media, communication, completion of syllabus, punctuality.
  2. Clinical teaching and supervision – guidance of students in wards and the community, demonstrations, clinical evaluations.
  3. Evaluation of students – fair, timely internal assessment; question-paper setting; feedback to students.
  4. Research and publications – projects, papers, presentations, guidance of student research.
  5. Administrative and committee work – coordination of classes, committees, examinations, records.
  6. Professional development – CNE, workshops, higher studies, registration renewal.
  7. Student mentoring and counselling, community service and extension activities.
  8. Personal qualities – teamwork, ethics, interpersonal relationships.

Methods

  • Self-appraisal – the faculty member reports activities and achievements against objectives set at the beginning of the year.
  • Student feedback – anonymous evaluation of teaching by students at the end of each course.
  • Peer review – observation of classroom and clinical teaching by colleagues or heads of departments.
  • Principal's (head's) assessment – based on observation, records and results.
  • Teaching portfolio – lesson plans, materials, feedback, publications and certificates.
  • Academic performance indicators or scoring systems where universities use them for promotion.

Process

  1. Set clear standards and objectives for each faculty member at the start of the year.
  2. Collect information from several sources during the year.
  3. Prepare the appraisal using the prescribed format.
  4. Hold an appraisal discussion – recognise strengths, discuss areas for improvement and agree on a development plan.
  5. Follow up with support (workshops, mentoring) and review in the next cycle.

Principles – objectivity, use of multiple sources, transparency, confidentiality, emphasis on development rather than punishment, and consistency for all faculty.

  • Use of results – planning faculty development, allotting responsibilities that match strengths, recommending promotions and awards, and improving the overall quality of teaching in the college.

Conclusion Faculty appraisal evaluates teaching, clinical supervision, evaluation of students, research, administrative work, professional development and mentoring, using self-appraisal, student feedback, peer review, the principal's assessment and portfolios. A fair, development-oriented process improves the quality of nursing education.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
question: Write the qualifications prescribed by the INC for the posts of tutor and assistant professor.
answer_html:
• Tutor (clinical instructor) – M.Sc. Nursing, or B.Sc. Nursing / Post Basic B.Sc. Nursing with at least one year of experience.
  • Assistant Professor (Lecturer) – M.Sc. Nursing with three years of teaching experience; a Ph.D. in Nursing is desirable.

  • Both must be registered nurses and midwives with the State Nursing Council, and qualifications must be from institutions recognised by the INC; the norms are revised from time to time, so current INC regulations should be followed.

  • Higher posts (associate professor, professor) require longer teaching experience after M.Sc. Nursing.

subject: Nursing Management and Leadership
unit_title: Directing and Controlling in an Educational Organisation
question: Define academic (educational) audit. Explain its purposes, types, areas, process and uses in a college of nursing.

diagram.caption: Academic audit cycle in a college of nursing
labels: constitute audit committee and schedule → departmental self-study reports → data collection (documents
observation of classroom and clinical teaching
employers) → analysis against standards → audit report (strengths
recommendations) → action plan and implementation → action taken report → next audit

answer_html:
Definition Academic (educational) audit is a systematic and objective examination of the academic activities and processes of an institution – curriculum delivery, teaching–learning, evaluation, research, resources and student support – against its stated objectives and accepted standards, carried out by internal or external peers, in order to assess quality and guide improvement.

  • It differs from a financial audit (which examines accounts) and from an inspection (which checks compliance with minimum norms); its main aim is quality enhancement.

Purposes

  1. To assess whether the INC curriculum is implemented as planned – hours, content, clinical experience and evaluation.
  2. To evaluate the effectiveness of teaching–learning and evaluation.
  3. To identify strengths, weaknesses and good practices of departments and faculty.
  4. To ensure accountability to students, the university, regulatory bodies and society.
  5. To prepare the institution for accreditation (such as NAAC) and inspections.
  6. To identify faculty development and resource needs and inform planning and budgeting.
  7. To promote a culture of continuous quality improvement.

Types

  • Internal academic audit – conducted by the college's own audit committee or Internal Quality Assurance Cell (IQAC), usually every year.
  • External academic audit – by peer experts from other institutions or the university; an academic and administrative audit covers both academic and administrative processes.
  • Departmental or programme audit – focused on one department or programme.

Areas audited (in line with NAAC criteria)

  1. Curricular aspects – planning (master plan, time tables), implementation, completion of syllabus, feedback on curriculum.
  2. Teaching–learning and evaluation – lesson plans, student-centred and active learning methods, use of ICT and simulation, clinical teaching, internal assessment and university results.
  3. Research, innovations and extension – faculty and student research, publications, CNE programmes, community health activities.
  4. Infrastructure and learning resources – classrooms, laboratories, library, computers, hostel, clinical facilities.
  5. Student support and progression – mentoring, counselling, scholarships, grievance redressal, pass rates, placements and higher studies.
  6. Governance, leadership and management – planning, committees, decision-making, finance, faculty appraisal.
  7. Institutional values and best practices – ethics, gender sensitivity, community service, green practices.

Nursing-specific indicators

  • Number of clinical hours completed by each student against INC requirements; adequacy of clinical areas and patient load.
  • Clinical teacher–student ratio and supervision; completion of logbooks, case studies and procedures.
  • Use of skills and simulation laboratories.
  • Results in university examinations; registration of graduates; employer feedback on graduates.

Process

  1. Planning – constitute the audit committee (senior faculty, IQAC coordinator, external expert), fix the schedule and prepare audit tools (checklists, rating scales, questionnaires).
  2. Self-study – each department prepares a self-appraisal report with data and evidence.
  3. Data collection
    • Review of documents and records – master plan, time tables, lesson plans, attendance, internal assessment, clinical records, minutes, research records.
    • Observation of classroom and clinical teaching, laboratories and the library.
    • Feedback from students, faculty, alumni, clinical staff and employers through questionnaires and interviews.
  4. Analysis – compare findings with standards, objectives and previous audits; identify strengths and gaps.
  5. Audit report – findings, good practices, deficiencies and specific recommendations, sometimes with a score or grade for each area.
  6. Action plan – departments plan corrective actions with responsibilities and time limits; the principal approves and provides resources.
  7. Implementation and follow-up – an action taken report is reviewed, and the next audit checks whether improvements have been made (closing the quality cycle).

Uses

  • Improvement of teaching, clinical experience and evaluation.
  • Planning faculty development, purchases and the budget.
  • Recognition of good teachers and practices.
  • Readiness for inspections and accreditation; evidence of accountability.
  • Basis for curriculum review and programme evaluation.

Problems and solutions

  • Faculty may see the audit as fault-finding – emphasise improvement, involve faculty in planning it and keep it non-punitive.
  • Incomplete records – maintain documentation throughout the year.
  • Lack of follow-up – link recommendations to the annual plan and budget and review them in staff meetings.

Role of the principal – lead the audit process, ensure honesty and objectivity, provide resources for improvement, recognise good practices and ensure that recommendations are implemented.

Example – internal academic audit of the Child Health Nursing department

  • Documents reviewed – course plan, lesson plans, time table, attendance registers, internal assessment records and clinical rotation plan for the semester.
  • Observation – two classroom sessions and one clinical teaching session in the paediatric ward; condition of the paediatric skills laboratory and its equipment.
  • Feedback – questionnaires from students on teaching and clinical supervision; discussion with the paediatric ward in-charge about students' work.
  • Findings – theory hours complete and lesson plans well prepared (strengths); but students received too little experience in the neonatal unit because of overcrowding, two simulation manikins were out of order, and case-study evaluation was delayed (gaps).
  • Recommendations and action – rotate small groups through the neonatal unit on alternate days, repair the manikins and add simulation sessions, and set deadlines for returning evaluated case studies; the next audit checks progress.

Characteristics of an effective academic audit – it is objective and evidence-based, uses clear standards, involves faculty and students, is constructive rather than punitive, is regular (not only before inspections), leads to specific, time-bound action and is followed up.

Academic audit and accreditation – the evidence and improvements generated by yearly audits form the basis of the self-study report required for accreditation, so institutions that audit regularly find external assessment much easier.

Tools commonly used in an academic audit

  • Checklists for documents and facilities (for example, whether each course has a course plan, lesson plans and a record of hours taught).
